title: The Man Who Walked into the Smoke
text:
On a summer night in 1916, a tunnel under Lake Erie, near the city of Cleveland, filled with gas after an explosion. Workers were trapped deep under the water, and the first men who went in to save them did not come back. Late that night, someone remembered a local inventor who had been showing a strange new mask at fairs. A messenger was sent to his house, and the inventor, Garrett Morgan, came quickly in his night clothes, together with his brother.

Morgan was born in Kentucky in 1877. His parents had been born into slavery, and the family had little money. He left school after only a few years, but he never stopped learning. As a teenager he moved north, first to Cincinnati and then to Cleveland, where he found work repairing sewing machines. He was good with his hands and even better at noticing small problems. Before long he opened his own repair shop, and later a clothing business with his wife.

His first successful product came almost by accident. While he was working on a sewing machine, he tried to find a liquid that would stop the needle from burning the cloth. He wiped the liquid on a cloth and later saw that it had changed the hairs on the material. Curious, he tested it on a neighbour's dog, and then on his own hair. The result was a hair cream that sold well for many years and gave him the money to try bigger ideas.

The biggest idea was the one that saved lives in the tunnel. Morgan had designed what he called a safety hood. It was a cloth cover for the head, with a long tube that hung down near the floor. Smoke and hot gas rise, so the cleanest air in a burning room is usually close to the ground. The tube collected this cleaner air, and a second tube carried the used air away. He received a patent for it in 1914 and showed it to fire departments, sometimes by sitting inside a tent full of thick smoke for twenty minutes.

In the Lake Erie tunnel, Morgan and his brother put on their hoods and went down. According to most accounts, they carried out several men, some alive and some already dead. It was dangerous, tiring work, and Morgan felt the effects of the gas for years afterwards. Yet the newspapers mostly praised other people, and the city was slow to recognise what he had done. Some historians believe that this was because he was a Black man. When he tried to sell his hood in the South, he sometimes hired a white actor to present it while he played the role of a helper.

Morgan did not give up. Cleveland was growing fast, and its streets were full of horses, bicycles, people on foot and the first cars. Crossings were chaotic, and accidents were common. The signals of the time simply switched between stop and go, with no warning in between. After seeing a serious crash, Morgan designed a signal with a third position that stopped traffic in every direction for a moment, so the crossing could clear. He received a patent in 1923 and is reported to have sold the rights to a large electric company for about forty thousand dollars.

Today the traffic light has many fathers, and Morgan was not the only person working on the problem. But the idea behind his design, a short pause to keep everyone safe, lives on in the yellow light we see every day. And firefighters still breathe through masks that follow the same simple principle as his hood: find the clean air and bring it to the person who needs it.

questions.q: Why did the safety hood have a long tube hanging down near the floor?
options: To carry water to the person wearing it
Because the cleanest air in a smoky room is close to the ground
So that the wearer could talk to people outside
To make the hood heavy enough to stay on the head
questions.explain: Metin, duman ve sıcak gaz yükseldiği için en temiz havanın yere yakın olduğunu söylüyor; bu yüzden doğru cevap "Because the cleanest air in a smoky room is close to the ground".

questions.q: What was new about Morgan's traffic signal?
options: It used electric lights for the first time
It was cheaper than all other signals
It worked only for horses and bicycles
It had a third position that stopped traffic in every direction for a moment
questions.explain: Dönemin sinyalleri yalnızca dur ve geç arasında geçiş yapıyordu; Morgan'ın tasarımı trafiği her yönde kısa süre durduran üçüncü bir konum ekledi: "It had a third position that stopped traffic in every direction for a moment".

title: The Cloudy Liquid Nobody Wanted
text:
Stephanie Kwolek never planned to become a famous chemist. As a girl growing up near Pittsburgh in the 1920s and 1930s, she loved two things: walking in the woods with her father, who collected plants and insects, and sewing clothes with her mother. For a while she dreamed of becoming a fashion designer. Later she decided she wanted to be a doctor, and she studied chemistry at college as a first step.

Medical school was expensive, so in 1946 she took a job at DuPont, a large American chemical company, planning to save money and leave after a year or two. Instead, she found that she enjoyed the work so much that she stayed for about forty years. In the laboratory she could ask her own questions, try things that might fail, and learn something new almost every day.

In the 1960s, many people feared that oil would become scarce and expensive. Car makers wanted lighter tyres, because lighter cars use less fuel. Kwolek's team was asked to look for a new fibre that was both very strong and very light, strong enough to replace the steel wires inside tyres.

One day in 1965, she made a solution from a group of long chemicals called polymers. Usually, solutions like this were thick and clear, like honey. Hers was thin and cloudy, almost like milky water. Many chemists would have decided it was a failure and thrown it away. Kwolek was not sure what it was, but she was curious. She asked the technician who ran the spinning machine, which turned liquids into fibres, to try it. He refused at first. He thought the cloudy liquid contained small solid pieces that would block his machine.

Kwolek kept asking, and finally he agreed. The liquid passed through the machine without any trouble, and the fibre that came out was surprising. It was stiff and extremely strong. Kwolek tested it again and again, because she did not trust the first results. She later said that she did not tell anyone at first, because she was afraid of being wrong.

She was not wrong. Other scientists at DuPont joined the work and developed the fibre further. In 1971 the company introduced it with the name Kevlar. By weight, it is about five times stronger than steel, and it does not burn easily. It was used in tyres, as planned, but soon people found many other uses. Today it is found in ropes for ships, cables under the sea, gloves that protect workers from cuts, sports equipment, and parts of aeroplanes and spacecraft.

Its most famous use, however, is in vests that protect police officers from bullets. Over the years, thousands of officers have survived attacks because they were wearing such vests. Kwolek received many letters from people who had been saved, and she said these letters meant more to her than any prize.

She did not become rich from her discovery. Like most company scientists, she had signed her patent rights over to her employer. But she received many honours, and she was one of the few women of her generation to be admitted to the National Inventors Hall of Fame in the United States. In her later years she spent much of her time encouraging young people, especially girls, to study science.

Her advice was simple. Do not be afraid to look at something strange, and do not throw away a result just because you did not expect it. Sometimes the most important discoveries hide inside a cloudy liquid that everyone else would pour down the sink.

questions.q: Why did the technician first refuse to put the liquid into his machine?
options: He thought it might contain solid pieces that would block the machine
He was told by the company not to help Kwolek
The machine was broken that week
He believed the liquid was dangerous to breathe
questions.explain: Teknisyen, bulanık sıvının makinesini tıkayacak katı parçalar içerdiğini düşünüyordu; doğru cevap "He thought it might contain solid pieces that would block the machine".

questions.q: According to the text, what meant the most to Kwolek?
options: The money she earned from Kevlar
Being admitted to the Hall of Fame
Letters from people whose lives had been saved
Becoming a doctor in the end
questions.explain: Metne göre kurtarılan insanlardan gelen mektuplar onun için her ödülden daha anlamlıydı: "Letters from people whose lives had been saved". Kevlar'dan zengin olmadı ve doktor olmadı.

title: A Secretary and a Bottle of White Paint
titleTr: Bir Sekreter ve Bir Şişe Beyaz Boya
text:
In the early 1950s, Bette Nesmith Graham worked as a secretary at a bank in Dallas, Texas. She was a single mother with a young son, and she needed the job. She was not, by her own account, a perfect typist. Like everyone who typed for a living, she made mistakes, and in those days a mistake was a serious problem.

Before computers, every letter and report was typed on paper. If you hit the wrong key, the wrong letter appeared in ink, and it stayed there. Typists used special erasers to rub the letter away, but this often left a grey mark or even a hole in the paper. With the new electric typewriters that offices were buying at the time, the problem became worse. Their ink was harder to remove, and the clean, sharp letters made every mistake easy to see. Sometimes a secretary had to type a whole page again because of a single wrong letter.

Graham had another skill besides typing. She was a talented amateur artist, and she earned extra money by painting holiday decorations on the bank's windows. She noticed that when artists made a mistake, they did not try to remove the paint. They simply painted over it. She wondered whether she could do the same thing on paper.

At home, she mixed some white paint in her kitchen, put it in a small bottle, and took it to the office with a thin brush. When she made a typing mistake, she quietly painted over the letter, waited a moment for it to dry, and typed the correct letter on top. Her boss did not notice. Before long, other secretaries did notice, and they asked for bottles of their own.

For several years Graham made the liquid at home, using her kitchen as a laboratory. She asked a chemistry teacher at her son's school and a man who worked at a paint shop for advice, and she kept improving the recipe so that it dried faster and looked more like real paper. Her son and his friends filled the bottles in the garage. At first she called the product Mistake Out. Later she changed the name to Liquid Paper.

The business grew slowly. In fact, Graham lost her bank job, reportedly because she typed the name of her own company on a letter by mistake, and she could not correct that error. She tried to sell her idea to a large company, but it was not interested. So she continued alone, sending samples to office supply magazines and travelling to meet buyers. By the late 1960s, her small kitchen business had become a real company with its own factory, and it was selling millions of bottles every year.

Graham cared about the people who worked for her. Her factory had a library and a space where children could be looked after, which was unusual for the time. In 1979 she sold the company to a large firm for about forty-seven million dollars. She died the following year, and she left much of her money to foundations that supported women in art and business.

Her son became famous too, as a musician in a popular band of the 1960s, but many people never knew that his mother had built her own success with a bottle of paint. Today most writing is done on screens, where the delete key does the work. Still, small bottles of white correction fluid can be found in many school bags and offices around the world, and the idea behind them came from a secretary who looked at a mistake and saw an opportunity.

questions.q: Where did Graham get the idea of painting over mistakes?
options: From a chemistry teacher at her son's school
From a magazine about office work
From the way artists cover their mistakes with paint
From her boss at the bank
questions.explain: Graham, ressamların hatayı silmeye çalışmadığını, üzerine boya sürdüğünü fark etti; doğru cevap "From the way artists cover their mistakes with paint". Kimya öğretmeninden ise yalnızca tarifi geliştirirken tavsiye aldı.

questions.q: Why did electric typewriters make the problem of mistakes worse?
options: Their ink was harder to remove and the sharp letters made mistakes easy to see
They were much slower than older machines
They used a special kind of paper that tore easily
They often typed the wrong letter by themselves
questions.explain: Metne göre elektrikli daktiloların mürekkebi daha zor çıkıyordu ve keskin harfler her hatayı belirgin kılıyordu: "Their ink was harder to remove and the sharp letters made mistakes easy to see".

title: The Wrong Part in the Right Place
text:
Many great inventions begin with a careful plan. The device that now keeps millions of hearts beating began with a mistake. In 1956, an American engineer named Wilson Greatbatch was building a machine to record the sounds and rhythms of the heart. He reached into a box for a small electrical part and took out the wrong one. When he put it into his circuit, the machine did not record anything. Instead, it began to produce short, regular electrical pulses, a little more than one every second.

Greatbatch stared at it. The rhythm sounded familiar. It was very close to the beat of a healthy human heart. Years earlier he had heard doctors talk about a condition called heart block, in which the natural electrical signals of the heart fail to reach the lower part of the heart. In serious cases the heart beats too slowly, or stops for dangerous moments. Doctors already knew that electricity could help, but the machines of the time were large boxes that stood next to the bed or were pushed around on a table. Patients were connected to them with wires through the skin, and if the electricity in the building failed, the patient could die.

Looking at his little circuit, Greatbatch had a bold thought. What if a device like this could be made small enough to put inside the body? Then the patient could go home and live a normal life.

Greatbatch was born in Buffalo, New York, in 1919. As a boy he loved radios, and during the Second World War he served in the navy, working with radio and electronic equipment. After the war he studied electrical engineering, and later he taught at a university. He was a practical man who liked to build things with his own hands.

For the next two years he worked on his idea in a workshop in his barn, often with very little money. He had to solve many difficult problems. The device had to be tiny and light. It had to be covered so that the body's liquids could not damage it. And it had to keep working for a long time, because nobody wanted to have an operation every few weeks. In 1958 he and a surgeon tested an early version in a dog, and it worked. In 1960 the first patients in Buffalo received pacemakers based on his design. One of them reportedly lived for many more years with the device inside his chest.

The early pacemakers had one big weakness: their batteries. They lasted only about two years, and every time they ran down, the patient needed another operation. Greatbatch spent much of the rest of his career on this problem. In the 1970s his company developed a new kind of battery based on the metal lithium, which could last ten years or more. This battery became the standard for pacemakers around the world.

Greatbatch was a modest man who liked to say that most of his ideas failed. He held well over a hundred patents, and in his old age he worked on projects as different as clean energy and a solar-powered canoe, which he paddled himself on a long trip through the lakes of New York State. He also enjoyed meeting young inventors and telling them about his famous mistake.

The lesson he took from that day in 1956 was not that mistakes are good in themselves. It was that you must notice them. Another engineer might have pulled out the wrong part, said something angry, and continued with the original plan. Greatbatch stopped, listened to the rhythm, and asked what it could be used for.

questions.q: What happened when Greatbatch used the wrong electrical part?
options: The machine broke and caught fire
The machine recorded the heart more clearly
The machine produced regular pulses similar to a heartbeat
The machine stopped working completely
questions.explain: Yanlış parçayı taktığında makine kayıt yapmadı; bunun yerine sağlıklı bir kalp atışına benzeyen düzenli elektrik atımları üretti: "The machine produced regular pulses similar to a heartbeat".

questions.q: Why was the lithium battery important?
options: It made the pacemaker much cheaper
It lasted much longer, so patients needed fewer operations
It allowed doctors to control the pacemaker by radio
It was the first battery small enough for a pacemaker
questions.explain: Eski piller yaklaşık iki yıl dayanıyordu ve her seferinde ameliyat gerekiyordu; lityum pil on yıl ya da daha fazla dayanabiliyordu: "It lasted much longer, so patients needed fewer operations".

title: The Draftsman Who Taught Himself
text:
In 1842, a young couple named George and Rebecca Latimer escaped from slavery in Virginia and made their way north to Boston. Soon afterwards George was arrested, and his former owner demanded that he be returned. The case caused anger across Massachusetts, thousands of people signed a petition, and in the end money was raised to buy his freedom. Six years later, in 1848, the couple had a son named Lewis. He would grow up to play a quiet but important part in bringing electric light into homes and streets.

The boy's childhood was not easy. When he was about ten, his father left the family, and Lewis had to work to help his mother. At sixteen he joined the navy and served during the American Civil War. When he came back to Boston, he found a job as an office boy at a firm of patent lawyers. These lawyers helped inventors protect their ideas, and every application needed exact technical drawings of the invention.

The young man watched the draftsmen who made these drawings and was fascinated. He could not afford lessons, so he bought second-hand drawing tools and practised at night. He studied books and copied the work he saw in the office. One day he asked his boss to let him try a real drawing. The boss was surprised by the quality, and over time Latimer was promoted from office boy to head draftsman.

During these years he made one of the most famous drawings in the history of technology. In 1876 a teacher named Alexander Graham Bell asked the firm to help him with a patent for a new machine that could carry the human voice along a wire. According to most accounts, Latimer prepared the drawings for the telephone patent, sometimes working late into the night, because Bell was racing against other inventors.

He was also an inventor himself. Electric lamps at that time used a thin thread, called a filament, that glowed when electricity passed through it. The early filaments were made of carbon and broke quickly, so the lamps were expensive and did not last. Working for a company that competed with Thomas Edison, Latimer developed a better way of making carbon filaments, and he received a patent for it in the early 1880s. His company sent him to cities such as New York, Philadelphia and Montreal to help set up electric lighting systems. In Montreal he even had to give his instructions in French.

Later he joined the company of Edison himself, where he worked as a draftsman and as an expert in patent cases. When other companies were accused of copying Edison's ideas, Latimer studied the drawings and explained them in court. In 1890 he wrote one of the first books on electric lighting for ordinary readers, and he became one of the small group of engineers known as the Edison Pioneers.

He was more than an engineer. He wrote poetry, played the flute, painted, and taught English and drawing to new immigrants in New York. He believed that education should be open to everyone, perhaps because he had worked so hard to get his own.

For many years his name appeared only in small print in histories of the telephone and the light bulb. Today schools, streets and a museum carry his name. His story reminds us that big inventions are rarely the work of one famous person. Behind every well-known name there are many skilled people who make the ideas work, and some of them, like Latimer, had to teach themselves everything they knew.

questions.q: How did Latimer learn to make technical drawings?
options: He studied engineering at a university
He learned in the navy during the war
His father taught him when he was a child
He watched the draftsmen at work and practised at night with second-hand tools
questions.explain: Latimer derse para veremediği için ikinci el aletler alıp geceleri çalıştı ve ofisteki teknik ressamları izledi: "He watched the draftsmen at work and practised at night with second-hand tools".

questions.q: What was Latimer's own invention about?
options: A better way of making carbon filaments for lamps
A new kind of telephone wire
A machine for copying drawings
A cheaper way to produce electricity
questions.explain: Latimer, çabuk kırılan karbon flamanları daha iyi üretmenin bir yolunu geliştirip patent aldı: "A better way of making carbon filaments for lamps". Telefon için ise yalnızca Bell'in çizimlerini hazırladı.

title: Salt, Bones and Too Many Cameras
text:
On a postcard, Hallstatt looks almost too perfect. Small wooden houses stand close together on a narrow piece of land between a steep mountain and a dark green lake in central Austria. A white church tower rises at the edge of the water, and in the morning thin clouds often hang above the surface. Many visitors say it looks like a scene from a fairy tale. However, the real story of the village is not about beauty. It is about salt.

People have taken salt from the mountain above Hallstatt for thousands of years. Archaeologists believe that mining here began at least seven thousand years ago, which would make it one of the oldest salt mines in the world. In the past, salt was extremely valuable, because people needed it to keep meat and fish from going bad. The miners of Hallstatt grew rich by selling it across Europe. Inside the mountain, scientists have even found ancient tools, pieces of clothing and leather shoes, all kept in good condition by the salt.

The village has always had one problem: space. There is so little flat land that the houses climb up the hillside, and for centuries the only easy way to reach Hallstatt was by boat. A proper road arrived only in the late nineteenth century. The small size of the village also created an unusual tradition. The church graveyard was too small for everyone, so after some years the bones were dug up to make room for new graves. The skulls were cleaned, and family members often painted them with flowers, leaves and the name of the dead person. Today around six hundred painted skulls can be seen in a small building called the Bone House. It may sound frightening, but many visitors find it surprisingly gentle and full of love.

In 1997, Hallstatt and the landscape around it were added to the UNESCO World Heritage list. Then something else happened. Photos of the village spread across the internet, and it became famous in East Asia. A company in China even built a copy of the village in the south of the country, with its own lake, church tower and wooden houses. The copy opened in 2012, and some people in the real Hallstatt were not sure whether to feel proud or annoyed.

Today the village has fewer than eight hundred residents, but on busy summer days it may receive up to ten thousand visitors. Tour buses fill the car park, and drones fly over the roofs. Some residents have put up signs asking tourists not to enter their gardens. In 2023, the village even built a wooden fence to block one of the most popular photo spots, although it was removed after people complained. Local leaders now limit the number of tour buses that can arrive each day.

If you visit, there is a simple way to see a different Hallstatt: stay for one night. In the early evening, the last buses leave, the noise disappears and the lake becomes still again. Then you can walk along the water, listen to the church bells and imagine the miners coming down the mountain after a long day, their hands white with salt.

questions.q: Why were the bones in Hallstatt's graveyard dug up?
options: Because the salt in the ground damaged them
Because the graveyard did not have enough space for new graves
Because scientists wanted to study the ancient miners
Because tourists wanted to see painted skulls
questions.explain: Metne göre köydeki düz alan çok azdı ve mezarlık herkese yetmiyordu; bu yüzden kemikler yeni mezarlara yer açmak için çıkarıldı. Doğru cevap: "Because the graveyard did not have enough space for new graves".

questions.q: What does the writer suggest to visitors who want a quieter Hallstatt?
options: Visiting the copy of the village in China
Arriving on one of the tour buses
Flying a drone over the lake
Staying in the village for one night
questions.explain: Yazar son paragrafta akşam otobüsler gidince köyün sessizleştiğini söylüyor ve bir gece kalmayı öneriyor. Doğru cevap: "Staying in the village for one night".

title: The Blue Town in the Mountains
text:
Walk through the old town of Chefchaouen in northern Morocco and you will soon lose any sense of direction. The narrow streets turn left and right, go up stairs and down again, and almost everything around you is blue. Walls, doors, steps and even some flower pots are painted in shades from pale sky blue to deep blue. Cats sleep on blue steps in the afternoon sun, and the light seems to change colour as you walk.

The town sits in the Rif Mountains, and it was founded in 1471 as a small fortress. For a long time it was a closed place. Outsiders were rarely welcome, and only a few European travellers managed to enter it before the twentieth century. Over the centuries, Muslim and Jewish families who had been forced to leave Spain settled here, and they brought their own building styles, crafts and recipes with them. Many of the houses still have the small windows and heavy wooden doors of that time.

So why is everything blue? Strangely, nobody knows for sure, and if you ask five people in the town, you may hear five different answers. One popular explanation is that Jewish families painted their houses blue, because in their tradition the colour reminds people of the sky and of God. Another says that blue keeps mosquitoes away, although scientists are not sure this is true. Some people say the colour keeps the houses cool in the hot summer. Others believe it simply represents water, which is precious in this dry region. There is also a more modern answer: blue walls attract tourists, and tourists bring money. Whatever the reason was in the past, residents today repaint their walls every year or two, usually in spring, to keep the colour bright.

Water, in fact, is an important part of daily life. Just outside the old town, a spring called Ras el-Maa comes out of the mountain. Local women have washed clothes there for generations, and on hot days children play in the cold water while their parents sit in the shade. The same water once turned small mills that ground grain for bread.

Chefchaouen has become very popular on social media, and photos of its blue streets travel around the world. As a result, the town is much busier than it was twenty years ago. Some residents complain that visitors take pictures of their front doors without asking, and a few have even put up signs asking for a little money in return. Others are happy, because tourism has created jobs in hotels, cafés and small shops that sell woven blankets, leather bags and goat's cheese.

The best time to explore the town is early in the morning. The shops are still closed, the streets are quiet and the only sound may be a man pushing a cart up the steps. If you climb the hill to the small white mosque above the town, you can watch the sun rise over the mountains and see the blue houses slowly appear out of the shadow, one by one.

questions.q: What does the text say about the reason for the blue colour?
options: Nobody knows for sure, and people give different explanations
The government ordered everyone to paint their walls blue
Scientists have proved that blue keeps mosquitoes away
European travellers brought the idea in the twentieth century
questions.explain: Metin mavinin nedenini kimsenin kesin bilmediğini ve beş kişiye sorarsanız beş farklı cevap alabileceğinizi söylüyor. Doğru cevap: "Nobody knows for sure, and people give different explanations".

questions.q: How do some residents feel about the growing number of tourists?
options: All of them want tourists to leave the town
None of them have noticed any change
Some are unhappy about photos of their doors, while others welcome the new jobs
They are worried that tourists will paint the walls a different colour
questions.explain: Metne göre bazı sakinler ziyaretçilerin izinsiz kapılarının fotoğrafını çekmesinden şikâyet ediyor, bazıları ise turizmin yarattığı işlerden memnun. Doğru cevap: "Some are unhappy about photos of their doors, while others welcome the new jobs".

title: The Islands Where Sheep Made the Map
text:
Halfway between Iceland and Norway, in the cold waters of the North Atlantic, lie eighteen rocky islands. They are the Faroe Islands, a self-governing part of the Kingdom of Denmark. About fifty-four thousand people live there, but they are not the largest group. The islands are also home to around seventy thousand sheep, and many people believe that the name Faroe itself comes from an old word meaning sheep islands.

The landscape is dramatic. There are almost no trees, because strong winds blow across the islands for most of the year. Instead, there are green hills, high cliffs and waterfalls that drop straight into the sea. The weather can change in minutes. A sunny morning may turn into heavy rain, thick fog and then sun again before lunch. People often joke that if you don't like the weather, you only have to wait five minutes.

Traditional houses here have roofs covered with grass. The grass keeps the houses warm in winter and protects them from rain. In summer the roofs need cutting, and sometimes a goat is sent up to eat the grass instead. Many houses are painted in bright colours, such as black, red and yellow, so they can be seen easily in the grey weather.

Travelling between eighteen islands was never easy. For centuries, people used small boats, and storms could cut villages off for days. Today the islands are connected by bridges, ferries and some very long tunnels, including several under the sea. The most surprising one opened in 2020. It is about eleven kilometres long and runs deep under the water between two islands. In the middle there is a roundabout, and the rock walls around it are lit with blue and green lights and decorated with a ring of human figures by a local artist. Driving through it feels a little like visiting an art gallery under the sea.

The sheep once helped to put the islands on the map, quite literally. In 2016, a local woman who worked in tourism was frustrated that Google's Street View service had not photographed the islands. She came up with an unusual idea. With the help of a farmer, she fixed small cameras on the backs of a few sheep and let them walk across the hills. The pictures were put online, and the project, which she called Sheep View, received attention from news websites around the world. Shortly afterwards, Google sent equipment to the islands, and residents and volunteers helped to photograph the roads and paths.

Not everything on the islands is gentle. A traditional hunt of pilot whales still takes place in some summers, and it causes strong debate both at home and abroad. Supporters say it is part of their culture and a local source of food, while critics argue that it is cruel and no longer necessary.

Most visitors, however, come for the walking. Paths lead to cliffs where thousands of seabirds, including puffins, build their nests in summer. Sitting on a cliff edge, with the wind in your face and the sea far below, it is easy to understand why the islanders love their remote home so much.

questions.q: Why did a local woman put cameras on sheep?
options: To study how sheep move across the hills
To find sheep that were lost in the fog
Because Google's Street View had not photographed the islands
Because farmers wanted to protect their animals from whales
questions.explain: Metne göre turizmde çalışan bir kadın, Google Street View'in adaları fotoğraflamamasından bıkmıştı ve koyunlara kamera takarak kendi çözümünü buldu. Doğru cevap: "Because Google's Street View had not photographed the islands".

questions.q: What is special about the tunnel that opened in 2020?
options: It is the only way to reach Iceland by car
It has a roundabout with lights and art in the middle
It was built by farmers without any machines
It is closed to cars and open only to walkers
questions.explain: Metin, 2020'de açılan deniz altı tünelinin ortasında ışıklandırılmış ve insan figürleriyle süslenmiş bir göbek kavşak olduğunu anlatıyor. Doğru cevap: "It has a roundabout with lights and art in the middle".

title: Walking on the Sky in Bolivia
text:
Imagine standing in the middle of a white plain so flat and so wide that you cannot see where it ends. There are no trees, no buildings and no hills, only white ground under a deep blue sky. This is the Salar de Uyuni in southwest Bolivia, the largest salt flat in the world. It covers more than ten thousand square kilometres and lies about three thousand six hundred metres above sea level, higher than most mountains in Europe.

Thousands of years ago, the area was part of a huge lake. Slowly, the climate became drier and the water disappeared, leaving behind a thick layer of salt. In some places the salt is several metres deep. Under the surface there is salty water, and it holds a large amount of lithium, the metal used in the batteries of phones and electric cars. Some people see this as a great chance for Bolivia, while others worry that mining could damage the fragile landscape.

The salt flat looks different in each season. In the dry months, the surface breaks into thousands of shapes with six sides, like tiles on a giant floor. In the rainy season, usually between December and March, a thin layer of water covers parts of the plain. Then something magical happens. The water becomes a perfect mirror, and the sky, with all its clouds, appears under your feet. People who walk there say it feels like walking on the sky. At night, if the air is still, the stars are reflected too, and visitors can feel as if they are floating in space.

Because the plain is so flat and empty, it has become famous for funny photographs. Without trees or buildings to compare sizes, the eye is easily tricked. A person standing far from the camera can appear to be tiny, so tourists take pictures of friends who seem to stand on a bottle or hide inside a shoe. Tour guides often carry plastic toy dinosaurs for this purpose.

The salt is also a building material. Near the edge of the flat, there are hotels made almost entirely of salt blocks. The walls, the beds and even the tables and chairs are cut from salt. Guests are usually asked politely not to lick the walls. Local families also collect salt by hand, pile it into small hills to dry in the sun and sell it for cooking.

Not far from the town of Uyuni there is a strange sight: a train cemetery. In the early twentieth century, trains carried minerals from the mines to ports on the Pacific coast. When mining in the area declined, old engines and carriages were simply left in the desert. Today they stand there rusting in the wind, and visitors climb over them to take photographs.

Life is hard at this height. The sun is strong, the nights are freezing and the air contains less oxygen, so newcomers can feel tired or get headaches. Still, every year thousands of travellers make the long journey, and in some seasons pink flamingos join them, standing in the shallow lakes nearby. For many visitors, the moment when the sky appears under their feet is one they will never forget.

questions.q: What happens to the salt flat in the rainy season?
options: It becomes too dangerous for visitors
The salt melts and a deep lake forms
Trains start to carry salt to the coast
A thin layer of water turns it into a huge mirror
questions.explain: Metne göre yağmur mevsiminde ince bir su tabakası düzlüğü kaplar ve gökyüzünü yansıtan kusursuz bir aynaya dönüştürür. Doğru cevap: "A thin layer of water turns it into a huge mirror".

questions.q: Why are tourists able to take funny photographs on the salt flat?
options: There is nothing nearby to compare sizes, so the eye is easily tricked
The salt changes the colours in their pictures
Tour guides use special cameras
The flamingos stand very close to visitors
questions.explain: Metin, düzlükte boyutları karşılaştırmaya yarayacak ağaç ya da bina olmadığı için gözün kolayca yanıldığını söylüyor. Doğru cevap: "There is nothing nearby to compare sizes, so the eye is easily tricked".

title: Opal Hunters of the Desert
text:
Drive north from Adelaide for about nine hours, through flat red desert, and you reach one of the strangest towns in Australia. At first, Coober Pedy does not look like much. There are a few shops, a petrol station and hundreds of small piles of white and grey earth scattered across the landscape. But much of the town is hidden. About half of the residents live under the ground, in homes dug into the hillsides.

The reason is the heat. In summer, temperatures often go above forty degrees, and the hot wind brings dust into everything. Under the ground, however, the temperature stays at around twenty-four degrees all year, day and night. People there do not need air conditioning in summer or heating in winter. These homes are called dugouts, and many of them are surprisingly comfortable, with kitchens, bathrooms, bedrooms and even swimming pools cut into the rock. The only thing missing is windows, so most rooms have soft electric lights that stay on all day.

The town exists because of a stone. In 1915, a fourteen-year-old boy who was searching for water with his father's group found a piece of opal lying on the ground. Opal is a beautiful stone that shows flashes of many colours, red, green and blue, when you move it in the light. Soon miners arrived from all over the world, and after the Second World War many came from southern Europe, especially Greece and Italy. Today the area produces a large share of the world's opal, and people of dozens of nationalities live there.

The name Coober Pedy is often said to come from local Aboriginal words meaning something like white man in a hole. Whether or not this is the exact meaning, it describes the town well. Even some of the churches are under the ground. One of them, a Serbian Orthodox church, has high walls of carved rock and coloured glass windows lit from behind.

Life in Coober Pedy has its own rules. Because there is hardly any grass, the golf course is made of sand and dirt, and players carry a small piece of artificial grass to hit the ball from. Sometimes they play at night with glowing balls, because it is too hot during the day. Water is precious: for many years it had to be brought in by truck, and today it comes from deep under the ground and is cleaned before people can drink it.

There are also dangers. The land around the town has thousands of old mine shafts, deep narrow holes that miners dug and then left open. Signs warn visitors not to walk backwards while taking photos, and not to run. Every year people are reminded to stay on the marked paths.

Filmmakers love the place, because the landscape looks like another planet, and scenes from several science fiction films were shot in the area. But for the people who live there, it is simply home. Many of them still dream that the next metre of rock will hold the one perfect stone that changes their lives.

questions.q: Why do many people in Coober Pedy live under the ground?
options: Because the land above ground belongs to the mines
Because it stays at a comfortable temperature all year
Because the government does not allow houses on the surface
Because they want to hide their opals from visitors
questions.explain: Metne göre yazın sıcaklık kırk derecenin üstüne çıkarken yer altında sıcaklık bütün yıl yaklaşık yirmi dört derecede kalıyor. Doğru cevap: "Because it stays at a comfortable temperature all year".

questions.q: Why are visitors told not to walk backwards while taking photos?
options: Because they might damage the opals in the ground
Because the golf players need the space
Because they might fall into an old, open mine hole
Because it is too hot to move slowly
questions.explain: Metin, kasabanın çevresinde madencilerin kazıp açık bıraktığı binlerce eski maden kuyusu olduğunu ve tabelaların bu yüzden uyardığını anlatıyor. Doğru cevap: "Because they might fall into an old, open mine hole".

title: The Zipper That Nobody Wanted
text:
Think about how many times you open and close a zipper in a normal day. Your coat, your bag, your pencil case, maybe your boots. It takes less than a second, and you never think about it. But this small piece of metal or plastic needed about thirty years, several inventors and a funny name before people finally accepted it.

The story usually begins with an American called Whitcomb Judson. In the early 1890s, Judson was a busy inventor in Chicago. According to one popular account, he had a friend with a bad back who found it hard to bend down and fasten his high boots. In those days, boots were closed with long rows of small hooks, and doing them up could take several minutes. Judson designed a "clasp locker" to make the job quicker. It was a line of hooks and eyes that a small slider pulled together.

Judson received patents for his idea in 1893, and he even started a company to sell it. Sadly, the clasp locker had a serious problem. It often opened by itself at the worst possible moment, or it got stuck halfway. Few customers trusted it, and for many years the company earned very little money. It seemed that the idea might simply disappear.

The man who saved it was Gideon Sundback, a young engineer who had moved to the United States from Sweden. He joined Judson's company and started to study the design carefully. His life at this time was not easy. He had married the daughter of the factory manager, but she died in 1911, only a few years later. Some writers believe that Sundback buried himself in his work after her death.

By 1913, he had made a much better fastener. Instead of hooks and eyes, he used many small metal teeth on two strips of cloth. When the slider moved up, the teeth on each side locked into each other. When it moved down, they came apart again. The new fastener was lighter, flatter and far more reliable. Sundback also built a machine that could produce it cheaply and in large numbers, which was just as important as the design itself.

Even then, people did not rush to buy it. At first, it was used mainly on money belts and tobacco bags. Things changed in the 1920s, when a large rubber company used the fastener on a new kind of boot. The company called the boots "Zippers", probably because of the sound the slider made. The name was so catchy that people soon used it for the fastener itself.

Clothes came last. For a long time, many people thought that a metal fastener on clothing looked strange, or even a little dangerous. In the 1930s, however, children's clothes with zippers were advertised as a way to help children dress themselves. Soon after that, some fashion designers started using zippers in trousers and dresses. By the middle of the century, the zipper was everywhere.

Today, factories around the world produce billions of zippers every year. Most people have never heard of Judson or Sundback. Yet every time you close your jacket on a cold morning, you are using an idea that almost failed, and that needed a second inventor to make it work.

questions.q: What was the main problem with Judson's first "clasp locker"?
options: It often opened by itself or got stuck
It was too expensive to make by hand
It was too heavy for boots
It made a loud and annoying sound
questions.explain: Metinde toka kilidinin sık sık kendiliğinden açıldığı ya da yarıda takıldığı anlatılıyor; doğru cevap "It often opened by itself or got stuck".

questions.q: Where did the name "zipper" come from?
options: From Gideon Sundback's family name
From a Swedish word for "teeth"
From the name of a boot sold by a rubber company
From Judson's first company
questions.explain: Bir kauçuk şirketi bu çizmelere "Zippers" adını verdi ve isim sonra fermuarın kendisi için kullanıldı; doğru cevap "From the name of a boot sold by a rubber company".

title: Three Hours and a Piece of Wire
titleTr: Üç saat ve bir parça tel
text:
In the spring of 1849, a New York mechanic called Walter Hunt had a problem that many people know well. He owed money. According to the most common version of the story, he owed a friend fifteen dollars, which was a real amount of money at that time. Hunt was clever, but he was not good at business, and he could not pay.

So he did what he always did when he was worried. He picked up something and started to play with it. This time it was a piece of brass wire, about twenty centimetres long. He bent it, twisted it and bent it again. After about three hours, he had made something new: a pin that could close safely.

Pins, of course, were not new. People had used straight pins for centuries to hold cloth together, and they often pricked their fingers. Even the idea of a pin with a spring was very old. In the Bronze Age, people across Europe used metal brooches with a kind of spring to fasten their clothes. Hunt's pin was different because it was cheap, simple and safe. One end of the wire was coiled into a small circle, which worked as a spring. The sharp point fitted into a little cover at the other end, so it could not open by accident or hurt anyone.

Hunt understood that this was useful. He applied for a patent and received it in April 1849. Then he did something that surprises people today. Instead of making the pins himself, he sold all the rights to a company for four hundred dollars. He paid his friend the fifteen dollars and, it seems, he was happy to have the rest. The company, however, went on to earn far more than that from his idea.

This was not the first time Hunt had missed his chance. Some years earlier, he had built one of the first sewing machines in America. But he decided not to patent it. According to his daughter, he was afraid that a machine like that would put many poor women who sewed by hand out of work. Later, other inventors made sewing machines famous and rich, while Hunt's name was mostly forgotten.

Hunt's list of ideas was long and colourful. Over his life, he worked on a repeating rifle, a better stove, a knife sharpener, a new kind of ink bottle and even a bicycle with a bell. Many of his inventions worked well. Very few made him money. He was the kind of person who loved solving problems more than selling the answers.

Today, safety pins are found in almost every home. Parents once used them to close babies' cloth nappies. Tailors use them to hold fabric before they sew it. Some people wear them as jewellery, and in the 1970s they became part of punk fashion. In a few countries, people even pin one inside their clothes for good luck.

The next time you hold a safety pin, look at the small spring at its end. It is a simple shape that has hardly changed since 1849. It was made in a single afternoon by a tired man who needed to pay back fifteen dollars, and who gave away a fortune without much regret.

questions.q: Why did Walter Hunt start playing with a piece of wire?
options: A company had asked him for a new product
He wanted to make jewellery for his daughter
He was worried about a small debt he could not pay
He was trying to repair a sewing machine
questions.explain: Hunt bir arkadaşına on beş dolar borçluydu ve ödeyemiyordu; endişelenince tel ile oynamaya başladı. Doğru cevap "He was worried about a small debt he could not pay".

questions.q: Why, according to his daughter, did Hunt not patent his sewing machine?
options: He feared it would take work away from women who sewed by hand
He thought it did not work well enough
He did not have enough money for a patent
Another inventor had already patented it
questions.explain: Kızına göre Hunt, makinenin elle dikiş diken yoksul kadınları işsiz bırakmasından korkuyordu; doğru cevap "He feared it would take work away from women who sewed by hand".

title: The Puzzle That Took Over America
text:
On Sunday, 21 December 1913, readers of the New York World newspaper found something unusual in the fun section. Next to the jokes and the comic drawings, there was a diamond-shaped pattern of empty squares. Under it was a list of short clues. The idea was to read each clue, think of the right word and write it into the squares, one letter in each box. The puzzle was called a "Word-Cross".

The man behind it was Arthur Wynne, a journalist who had been born in Liverpool in England and had moved to the United States as a young man. His editor had asked him to create a new game for the Christmas edition. Wynne remembered a children's word game from his childhood, in which words were arranged in a square so that they could be read both across and down. He made the idea bigger and more flexible, and he added clues.

Wynne's first puzzle looks very simple to modern eyes. It had no black squares, and some of the clues were rather easy, such as "the fibre of the gomuti palm" and "what we all should be". But readers loved it. They wrote letters to the paper asking for more, and soon there was a new puzzle every week. A few weeks later, the name changed. Some people say a typesetter made a mistake and printed "Cross-Word" instead of "Word-Cross". Whatever the reason, the new name stayed.

For about ten years, the crossword lived quietly in this one newspaper. Then, in 1924, two young men who had just started a publishing company decided to print a whole book of crossword puzzles. Their names were Richard Simon and Max Schuster. Other publishers thought the idea was silly, and the young men were not sure either. To be safe, they did not put their company's name on the first book. They attached a small pencil to each copy.

The book was an enormous success. It sold hundreds of thousands of copies, and the young company became one of the biggest publishers in America. Suddenly, crosswords were everywhere. People did them on trains, in cafés and at work. Songs were written about them. Dictionaries sold out in some shops, and, according to newspaper reports of the time, some libraries had to limit how long a visitor could use the dictionary.

Not everyone was happy. Some newspapers wrote that the crossword was a silly fashion that wasted people's time and would soon be forgotten. One serious paper, the New York Times, was especially critical. Interestingly, the same paper changed its mind later. It started its own Sunday crossword in 1942, during the Second World War. Its editors thought that readers needed something calm to do during the long, dark evenings of the war.

From America, the crossword travelled around the world. British puzzles developed their own style, with clever clues that often hide a word inside a joke. Other countries changed the shape and the rules to suit their own languages. In Turkey, many newspapers still print a bulmaca every day.

Today, millions of people solve crosswords on paper or on their phones. Some do them to relax, and others believe they help to keep the mind sharp. Very few of them have heard of Arthur Wynne. Yet each time someone fills in the last empty square with a smile, they are enjoying a small Christmas gift from 1913.

questions.q: Where did Arthur Wynne get the basic idea for his puzzle?
options: From a Turkish newspaper
From a word game he knew as a child
From a book by Simon and Schuster
From a letter sent by a reader
questions.explain: Wynne, çocukluğunda bildiği ve kelimelerin hem yatay hem dikey okunduğu bir kelime oyununu hatırladı; doğru cevap "From a word game he knew as a child".

questions.q: Why did the New York Times start a crossword in 1942?
options: Because its readers had stopped buying dictionaries
Because Arthur Wynne asked it to
Because the New York World had closed
Because its editors felt readers needed something calm during the war
questions.explain: Gazetenin editörleri, savaşın uzun ve karanlık akşamlarında okuyucuların sakin bir uğraşa ihtiyacı olduğunu düşündü; doğru cevap "Because its editors felt readers needed something calm during the war".

title: Wallpaper Nobody Hung
text:
Few things are as satisfying as a sheet of bubble wrap. You press one bubble between your fingers, it makes a small pop, and you immediately want to press another one. Most of us meet bubble wrap when a parcel arrives and something fragile is safely inside. But this famous packing material was not invented for packing at all. It began as a failed idea for decorating homes.

In 1957, two engineers in New Jersey, in the United States, were working in a small workshop. One was an American called Alfred Fielding. The other, Marc Chavannes, had come from Switzerland. They were interested in new plastic materials and wanted to create something modern for people's houses. Their plan was a plastic wallpaper with a textured surface. They sealed two layers of plastic together in a way that trapped small pockets of air between them. The result was a sheet covered in little round bubbles.

The two men thought it looked fresh and exciting. Customers did not agree. Very few people wanted their living room walls to be covered in plastic bubbles, and the wallpaper did not sell. Many inventors would have given up at this point. Fielding and Chavannes decided to look for a different use.

Their next idea was to sell the material as insulation for greenhouses. The air in the bubbles, they hoped, would keep the plants warm in winter. The sheets did hold some heat, but the plan still did not work well as a business. Farmers were not very interested, and the two men were running out of time and money.

The answer came from a completely different direction. In 1959, the computer company IBM introduced a new machine that was very expensive and easily damaged. The company needed a safe way to send these computers to customers. According to the usual account, someone at Fielding and Chavannes's young company, Sealed Air, saw the chance and suggested their bubble sheets. The air pockets were light, but they protected delicate objects from shocks during the journey. IBM agreed to use them, and suddenly the material had a real purpose.

After that, bubble wrap spread quickly. Shops used it to send glasses, plates, electronics and works of art. Moving companies wrapped furniture in it. As online shopping grew, the demand grew with it. Today, the company makes much more than bubble wrap, but this is still the product most people connect with its name.

Of course, the story has a second, more playful side. People quickly discovered that popping the bubbles was fun, and possibly even relaxing. Some studies have suggested that it can reduce stress, although scientists do not agree on how strong the effect is. In the United States, there is even a Bubble Wrap Appreciation Day on the last Monday of January.

There is also a less happy side. Bubble wrap is made of plastic, and most of it is used only once and then thrown away. For this reason, some companies now use paper padding or wrap made from recycled materials. Even the makers of the original product have worked on versions that use less plastic. One day, the satisfying pop may have to come from a greener kind of bubble.

questions.q: What were Fielding and Chavannes first trying to make?
options: A safe box for computers
A plastic wallpaper for homes
A toy for children
A cover for greenhouses
questions.explain: İki mühendis önce evler için dokulu plastik bir duvar kâğıdı yapmak istiyordu; doğru cevap "A plastic wallpaper for homes". Sera fikri ikinci denemeydi.

questions.q: What finally gave bubble wrap a real purpose?
options: Farmers started buying it for their plants
Scientists proved that it reduces stress
Online shops asked for a cheaper material
A computer company needed to send its machines safely
questions.explain: IBM pahalı ve kolay hasar gören bilgisayarlarını güvenle göndermek için bu malzemeyi kullanmaya karar verdi; doğru cevap "A computer company needed to send its machines safely".

title: Who Really Invented the Paper Clip?
text:
Some objects are so simple that it is hard to believe anyone invented them. The paper clip is one of these. It is just a short piece of steel wire, bent into two loops, one inside the other. Yet this tiny object has an interesting history, a national legend and even a role in a war.

Before the paper clip, people held papers together in other ways. They used straight pins, which left small holes and could hurt fingers. Sometimes they tied documents with ribbon, or simply folded the corners together. In the second half of the nineteenth century, however, factories learned to produce cheap steel wire that was both strong and springy. Suddenly, many people tried to bend this wire into a useful shape for holding paper.

If you ask people in Norway who invented the paper clip, many will give you a name: Johan Vaaler. Vaaler was a Norwegian who worked in an office, and in 1899 he received a German patent for a paper clip. A year or two later, he received an American patent too. For a long time, Norwegians proudly believed that he had given this little object to the world.

The truth is a bit more complicated. Vaaler's design was not the one we use today. His clip had only one and a half loops, and it was not very good at holding papers. The famous double-loop shape, which most people now picture, was already being made in Britain in the 1890s. It was known as the Gem clip, after the company that probably first produced it. Strangely, nobody seems to have patented the Gem design, so we do not know the name of the person who first bent it.

So how did Vaaler become a hero? Part of the answer is that an encyclopedia mentioned him in the 1920s, and the story was repeated many times after that. The other part of the answer comes from the Second World War.

During the war, Germany occupied Norway. Norwegians were not allowed to show support for their king or their government, which had escaped to London. According to many accounts, some people began to wear paper clips on their jackets. It was a quiet way of saying "we stick together". The clip was small, ordinary and easy to hide, but everyone understood its meaning. Some people were punished for wearing one. Historians still discuss how common this was, but the paper clip became a powerful symbol in Norwegian memory.

After the war, the legend of Vaaler grew even stronger. In 1989, a giant paper clip, about seven metres tall, was built outside a business school near Oslo to honour him. Ironically, the statue shows the Gem shape, not his own design. Later, his picture also appeared on a Norwegian stamp.

Does it matter who really invented the paper clip? In one way, not very much. Millions of clips are used every day, and they work perfectly well without a famous inventor. But the story shows how history is sometimes shaped by what people want to believe. A country under pressure needed a small, proud symbol, and a piece of bent wire was ready to help.

questions.q: What was different about Johan Vaaler's design?
options: It was made of plastic instead of steel
It was much bigger than modern clips
It had only one and a half loops and held paper less well
It was used only by the Norwegian government
questions.explain: Vaaler'ın ataşında yalnızca bir buçuk halka vardı ve kâğıtları iyi tutmuyordu; doğru cevap "It had only one and a half loops and held paper less well".

questions.q: What did wearing a paper clip mean for some Norwegians during the war?
options: That they wanted to stay united against the occupation
That they worked in an office
That they supported the German government
That they had invented something new
questions.explain: Ataş takmak "birbirimize kenetleniriz" demenin sessiz bir yoluydu; doğru cevap "That they wanted to stay united against the occupation".

title: The Plant That Counts
text:
In a small corner of the south-eastern United States, along the coast of North and South Carolina, grows one of the strangest plants on Earth. It is only a few centimetres tall, and it would be easy to walk past it. But when an insect lands on one of its leaves, the leaf snaps shut like a pair of jaws. This is the Venus flytrap, and it has fascinated people for more than two hundred years.

Charles Darwin was one of its biggest fans. In the 1870s he studied it closely and called it one of the most wonderful plants in the world. Darwin wanted to know why a plant would eat animals at all. The answer lies in the ground. The flytrap lives in wet, sandy soil that contains very little nitrogen, a substance all plants need in order to grow. Insects are full of nitrogen, so catching them is a clever way to get what the soil cannot give.

Each trap is made of two leaf halves joined in the middle. On the inside of each half there are a few tiny hairs, usually three. These hairs work like switches. If an insect touches one hair, nothing happens. If it touches a hair a second time, or touches another hair within about twenty seconds, the trap closes in a fraction of a second. This rule protects the plant from wasting energy. A falling raindrop or a piece of dust will probably touch a hair only once, so the trap stays open.

In 2016, a team of scientists in Germany looked at this behaviour more closely. They touched the hairs again and again with a thin tool and measured the electrical signals inside the leaf. Their results suggested that the plant was, in a simple way, counting. Two touches closed the trap. After that, the struggling insect kept touching the hairs from inside. When the count reached about five, the plant began to produce the special juices that break down food. The more the prey moved, the more juice the plant produced. A small, weak insect received a small amount; a large one that fought hard received a lot.

Of course, the plant has no brain and cannot count in the way that we do. The scientists explained that each touch sends a small electrical signal through the leaf, and the signals add up. Still, the result is remarkable: a plant that can tell the difference between one touch, two touches and five.

Once the trap is sealed, digestion takes around a week or more. Then the leaf opens again, and only the dry outer shell of the insect is left behind. The wind or the rain carries it away. A single trap can only close a few times in its life before it turns black and dies, so every false alarm is expensive. New traps grow to take its place.

Sadly, the flytrap is in trouble in the wild. Its home has shrunk as towns have grown and as wetlands have been drained. Another problem is that people dig up wild plants to sell them. In North Carolina this is now a serious crime that can lead to a large fine or even prison. Interestingly, the flytrap also depends on fire. Natural fires clear away taller plants that would otherwise block the sunlight. When fires are stopped, the little flytrap slowly disappears.

Next time you see a Venus flytrap in a garden shop, remember that you are looking at a plant that can sense, remember and, in its own way, count. It is a small reminder that plants are often far more active than they seem.

questions.q: Why does the Venus flytrap catch insects?
options: Because it cannot make its own sugar from sunlight
Because the soil it grows in has very little nitrogen
Because insects damage its leaves if it does not
Because fire has destroyed its usual food
questions.explain: Metin bitkinin azotça çok fakir, ıslak ve kumlu toprakta yaşadığını, böceklerin ise azot dolu olduğunu söylüyor; doğru cevap 'Because the soil it grows in has very little nitrogen'.

questions.q: What did the scientists in Germany discover in 2016?
options: The plant closes its trap after a single touch
The plant has a very small brain inside each leaf
The plant starts producing digestive juices after about five touches
The plant can open and close a trap hundreds of times
questions.explain: Araştırmacılar iki dokunuşun kapanı kapattığını, sayı yaklaşık beşe ulaşınca bitkinin sindirim sıvısı üretmeye başladığını buldu: 'The plant starts producing digestive juices after about five touches'.

title: The Frog That Turns to Ice
text:
Imagine walking through a forest in Alaska in the middle of winter. Under a thin layer of dead leaves and snow, you find a small brown frog. It is as hard as stone. Its heart is not beating, it is not breathing, and its blood is not moving. By any normal measure, it is dead. But when spring arrives, the frog will slowly soften, its heart will start beating again, and within a day or so it will hop away to look for a partner.

This is the wood frog, a small animal that lives across much of North America, from the eastern United States to Canada and Alaska. It has one of the most surprising survival methods in the animal world: it allows its body to freeze.

For most animals, freezing is deadly. When water turns to ice, it forms sharp crystals. These crystals can break the walls of cells, and they also pull water out of cells, which then dry out and collapse. That is why frozen fruit often becomes soft and watery after it thaws. A frog's body, like ours, is mostly water, so you might expect it to be destroyed by the cold.

The wood frog has found a clever solution. When ice first touches its skin in autumn, its body reacts within minutes. The liver starts to release huge amounts of sugar into the blood. This sugar travels to the cells and fills them, working rather like the antifreeze that people put in car engines. Because the inside of the cells is full of sugar, it does not freeze easily. The ice forms mainly in the spaces between the cells and around the organs, while the cells themselves stay protected. In the end, as much as two-thirds of the water in the frog's body may turn to ice.

In this state, the frog uses almost no energy. It does not need to find food, and it is safe from many enemies that have left the area or are sleeping themselves. Scientists who studied frogs in Alaska found that some of them stayed frozen for more than half of the year and survived temperatures far below zero. Frogs from further south, where winters are milder, do not survive such low temperatures in the laboratory. It seems that the northern frogs have stronger protection, perhaps because they store more sugar.

When the weather warms up, the process runs in reverse. The ice melts, and the heart starts to beat again, at first slowly and then normally. Breathing returns, and the frog wakes up. Scientists still do not fully understand what makes the heart start again, and this is one of the most exciting questions in the field.

Waking up early is important for the wood frog. It is one of the first frogs to breed in spring. The males gather in small pools formed by melting snow and call to the females with a sound that resembles a group of ducks. Because these pools dry out by summer, the eggs must develop quickly, and the young frogs must leave the water before it disappears.

The wood frog is not only a curiosity. Doctors have long wanted to store human organs, such as hearts or kidneys, for longer before they are given to patients. At present, many organs can survive outside the body for only a few hours. If we could learn to freeze organs safely, as the wood frog does with its whole body, many more lives could be saved. Researchers are studying the frog's chemistry in the hope of copying some of its tricks.

So the next time you feel cold on a winter day, think of the little wood frog, which spends the season as a block of ice and still wakes up ready for spring.

questions.q: How does the wood frog protect its cells from ice?
options: It moves to warmer water before the winter begins
It grows a thick layer of fat under its skin
It keeps its heart beating slowly all winter
Its liver fills the cells with sugar so they do not freeze easily
questions.explain: Metne göre karaciğer kana büyük miktarda şeker salar; şeker hücreleri doldurur ve antifriz gibi çalışır: 'Its liver fills the cells with sugar so they do not freeze easily'.

questions.q: Why are doctors interested in the wood frog?
options: They hope to learn how to store human organs for longer
They want to use its sugar as a new medicine
They believe it can cure heart disease
They need its skin for treating burns
questions.explain: Doktorlar organları hastaya nakledilmeden önce daha uzun süre saklamak istiyor; kurbağanın kimyası bu konuda ipucu verebilir: 'They hope to learn how to store human organs for longer'.

title: The Fish That Shoots Its Dinner
text:
In the warm, muddy waters of mangrove forests in South-East Asia and northern Australia, a fish waits just below the surface. Above it, a small insect is resting on a leaf. Suddenly, a thin jet of water flies up from the river. It hits the insect, which falls into the water, and the fish swallows it almost before it lands. This hunter is the archerfish, and it is one of the best shooters in nature.

An archerfish is not large; most are about the size of a man's hand. Its secret is in its mouth. Along the roof of its mouth there is a narrow groove. When the fish presses its tongue against this groove, it forms a kind of tube. Then the fish closes its gills quickly and pushes water out through the tube. The result is a jet that can travel a metre or more, and the best shooters can hit targets even further away.

Shooting from under water is much harder than it sounds. When light passes from air into water, it bends. You have probably noticed this if you have ever put a pencil into a glass of water: the pencil seems to break at the surface. For the fish, this means that the insect is not where it appears to be. Yet archerfish correct for this problem and hit their targets with great accuracy. Young fish miss often, but they improve with practice, and they also seem to learn by watching more experienced fish.

Scientists in Germany have studied archerfish for many years and found even more surprising skills. The fish can change the shape of the jet depending on how far away the target is. The water at the back of the jet leaves the mouth slightly faster than the water at the front. As a result, the back of the jet catches up with the front, and the water gathers into a heavy drop just as it reaches the insect. In this way, the force is greatest at exactly the right moment.

There is another problem to solve. When the insect falls, other fish are waiting to steal it. So an archerfish must work out very quickly where its prey will land. Researchers found that the fish needs only about a tenth of a second after the shot to decide where to swim, and then it races to that spot. It does not wait to watch the whole fall; it calculates the place from the first moments.

In 2016, researchers at the University of Oxford tested something even stranger. They trained archerfish to spit at a picture of one human face on a screen above their tank. Then they showed the fish this face among many new faces. The fish chose the correct face most of the time, even though human faces are not something fish meet in nature. This was surprising because many people believed that recognising faces needed a large and complex brain.

Some aquarium owners have their own stories. Archerfish in home tanks have been known to shoot at lamps, at fingers, and sometimes at the faces of the people looking at them. Whether this is curiosity or a hope for food is hard to say.

The archerfish reminds us that intelligence takes many forms. A small fish with a small brain can solve problems of physics that people need calculators for. It does not know the rules of light, but its body and brain have learned to work with them perfectly.

questions.q: Why is it difficult for the archerfish to hit an insect?
options: Insects above the water move too fast to see
Light bends between air and water, so the insect is not where it seems
The fish has very poor eyesight
The water in mangrove forests is too cold
questions.explain: Işık havadan suya geçerken kırılır; bu yüzden böcek göründüğü yerde değildir: 'Light bends between air and water, so the insect is not where it seems'.

questions.q: What did the Oxford experiment show?
options: Archerfish prefer to shoot at lamps rather than insects
Archerfish can only learn by watching older fish
Archerfish can recognise a particular human face
Archerfish need a large brain to hunt successfully
questions.explain: Oxford deneyinde balıklar öğrendikleri yüzü birçok yeni yüz arasından çoğu zaman doğru seçti: 'Archerfish can recognise a particular human face'.

title: Rolling by Starlight
text:
On a warm night in the dry grasslands of South Africa, a small black beetle is busy. In front of it lies a ball of animal dung, larger than the beetle itself. The beetle stands on its front legs, pushes the ball with its back legs, and rolls it away across the ground. What makes this ordinary scene special is the direction the beetle chooses. It rolls in an almost perfectly straight line, even in the dark. For a long time, nobody knew how it managed this.

Dung may not sound very attractive, but for dung beetles it is a treasure. It contains water and food, and some beetles also lay their eggs inside it. Fresh dung attracts many beetles at once, and they fight over it. So a beetle that has made its ball wants to leave the crowd as quickly as possible. The fastest way to escape is to travel in a straight line. If it went round in circles, it might end up back at the crowded pile, where another beetle could take its prize.

Before starting, the beetle often climbs on top of its ball and turns around, as if it is dancing. Scientists believe it is taking a kind of picture of the sky to find its direction. During the day, dung beetles use the sun. On moonlit nights, they use the moon and the patterns of light around it. But researchers in Sweden and South Africa noticed that some beetles could keep a straight path even on clear nights with no moon. Where were they getting their direction from?

In a series of clever experiments, published in 2013, a team led by the Swedish biologist Marie Dacke found an answer. First, they put tiny caps on the beetles' heads so that the insects could not see the sky. With the caps on, the beetles wandered in all directions. Without them, they rolled straight. So the sky was clearly important.

Next, the team took the beetles into a special theatre in Johannesburg, where an artificial night sky can be shown on the ceiling. When the full sky with all its stars was shown, the beetles rolled straight. When only the Milky Way was shown, a bright band of light formed by billions of distant stars, they still rolled straight. When only a few of the brightest single stars were shown, they became lost. The conclusion was clear: the beetles were using the Milky Way as a guide.

This was an exciting discovery. Seals and humans are known to use the stars to find their way, but this was the first time scientists had shown that an insect uses the Milky Way. Dung beetles have very small eyes, too small to see most single stars. However, the soft band of the Milky Way is bright enough for them to notice. The beetles do not use it to travel to a particular place; they simply use it to keep going in one direction.

The discovery also raises a worry. In many parts of the world, the night sky is no longer dark. Light from cities hides the stars, and today many people living in towns have never seen the Milky Way. Later studies suggested that city light makes it harder for dung beetles to find their way, and some begin to follow bright lamps instead.

Dung beetles are not glamorous animals. Yet they play an important role, burying waste, returning goodness to the soil and keeping flies under control. And on dark nights, these small cleaners look up at the same river of stars that has guided travellers for thousands of years.

questions.q: Why does a dung beetle roll its ball in a straight line?
options: To get away from other beetles as fast as possible
To follow the smell of fresh dung
To reach a particular nest it has built
To find water before the sun rises
questions.explain: Taze dışkının başında birçok böcek kavga eder; düz bir çizgi kalabalıktan kaçmanın en hızlı yoludur: 'To get away from other beetles as fast as possible'.

questions.q: What happened when only the Milky Way was shown on the ceiling?
options: The beetles stopped moving completely
The beetles wandered in all directions
The beetles climbed on their balls and danced all night
The beetles still rolled in a straight line
questions.explain: Tavanda yalnızca Samanyolu gösterildiğinde böcekler yine düz yuvarladı; bu da Samanyolu'nu rehber olarak kullandıklarını gösterdi: 'The beetles still rolled in a straight line'.

title: Tiny Engines That Switch Off at Night
text:
A hummingbird is a small bird with a huge appetite for life. Hummingbirds are found only in the Americas, from Alaska to the southern tip of South America, and there are more than three hundred species. The smallest, the bee hummingbird of Cuba, is only about five centimetres long and weighs less than a small coin. Yet these tiny birds live faster than almost any other animal on Earth.

Watch a hummingbird at a flower and you will see its wings as a grey blur. In many species, the wings beat around fifty times every second, and even more in the smallest ones. This allows the bird to hover in one place, like a helicopter, while it drinks. It can also fly sideways, upwards and even backwards, something no other bird can do for long. Its heart is just as busy. When a hummingbird is active, its heart may beat more than a thousand times a minute. A human heart, by comparison, beats around seventy times a minute at rest.

All this activity needs fuel. Hummingbirds drink nectar, the sweet liquid inside flowers, and they also catch small insects for protein. A hummingbird may visit hundreds or even thousands of flowers a day. Its long tongue is split at the end. When it enters the nectar, the two halves open and then close around the liquid, trapping it. The bird can do this many times per second. In one day, a hummingbird may drink as much nectar as its own body weight, or even more.

Hummingbirds also have excellent memories. A bird seems to remember which flowers it has already visited and roughly how long each one takes to fill up again. This saves it from wasting energy on empty flowers.
