The real problem comes at night. A hummingbird cannot feed in the dark, and it has very little fat stored in its tiny body. Small animals lose heat quickly, and keeping a body warm uses a lot of energy. If a hummingbird stayed fully active all night, it could run out of fuel before morning and die.

The solution is a state called torpor, a kind of deep, short sleep. As night falls, the bird lets its body temperature drop. Its heart slows from hundreds of beats a minute to perhaps fifty, and its breathing becomes very slow, sometimes with pauses. In this state, it may use only a small part of the energy it would normally need. A bird in torpor hangs quietly on a branch and does not respond to sound or touch. People who find one sometimes think it is dead.

A study published in 2020 measured the body temperature of hummingbirds living high in the Andes mountains of Peru, where nights are very cold. One species, the black metaltail, cooled its body to just over three degrees Celsius. This was the lowest temperature ever recorded in a bird, and lower than in any mammal that was not hibernating. Its normal daytime temperature is around forty degrees.

Waking up takes work. Before dawn, the bird starts to shiver, using its flight muscles to produce heat. Over about twenty minutes to an hour, its body warms up again, and its heart returns to full speed. By sunrise it is ready to fly to its first flower of the day.

Scientists think torpor may help explain how such small animals can survive at all. Living at full speed every hour of the day and night would simply cost too much. By switching off at night, the hummingbird can live a life of extremes: incredibly fast by day and almost still by night.

questions.q: Why can't a hummingbird stay fully active all night?
options: Its wings become too tired to beat
Flowers close their nectar at night
It would use up its small energy store before morning
Its enemies hunt mainly in the dark
questions.explain: Kuş karanlıkta beslenemez ve çok az yağ depolar; bütün gece tam aktif kalırsa sabaha kadar yakıtı bitebilir: 'It would use up its small energy store before morning'.

questions.q: What is special about the black metaltail?
options: It is the smallest bird in the world
It cooled its body to the lowest temperature ever recorded in a bird
It can fly backwards for several hours
It drinks nectar only at night
questions.explain: 2020 çalışmasında bu tür vücudunu üç derecenin biraz üzerine kadar soğuttu; bu, bir kuşta ölçülen en düşük sıcaklık: 'It cooled its body to the lowest temperature ever recorded in a bird'.

title: The Season of Kimchi
text:
Every year, when the first cold winds arrive in late autumn, millions of Korean families prepare for a very busy weekend. Grandmothers, aunts, cousins and neighbours gather in one house, and the floor slowly disappears under piles of cabbages. This yearly event is called kimjang, and its aim is simple: to make enough kimchi to last the whole winter.

Kimchi is a dish of vegetables that are salted and then left for some time until they slowly turn sour. There are hundreds of kinds, made with radish, cucumber or green onion, but the best-known version uses napa cabbage, a pale, long cabbage with soft leaves. In Korea, kimchi is not a side dish that people eat now and then. It appears at almost every meal, including breakfast, and many Koreans say a meal without it feels unfinished.

The work starts a day or two before the main event. The cabbages are cut in half and covered with coarse salt, then left in large tubs overnight. The salt pulls water out of the leaves, so they become soft and bendy. The next morning, everyone washes the cabbages again and again in cold water to remove the extra salt. Hands turn red and the kitchen smells like the sea.

Meanwhile, someone prepares the paste. It is usually a mixture of red chilli powder, garlic, ginger, sliced radish, green onion and a little fish sauce or salted shrimp. Every family has its own recipe, and arguments about the right amount of garlic are part of the fun. Then the real job begins. Sitting on the floor in a circle, often wearing rubber gloves, people spread the red paste between every single leaf. It is slow, careful work, and it gives everyone time to talk, gossip and laugh.

In the past, the finished kimchi went into large clay pots, which were buried in the garden up to their necks. Under the ground, the temperature stayed cool but did not drop too low, so the kimchi slowly changed through the winter. Its taste changed week by week, from fresh and crunchy to sour and strong. Today, most people live in flats, so the clay pots have been replaced by a special machine: the kimchi refrigerator. Many Korean homes have one next to their normal fridge, and it keeps the kimchi at exactly the right temperature.

Interestingly, the bright red colour that we now link with kimchi is fairly new. Chilli peppers came from the Americas, and they probably reached Korea only around the sixteenth or seventeenth century. Before that, kimchi was made with salt, garlic and other spices, and it looked much paler. Over time, chilli became so popular that it is now hard to imagine kimchi without it.

Kimjang is about more than food. Families who do not have time often receive boxes of kimchi from their parents, and many towns and companies organise large kimjang events where volunteers make kimchi for elderly people living alone. In 2013, UNESCO added the tradition to its list of the world's intangible cultural heritage, describing it as a way of sharing and building community.

People who have taken part in kimjang often remember the aching backs, the red fingers and the cold water. But they also remember the first warm bite of fresh kimchi wrapped around a piece of boiled pork, which is the traditional reward at the end of the long day. For many Koreans, that taste means that winter can come.

questions.q: Why were kimchi pots buried in the garden in the past?
options: To hide them from neighbours
To keep the kimchi at a cool but steady temperature
To make the kimchi turn red more quickly
To save space inside small flats
questions.explain: Metne göre toprak altında sıcaklık serin kalıyor ama çok düşmüyordu; bu yüzden doğru cevap 'To keep the kimchi at a cool but steady temperature'.

questions.q: What does the text say about the red colour of kimchi?
options: It comes from the fish sauce
It has always been part of the dish
UNESCO asked Koreans to keep it
It probably appeared only after chilli reached Korea a few centuries ago
questions.explain: Acı biber Amerika kıtasından geldi ve Kore'ye muhtemelen 16.-17. yüzyılda ulaştı; öncesinde kimçi daha soluktu. Doğru cevap 'It probably appeared only after chilli reached Korea a few centuries ago'.

title: Spring at the Sugar Shack
text:
In the forests of Quebec, in eastern Canada, spring does not begin with flowers. It begins with a sound: the soft drip, drip, drip of liquid falling into metal buckets. For a few weeks in March and April, the maple trees wake up from the winter, and families who make maple syrup work almost day and night.

The liquid inside the trees is called sap. It looks like water and tastes only a little sweet, because it is about ninety-seven per cent water and just two or three per cent sugar. To collect it, producers drill a small hole in the trunk and push in a short tube called a spout. The tree is not seriously harmed, and the same tree can be used for many decades.

The sap does not flow at any time. It needs a special kind of weather: nights below freezing and days above it. When the temperature rises in the afternoon, pressure builds inside the tree and pushes the sap out. At night, the cold pulls water back up from the roots. If the spring is too warm or too cold, the season can be short and disappointing, so producers watch the weather forecast very closely.

Indigenous peoples of the region were making maple sugar long before Europeans arrived. They cut the bark, collected the sap in containers made of bark and boiled it, possibly by dropping hot stones into it. French settlers learned the method from them and later began using iron pots. Today, many large farms collect sap through kilometres of plastic tubes that run from tree to tree down to the sugar house, but some small producers still walk through the snow with buckets.

The most important step is boiling. Because sap is mostly water, producers need about forty litres of it to make a single litre of syrup. The sap is heated in a long, flat pan, and clouds of sweet steam rise through the roof of the sugar house. Slowly the liquid becomes thicker and darker. The person in charge must watch it carefully: a few minutes too long and the syrup turns into sugar; a few minutes too short and it will go bad in the bottle.

For people in Quebec, the season is also a time for a party. Families and groups of friends visit a cabane à sucre, or sugar shack, where they sit at long wooden tables and eat a huge, heavy meal: pea soup, eggs, beans, ham and pancakes, with maple syrup poured over almost everything. The favourite part for children comes outside. Hot syrup is poured in lines onto clean snow, where it cools into a soft, sticky toffee. Children roll it up on a wooden stick and eat it straight away.

Quebec produces roughly seventy per cent of the world's maple syrup, and the province takes this business seriously. Producers sell through a central organisation, which even keeps a large reserve of syrup in storage. In good years, extra barrels go into the reserve, and in bad years they come out, so prices stay fairly steady.

Still, the future worries some producers. Warmer winters may change the pattern of freezing nights and mild days, and in some areas the season already seems to start earlier than before. Scientists are studying how the forests will react. For now, though, every spring the buckets fill again, the steam rises over the trees, and the smell of hot syrup tells everyone that winter is finally over.

questions.q: What kind of weather makes the sap flow?
options: Freezing nights followed by days above freezing
Long periods of warm, dry weather
Heavy rain at the end of winter
Very cold days and very cold nights
questions.explain: Özsu akışı için geceleri donma noktasının altında, gündüzleri üstünde hava gerekir; doğru cevap 'Freezing nights followed by days above freezing'.

questions.q: Why does Quebec keep a reserve of maple syrup?
options: To give it to children at sugar shacks
Because the syrup tastes better after many years
Because the law forbids selling it abroad
To keep prices fairly steady between good and bad years
questions.explain: İyi yıllarda fazla variller stoğa girer, kötü yıllarda çıkar; böylece fiyatlar sabit kalır. Doğru cevap 'To keep prices fairly steady between good and bad years'.

title: Drawing with Hot Wax
text:
In a small workshop in Yogyakarta, on the Indonesian island of Java, a woman sits on a low stool in front of a piece of white cotton. Next to her, a little pot of wax is warming over a fire. She dips a tiny copper tool into the pot, blows on it gently, and begins to draw. A thin line of hot wax runs across the cloth, forming the edge of a leaf. She will work like this, line by line, for several weeks.

This is batik, one of the best-known textile arts of Indonesia. The idea behind it is simple, even if the work is not. Wax does not let dye pass through it. So wherever the artist puts wax, the cloth stays the original colour. When the cloth is dipped into a dye bath, only the uncovered parts change colour.

To make a pattern with several colours, the process is repeated many times. First, the artist covers every part that should stay white. Then the cloth goes into the first dye, perhaps a light yellow. After it dries, she covers the parts that should stay yellow and dips it into a darker colour, such as brown or blue. At the end, the cloth is put into boiling water, the wax melts away, and the full design appears. The fine cracks in the wax often let a little dye through, leaving thin lines that many people see as the mark of real, hand-made batik.

The copper tool is called a canting. It has a small cup for the wax and a thin spout, a little like a tiny teapot on a handle. Good batik artists own several, with spouts of different sizes for thick and thin lines. In the nineteenth century, workshops also began using copper stamps to print wax onto the cloth. This was much faster, and it made batik cheaper and more common, but hand-drawn pieces are still considered the most valuable.

Traditional patterns carry meaning. Some designs were once worn only by members of the royal courts of central Java. One famous example is parang, a pattern of diagonal lines that some compare to waves or to a knife. Other regions developed their own styles. Batik from the northern coast of Java, where traders from China, India, Arabia and Europe arrived, is often brighter and uses flowers, birds and even ships.

In Indonesia, batik is far from a museum object. People wear it to weddings, to job interviews and to the office; some companies ask their staff to wear batik on Fridays. Babies are carried in batik slings, and in some traditions people are buried wrapped in batik. In 2009, UNESCO added Indonesian batik to its list of intangible cultural heritage, and since then the country has celebrated National Batik Day every year on the second of October.

The craft faces challenges, though. Cheap printed cloth with batik-style patterns is produced in factories and sold at a fraction of the price. Many young people prefer office jobs to sitting over hot wax for weeks. On the other hand, some young designers are bringing new life to the tradition, mixing classic patterns with modern clothes and selling them online.

For the woman in the Yogyakarta workshop, the slow work is not a problem. She says the cloth teaches patience. Each line, she explains, must be drawn only once, because wax cannot be rubbed out.

questions.q: What is the basic idea that makes batik possible?
options: Copper tools change the colour of cotton
Hot water makes dye stronger
Wax stops dye from reaching the parts of the cloth it covers
Patterns are printed by machines in factories
questions.explain: Mum boyanın geçmesine izin vermez; mumlu yerler orijinal rengini korur. Doğru cevap 'Wax stops dye from reaching the parts of the cloth it covers'.

questions.q: According to the text, what is one challenge for batik today?
options: UNESCO has stopped supporting it
Cheap factory cloth with batik-style patterns is sold for much less
People in Indonesia are not allowed to wear it to work
There is no more copper for the tools
questions.explain: Fabrikada üretilen ucuz, batik desenli kumaşlar çok daha düşük fiyata satılıyor; doğru cevap 'Cheap factory cloth with batik-style patterns is sold for much less'.

title: A Doll Inside a Doll
text:
Almost everyone has seen one. You hold a round wooden doll, painted as a smiling woman in a colourful scarf. You twist her in the middle, and she opens into two halves. Inside is a smaller doll, and inside that one is another, and another, until the last tiny doll, often no bigger than a grain of rice, sits in your hand. This is the matryoshka, the Russian nesting doll.

Many people think the matryoshka is very old, but the first one was probably made only around 1890. At that time, a wealthy businessman named Savva Mamontov and his wife supported Russian artists and craftsmen at their country estate of Abramtsevo, near Moscow. They wanted to protect and develop traditional Russian folk art. According to the usual story, a woodworker named Vasily Zvyozdochkin carved the first set, and a painter named Sergey Malyutin designed the decoration. That first set had eight dolls: a girl holding a black rooster, several sisters, a boy, and a baby at the centre.

Where did the idea come from? A popular explanation is that someone brought a set of wooden figures from Japan, where a similar toy may have existed, and the Russian artists were inspired by it. Historians are not completely sure, and some museum workers in Russia and Japan tell slightly different versions. What is clear is that the Russian version quickly took on a character of its own.

The name comes from Matryona, a common name for country women in old Russia. It sounded warm and motherly, and it fitted a toy that held a family inside itself. In 1900, the dolls were shown at the World's Fair in Paris and won a medal. Soon, orders came from abroad, and workshops in several Russian towns began producing them.

Making a good matryoshka is harder than it looks. The wood, usually lime, is cut in winter and left to dry for a long time, sometimes for two years, so that it will not crack later. The smallest doll, which cannot be opened, is turned first on a lathe. Then each larger doll is made to fit around the one before it. The craftsman measures by eye and by hand, and the two halves of each doll must close tightly without forcing. Finally, the dolls are painted, often in bright red, yellow and gold, and covered with a protective layer.

Over the years, the matryoshka has changed with the times. Some sets show scenes from Russian fairy tales; others show famous writers. In the 1990s, sets showing political leaders, one inside the other, became popular with tourists. Today, you can find nesting dolls painted as football players, cats or characters from films.

The doll has also become a useful image in everyday language. Writers use the word to describe a story inside a story, and engineers sometimes talk about a matryoshka design when one part fits neatly inside another. Perhaps this is why the toy is so loved. It is simple enough for a small child, yet it carries a little surprise every time you open it, and it reminds us that there is often more inside than we can see from the outside.

questions.q: Why is the wood for a matryoshka left to dry for a long time?
options: So that the paint will be brighter
So that the wood becomes heavier
So that it will not crack later
So that it smells like the forest
questions.explain: Ahşap daha sonra çatlamasın diye uzun süre, bazen iki yıl kurutulur; doğru cevap 'So that it will not crack later'.

questions.q: What does the text say about where the idea of the doll came from?
options: It certainly came from a Paris toy shop
It is often linked to a Japanese toy, but historians are not completely sure
Savva Mamontov invented it as a child
It was copied from an ancient Russian museum object
questions.explain: Yaygın açıklamaya göre fikir Japonya'dan gelen bir oyuncaktan çıktı, ama tarihçiler emin değil; doğru cevap 'It is often linked to a Japanese toy, but historians are not completely sure'.

title: A Path of Orange Petals
text:
At the end of October, the markets of Mexico turn orange. Farmers arrive with huge bundles of marigolds, and the strong, slightly bitter smell of the flowers fills the streets. Next to them, bakers sell round sweet bread decorated with shapes like bones, and small shops display skulls made of sugar, each with a name written on its forehead. The country is getting ready for the Day of the Dead.

Despite its name, the Day of the Dead, or Día de Muertos, is not a sad or frightening festival. It is held mainly on the first and second of November, and its central idea is that the dead come back for a short visit to the world of the living. Families prepare to welcome them as honoured guests, with their favourite food, music and stories.

The heart of the celebration is the ofrenda, a home altar. Families usually build it on a table covered with a colourful cloth, sometimes with several levels. On it they place photographs of relatives who have died, candles, flowers, and plates of the food and drinks those people loved in life: perhaps a bowl of mole, a few tamales, a bottle of soda or a packet of cigarettes. Paper with cut-out patterns, called papel picado, hangs above the altar and moves in the slightest wind.

The marigolds have a special job. Many people believe that their bright colour and strong smell help the souls find their way home. In some villages, families spread a path of orange petals from the street to the front door, or even from the cemetery to the house. Candles are lit for the same reason, so that the visitors can see the way in the dark.

On the night of the first or second of November, many families go to the cemetery. They clean the graves, decorate them with flowers and candles, and stay there for hours, sometimes all night. People eat, play music, and tell stories about the person they have lost: how he laughed, what she cooked, the funny mistakes they made. Children run between the graves, and the atmosphere is closer to a family picnic than a funeral.

The festival as we know it today is a mixture of traditions. Long before the Spanish arrived in the sixteenth century, peoples such as the Aztecs held ceremonies for the dead. The Spanish brought the Catholic days of All Saints and All Souls, which fall on the same dates. Over the centuries, the two traditions came together, and each region of Mexico developed its own customs.

The famous image of La Catrina, an elegant female skeleton in a large hat, came later. It was drawn in the early twentieth century by the artist José Guadalupe Posada, partly to laugh at rich people who tried to look European. Today, many people paint their faces like her for the festival. In 2008, UNESCO added the indigenous festivity dedicated to the dead to its list of intangible cultural heritage.

Recently, the festival has become popular around the world, especially after it appeared in films. Mexico City even began holding a large parade, which had not been a traditional part of the celebration. Some people worry that the festival is becoming a show for tourists. But in most homes, the old meaning remains: for one night, the people we miss are not forgotten, and they are invited to sit at the table again.

questions.q: Why do some families make a path of marigold petals?
options: To keep animals away from the house
To decorate the street for tourists
Because the petals are used later to make bread
To help the souls of the dead find their way home

options: It was not a traditional part of the celebration
It began with the Aztecs

title: The Jump That Looked Like a Mistake
text:
In the autumn of 1968, tens of thousands of people sat in the Olympic stadium in Mexico City and watched something that looked like a mistake. A tall American student ran towards the high-jump bar, turned his body at the last moment and went over it backwards, head first, with his face looking at the sky. Then he landed on his shoulders and back. Some people laughed, and a few were worried. But the judges checked the bar, and it was still in place. The young man was Dick Fosbury, and his strange jump would soon change the sport for ever.

For most of the twentieth century, high jumpers went over the bar in other ways. In the "scissors" style, they lifted one leg and then the other, almost like stepping over a fence. Later, the "straddle" became the favourite technique of the best athletes. In the straddle, the jumper went over face down, rolling around the bar with one leg leading. It was efficient, but it was also difficult to learn, and it needed a lot of strength.

Fosbury, who grew up in the US state of Oregon, was not very good at the straddle. As a teenager he struggled to clear even modest heights, and he was close to giving up. So he went back to the old scissors style, which felt more natural to him. During competitions, he began to change it little by little. To get higher, he leaned back further and further. After a while, his body was almost flat in the air, with his back towards the bar. He was not following a plan from a book; he was simply listening to his own body.

There was also a practical reason why his style became possible at that time. In the past, jumpers landed in sand or in a low pile of wood chips. Landing on your neck in sand would be very dangerous. But in the 1960s, many schools started to use thick, soft landing mats made of foam. Without them, the new jump would probably never have spread, because no coach would have allowed it.

At first, many coaches did not like what they saw. Some said it looked lazy. Others warned that young athletes would hurt themselves if they copied it. A local newspaper is said to have described Fosbury as looking like a fish flopping in a boat, and the name "Fosbury Flop" stayed. But Fosbury kept winning. At university he improved quickly, and in 1968 he won a place in the US Olympic team.

In Mexico City, the final lasted for hours. One by one, the other jumpers failed and went out. In the end, Fosbury cleared 2.24 metres, a new Olympic record at the time, and won the gold medal. Millions of people saw the jump on television, and young athletes around the world went outside to try it.

The change did not happen overnight. Some of the best jumpers continued to use the straddle into the 1970s. But by the 1980s, almost every top high jumper in the world went over the bar backwards. Scientists later explained part of the reason. When the body bends over the bar in an arch, its centre of mass can stay slightly below the bar, even though each part of the body goes over it. In other words, the jumper does not need to lift the whole body quite as high.

Fosbury himself never competed in another Olympic Games. He became an engineer and later spoke about his jump with humour and modesty. He liked to explain that he had not invented it in a laboratory; it had grown slowly, competition by competition. His story is a reminder that a new idea does not always come from a clever theory. Sometimes it comes from a person who is not good at the usual way and is brave enough to look a little silly.

questions.q: How did Fosbury develop his new style of jumping?
options: A university coach designed it for him after studying science.
He copied it from a book about the straddle technique.
He slowly changed the old scissors style during competitions.
He practised it secretly on sand before the Olympics.
questions.explain: Metne göre Fosbury, kendisine daha doğal gelen eski makas stilini yarışmalarda azar azar değiştirdi; yani doğru cevap "He slowly changed the old scissors style during competitions."

questions.q: Why were soft foam mats important for the new jump?
options: Landing on the back or neck in sand would have been too dangerous.
They made the bar easier to see from the run-up.
Judges required them at the 1968 Olympic Games.
They helped jumpers run faster towards the bar.
questions.explain: Metin, kumda boyun üstüne düşmenin çok tehlikeli olacağını, köpük minderler olmasaydı yeni atlayışın yayılmayacağını söylüyor: "Landing on the back or neck in sand would have been too dangerous."

title: Twenty Minutes in a Paris Basement
text:
On the evening of 28 December 1895, a small group of people paid one franc each and walked down the stairs into a basement room under a café in Paris. The room was called the Indian Salon, and it was part of the Grand Café on the Boulevard des Capucines. There were a few dozen chairs and a white screen at the front. Nobody was quite sure what they were going to see. When the lights went down, a picture appeared on the screen, and then, to everyone's surprise, it began to move.

The show was organised by two brothers from Lyon, Auguste and Louis Lumière. Their father, Antoine, ran a successful factory that made photographic plates, and the brothers had worked in the family business since they were young. Louis in particular was a gifted inventor. In 1895 the brothers patented a machine they called the Cinématographe. It was light enough to carry, and it could do three jobs: it could record moving pictures, print them and project them onto a screen.

Other inventors were working on similar ideas at the same time. In the United States, Thomas Edison's company had built the Kinetoscope, a wooden box with a small window. Only one person at a time could look inside and watch a short film. The Lumières' idea was different and, as it turned out, more powerful. They wanted many people to sit together in the dark and watch the same pictures on a big screen. That shared experience is still at the heart of going to the cinema today.

The programme that night lasted only about twenty minutes. It included ten very short films, each less than a minute long. The first showed workers, many of them women, leaving the Lumière factory at the end of the day. Others showed a baby having breakfast, a blacksmith at work and a gardener who gets wet when a boy steps on his hose. There was no sound and no story in the modern sense. Yet the audience was amazed by small details: leaves moving in the wind, smoke rising, waves breaking on the shore.

A famous legend says that when the brothers showed a film of a train arriving at a station, people screamed and ran to the back of the room. They were afraid, the story goes, that the train would come through the screen. Historians are doubtful about this. The train film was probably not part of the first programme, and there is little evidence that anyone really ran away. Still, the legend tells us something true: for the first audiences, moving pictures felt shockingly real.

News of the show spread quickly. Within weeks, long lines of people were waiting outside the café, and the brothers were giving many shows a day. They trained camera operators and sent them around the world, to cities such as London, New York and Moscow. These operators showed films, but they also filmed local streets and festivals, so audiences could see faraway places for the first time.

Surprisingly, the Lumières did not seem to believe that cinema had a great future. Louis is often quoted as saying that it was "an invention without a future". Whether or not he really said these words, the brothers soon turned their attention back to photography, especially to colour photographs, and left film-making to others. People like Georges Méliès, a magician who is said to have been in the audience in 1895, went on to tell stories with film and to invent special effects.

Today the Lumière brothers are remembered as two of the parents of cinema. Their films are short and simple, but if you watch them now, you may feel a little of what that first audience felt in a dark basement in Paris: the strange pleasure of seeing ordinary life move on a wall.

questions.q: What made the Lumières' machine different from Edison's Kinetoscope?
options: It could record sound as well as pictures.
It allowed many people to watch the same film together on a screen.
It was the first machine that could show colour films.
It was much cheaper because it was made of wood.
questions.explain: Kinetoscope'a aynı anda tek kişi bakabiliyordu; Lumière kardeşler ise çok kişinin karanlıkta birlikte büyük perdeye bakmasını istedi: "It allowed many people to watch the same film together on a screen."

questions.q: What does the text say about the story of people running away from the train?
options: It is proved by many newspaper reports from 1895.
It happened during the gardener film, not the train film.
It was invented by Louis Lumière to sell tickets.
Historians doubt it, but it shows how real the films felt.
questions.explain: Metne göre tarihçiler bu hikâyeden şüphe ediyor, ama efsane ilk izleyicilere filmlerin çok gerçek geldiğini gösteriyor: "Historians doubt it, but it shows how real the films felt."

title: When the Scoreboard Said 1.00
text:
On 18 July 1976, at the Olympic Games in Montreal, a fourteen-year-old girl from Romania finished her routine on the uneven bars, landed cleanly and raised her arms. The crowd cheered. Then everyone turned to look at the scoreboard, and the cheering became confused. The board showed 1.00. For a moment, people did not understand. Had the judges given her a score of one? Then the truth spread through the hall: Nadia Comăneci had received a perfect ten, the first ever awarded in Olympic gymnastics, and the scoreboard simply could not show it.

According to the usual account, the company that made the scoreboard had been told that a perfect score was not going to happen. The board could show only three digits, so the highest number it could display was 9.99. When the judges decided that her routine had no faults at all, the machine showed the ten as 1.00. This small technical failure became one of the most famous images in the history of sport.

Comăneci was born in 1961 in Onești, a small town in the east of Romania. As a little girl she was full of energy, and she liked to climb trees and jump on furniture. When she was about six, a coach named Béla Károlyi visited her school. According to the well-known story, he saw her and a friend doing cartwheels in the schoolyard. When the bell rang, the two girls ran inside before he could find out their names, so he went from class to class looking for them. Whether every detail is true or not, Károlyi did find her, and she began to train at his new gymnastics school.

The training was very hard. Young gymnasts practised for many hours a day, repeating the same movements again and again. Comăneci was known for her concentration. She rarely smiled during competitions, and journalists sometimes described her as serious or cold. But she later explained that she was simply focused on her work. She was not trying to impress people with her face; she wanted her body to be exact.

In Montreal, the first perfect ten was only the beginning. During the Games she received seven perfect scores in total and won three gold medals. One of them was the all-around title, which goes to the best gymnast across all the events. She became the youngest all-around Olympic champion in gymnastics history. Today the rules no longer allow gymnasts that young to compete at the Olympics, so her record is likely to stand.

Her life after Montreal was not easy. Romania at that time was ruled by Nicolae Ceaușescu, and famous athletes were watched closely by the government. She won more medals at the 1980 Olympics in Moscow, but later she was not allowed to travel freely. In late 1989, only weeks before the government fell, she escaped across the border to Hungary at night and then travelled on to the United States. There she later married the American gymnast Bart Conner and started a new life.

Since then, the sport itself has changed. In 2006, gymnastics replaced the old system, in which ten was the highest score, with a new one that has no upper limit. Some fans miss the perfect ten, because everyone could understand it immediately. Others say the new system is fairer, because it rewards difficult routines more clearly.

Either way, the image of that scoreboard remains. It shows a moment when a young athlete went beyond what the people who designed the machine had expected. Sometimes progress means doing something so well that the old tools cannot measure it.

questions.q: Why did the scoreboard show 1.00?
options: The judges made a mistake and gave her a very low score.
Her routine had one small fault, so she lost nine points.
Gymnastics scores at that time were always shown as numbers below two.
It could only show three digits and was not ready for a ten.
questions.explain: Tabela yalnızca üç basamak gösterebiliyordu ve en yüksek 9.99 yazabiliyordu, bu yüzden 10 puanı 1.00 olarak çıktı: "It could only show three digits and was not ready for a ten."

questions.q: Why does the text say that her record as the youngest all-around champion is likely to stand?
options: Nobody has received a perfect ten since 1976.
Gymnasts of her age are no longer allowed to compete at the Olympics.
The all-around title no longer exists in gymnastics.
Romania stopped sending gymnasts to the Olympics after 1989.
questions.explain: Metne göre bugünkü kurallar o yaştaki cimnastikçilerin olimpiyatlarda yarışmasına izin vermiyor: "Gymnasts of her age are no longer allowed to compete at the Olympics."

title: Two Peach Baskets and a Football
titleTr: İki Şeftali Sepeti ve Bir Top
text:
In December 1891, a young teacher in the American city of Springfield, Massachusetts, had a difficult problem. Winter had arrived, and the students at his college could no longer play sports outside. Indoors, they did exercises and marched around the gym, and they were bored. Some of them were becoming angry and hard to manage. The head of the department gave the teacher a clear task: invent a new game that could be played inside, in a small hall, during the cold months. He had about two weeks.

The teacher was James Naismith, a Canadian who had grown up on a farm in Ontario. He had lost both of his parents when he was a child and was raised partly by an uncle. As a boy, he had played a simple outdoor game in which children tried to knock a small stone off a large rock by throwing other stones at it. Players soon learned that a soft, high throw worked better than a hard, straight one. Years later, this memory would help him.

Naismith thought carefully about the games he already knew. Football and rugby were too rough for a wooden floor, because players tackled each other and fell hard. He decided that his game should have very little physical contact. Players would not be allowed to run while holding the ball; they would have to pass it. And instead of a goal on the ground, which players could protect with their bodies, the goal would be high above their heads. To score, a player would need skill and a gentle throw rather than strength.

When Naismith asked the building manager for two boxes to use as goals, the man did not have any. He offered two old peach baskets instead. Naismith nailed them to the railing of a balcony at each end of the gym, about three metres above the floor. That height is still the standard height of a basketball hoop today. He wrote thirteen simple rules, and a secretary typed them on two pages, which he pinned to the wall.

The first game, played with an ordinary football, was not a great show. There were nine players on each side, and many of them did not yet understand the rules. According to most accounts, only one goal was scored, so the final result was 1–0. There was also a practical problem: the baskets still had their bottoms. Every time someone scored, a person had to climb up and take the ball out. Only some years later were the baskets replaced by metal rings with open nets.

Even so, the students loved the game. They took it home to their towns during the holidays, and it spread through the network of similar colleges in the United States and other countries. Within a few months, women were playing too. A teacher named Senda Berenson changed some of the rules for her female students, and women's basketball grew at almost the same speed as the men's game. Someone suggested calling the new sport "Naismith ball", but Naismith himself is said to have laughed at the idea. The name basketball, he thought, described it well enough.

Naismith did not become rich from his invention, and he never tried to. He later trained as a doctor and worked for many years at the University of Kansas, where he coached the basketball team. Interestingly, he is often described as the only coach in the history of that university with more losing seasons than winning ones. For him, sport was mainly about health and character, not about winning.

In 1936, basketball was played at the Olympic Games in Berlin for the first time. Naismith, then in his seventies, travelled to Germany to watch. The final was played outdoors on a court of clay and sand, and heavy rain turned it into mud. It was hardly the elegant game we see today, but the old teacher was reportedly very proud. The game he had invented in two weeks, with two fruit baskets and a borrowed ball, had reached the whole world.

questions.q: Why did Naismith put the goals high above the players' heads?
options: So that scoring would need skill and a soft throw, not strength.
Because the building manager wanted to keep the floor free.
Because the peach baskets were too heavy to stand on the ground.
So that the audience on the balcony could catch the ball.
questions.explain: Naismith, yerdeki bir kaleyi oyuncular vücutlarıyla koruyabileceği için kaleyi yukarı koydu; böylece gol için güç değil beceri ve yumuşak atış gerekecekti: "So that scoring would need skill and a soft throw, not strength."

questions.q: What practical problem did the first game have?
options: The football was too small for the baskets.
There were not enough players to make two teams.
Someone had to climb up and take the ball out after every goal.
The rules were written in a language the students did not know.
questions.explain: Sepetlerin dibi hâlâ yerindeydi, bu yüzden her golden sonra birinin yukarı tırmanıp topu çıkarması gerekiyordu: "Someone had to climb up and take the ball out after every goal."

title: Listening with Bare Feet
text:
When Evelyn Glennie walks onto a concert stage, she usually takes off her shoes. People in the audience sometimes think this is a fashion choice or a sign of an artist's free spirit. In fact, the reason is more practical. Glennie, one of the best-known percussionists in the world, has been profoundly deaf since the age of about twelve, and she says she feels a great deal of the music through her feet and the rest of her body.

Glennie grew up on a farm in the north-east of Scotland. As a child she loved music and learned the piano. But when she was around eight, her hearing began to get worse because of nerve damage. By her early teens, she could hear very little. Doctors suggested special hearing aids and a school for deaf children. Many people around her assumed that her musical life was over.

Glennie did not accept this. At school, she became interested in the percussion instruments: drums, xylophones and the timpani, the large kettle-shaped drums of an orchestra. A teacher named Ron Forbes helped her to discover something important. He asked her to put her hands on the wall of the practice room while he played two timpani tuned to different notes. Slowly she realised that she could feel the difference. A low note seemed to vibrate in her legs and feet, while a higher note was felt in her face, neck and chest. Hearing, she began to think, is not only something that happens in the ears.

Her next challenge was getting into a music college. When she applied to the Royal Academy of Music in London, there were doubts about whether a deaf student could follow the course. According to her own account, the academy changed the way it auditioned students and decided to judge applicants on their playing, not on their medical history. She was accepted, and she graduated with high marks.

At that time, there was a problem with her plan to be a solo percussionist: the job hardly existed. Orchestras had percussion players at the back, but very few concerts had a percussionist standing at the front like a violin or piano soloist. There was simply not enough music for it. So Glennie began asking composers to write new works for her. Over the following decades, she commissioned and performed a huge number of new pieces. Today young percussionists study music that did not exist before she asked for it.

Glennie has often said that she does not like it when newspapers describe her as "the deaf percussionist", as if her deafness were the most interesting thing about her. She points out that every musician listens in a personal way. For her, listening means using her whole body. She watches the movements of other players, feels vibrations through the floor and pays attention to the tiny changes in the instrument under her hands. She even argues that everybody could become better listeners if they paid more attention to touch and vibration.

Her work has received many awards. She has been honoured by the British state, and she played at the opening ceremony of the 2012 Olympic Games in London, leading a large group of drummers in front of a huge television audience. She has also spent years teaching and speaking about her wish to teach the world to listen.

Glennie's career is a story about talent and hard work, but it is also a story about questions. What does it mean to hear? Who decides what a disabled person can or cannot do? By standing on stage with bare feet, she has shown audiences that music can reach people by more than one road.

questions.q: What did Glennie learn when she put her hands on the wall?
options: That the practice room was too small for timpani.
That her hearing was slowly coming back.
That she could feel different notes in different parts of her body.
That low notes were impossible for her to notice.

questions.q: Why did Glennie ask composers to write new pieces?
options: She could not read the old music because of her deafness.
Orchestras refused to let her play at the back.
The Royal Academy of Music asked her to do it as a student.
There was very little music for a solo percussionist.

title: On the Tip of the Tongue
text:
You are telling a friend about a film you saw last year. You can see the main actor's face clearly. You know he was also in a famous war film, and you are almost sure his name starts with a B. But the name itself will not come. It is right there, on the tip of your tongue, and yet you cannot say it. A few hours later, while you are washing the dishes, the name suddenly appears in your head, and you have nobody to tell.

This experience is so common that scientists have studied it for more than fifty years. In 1966, two psychologists at Harvard University, Roger Brown and David McNeill, decided to create the feeling on purpose. They read out the definitions of rare words to a group of students. For example, they described an instrument that sailors once used to measure the position of the sun and stars. Many students knew that they knew the word, but they could not find it. While they were in this state, the researchers asked them questions. Which letter does it start with? How many syllables does it have? What does it sound like?

The answers were surprising. The students were often right about the first letter and the number of syllables, even though the word itself was missing. Some offered words that sounded similar, such as 'secant' or 'sextet' for the word 'sextant'. So the memory was not completely lost. Parts of it were available, like the outline of a picture with the colours missing.

Today most researchers explain the feeling in a simple way. When we speak, our brain does two jobs. First it finds the meaning of the word we want, and then it finds the sounds that go with that meaning. Usually these two steps happen so quickly that we never notice them. In a tip-of-the-tongue moment, the first step works but the second step fails. We have the meaning, and even a little of the sound, but the link between them is too weak at that moment.

Several things seem to make these moments more frequent. Names of people and places are the most common problem, probably because a name has no meaning that helps us reach it. The word 'baker' is connected to bread, ovens and early mornings, but the name 'Baker' is connected to almost nothing. Tiredness and stress also play a part. And the moments become more common as people get older. Older adults often worry that this is a sign of a serious memory problem, but research suggests that it is usually normal. Older people also know many more words, so their brain simply has more to search through.

There is also an annoying side to the experience. Once you get stuck on a word, you are more likely to get stuck on the same word again in the future. It seems that every failed search makes the wrong path a little stronger. Some researchers suggest a small trick to avoid this. When the word finally comes back, say it aloud or repeat it to yourself a few times. This strengthens the right connection.

What should you do when you are stuck? Trying harder does not always help, because the wrong words keep coming back. Thinking about the first letter, or saying the alphabet slowly, sometimes works. But often the best advice is the hardest to follow: stop looking. Go and wash the dishes. The word will probably find you.

questions.q: What did Brown and McNeill find when students could not remember a word?
options: The students had forgotten the meaning of the word completely
The students often knew the first letter and the number of syllables
The students remembered better when they were tired
The students could always find the word by saying the alphabet
questions.explain: Öğrenciler kelimeyi bulamasalar da çoğu zaman ilk harfini ve hece sayısını doğru biliyordu; yani doğru cevap 'The students often knew the first letter and the number of syllables'.

questions.q: Why are names especially hard to remember, according to the text?
options: They are usually longer than other words
They are learned later in life
They have no meaning that helps us reach them
They are rarely used in conversation
questions.explain: Metne göre isimlerin bizi ona götürecek bir anlamı yoktur; 'baker' kelimesi ekmeğe, fırına bağlıyken 'Baker' ismi neredeyse hiçbir şeye bağlı değildir. Doğru cevap 'They have no meaning that helps us reach them'.

title: Tiny Hills on Your Skin
text:
Think of the last time you stepped out of a warm shower into a cold bathroom, or heard a piece of music that moved you deeply. You may have noticed small bumps rising on your arms, and the hairs on your skin standing up. In English, these bumps are called goosebumps, because the skin looks like the skin of a bird after its feathers have been removed. In Turkish, people say that their hairs are standing up like thorns.

Goosebumps are made by very small muscles. Each hair on your body grows from a tiny hole in the skin, and next to each one there is a muscle thinner than a thread. When this muscle tightens, it pulls the hair upright and pushes up the skin around it. You cannot control these muscles yourself. They are controlled by the same part of the nervous system that makes your heart beat faster when you are afraid.

For our distant ancestors, who had much more hair, this reaction was useful in two ways. First, it helped them stay warm. When hair stands up, it traps a layer of air close to the skin, and this air acts like a blanket. Birds do the same thing on cold days, which is why they look bigger and rounder in winter. Second, it helped them look larger. A cat that meets a dog raises the hair on its back, and suddenly it seems bigger and more dangerous. A frightened animal with its hair up is sending a clear message: think twice before you attack me.

Humans have lost most of their body hair, so goosebumps no longer keep us warm or make us look frightening. For a long time, scientists thought the reaction was simply left over from the past, like a door that still exists in a house even though the room behind it has gone. But a study published in 2020 by researchers at Harvard University suggested a different story. Working with mice, they found that the tiny hair muscle and the nerve that controls it also support special cells in the skin. These cells are responsible for growing new hair. When the mice were kept in the cold for a long time, the system did not only lift the hair. It also seemed to help them grow thicker fur. If something similar happens in humans, goosebumps may still have a quiet job to do.

Then there is the strangest kind of goosebumps: the kind that comes from emotion. Many people feel a shiver when a choir reaches a high note, when a film hero returns home, or when they hear a speech that touches them. Some researchers have studied this using music. They found that only some people get these feelings regularly, and that these people may be more open to new experiences. Brain scans have shown that areas linked to reward become active during these moments, the same areas that respond to good food.

Why should a beautiful song produce the same reaction as a cold wind or an angry dog? Nobody knows for sure. One idea is that powerful music works a little like a sudden change in the world around us. It surprises the body and wakes it up, and the old system answers in the only way it knows.

So the next time the hairs on your arm stand up during a song, you can enjoy a small piece of history. Your body is reacting as if you were a furry animal on a cold night, even when you are only sitting in a concert hall.

It made the skin produce more sweat

It changed the colour of the skin

title: Brain Freeze
text:
It is a hot summer afternoon, and you are eating ice cream a little too fast. Suddenly a sharp pain shoots across your forehead. For a few seconds it is so strong that you close your eyes and stop moving. Then, almost as quickly as it came, it disappears. Doctors have a long name for this experience, but most people simply call it 'brain freeze'.

The name is a little misleading, because your brain does not actually freeze. It does not even feel pain directly, since the brain itself has no pain sensors. The pain comes from the area around it. The story starts in the roof of your mouth. When something very cold touches the back of it, the blood vessels there react quickly to the sudden change in temperature. First they become narrower, and then they open wide again as the body tries to warm the area up. This rush of blood seems to be what causes the pain.

But why do you feel it in your forehead and not in your mouth? The answer lies in a large nerve in the face. This nerve carries messages from the mouth, the eyes and the forehead to the brain. When it sends a sudden alarm from the roof of the mouth, the brain is not very good at telling exactly where the message came from. It makes a guess, and the guess is often the forehead. This is called referred pain. Something similar happens during a heart attack, when some people feel pain in their left arm or jaw, far from the heart itself.

In 2012, a small study in the United States tried to watch a brain freeze as it happened. Researchers asked thirteen adults to drink ice water through a straw, pressed against the roof of the mouth. At the same time, they measured the blood flow in the brain. When the pain began, the flow of blood in one important artery increased quickly. When it went back to normal, the pain went away too. The researchers suggested that the brain may be protecting itself. It is a very important and sensitive organ, so it may try to keep itself warm by bringing in extra blood. The sudden increase in pressure inside the head may then cause the pain. The study was small, so its results should be treated with care, but it gave a clear picture of the process.

Interestingly, not everyone gets brain freeze. Some studies have found that only about a third of people experience it, while others report higher numbers. People who suffer from migraines, a type of strong and long headache, seem to get brain freeze more often. This suggests that the two kinds of pain may share some of the same paths in the body.

The good news is that brain freeze is completely harmless, and it is easy to stop. The simplest method is to warm the roof of your mouth. You can press your tongue against it, or drink some water that is warm or at room temperature. You can also hold your hands over your mouth and nose and breathe out, so that warm air fills your mouth. Most of the time, the pain will be gone in less than a minute anyway.

Of course, the best solution is to avoid the problem in the first place. Eat slowly, keep cold food at the front of your mouth for a moment, and let it warm up a little before you swallow. Then you can enjoy your ice cream without any surprises.

questions.q: Why do people feel the pain of brain freeze in the forehead?
options: Because the forehead gets cold before the mouth
Because the brain really freezes for a few seconds
Because the brain guesses wrongly where the nerve's message came from
Because the ice cream touches the eyes

title: I Know Your Face, But…
text:
You walk into a shop and someone smiles at you. You know that face. You are sure you have met this person before, perhaps at a wedding or at your child's school. You smile back and chat about the weather, but the whole time you are desperately searching for a name. It never comes. Afterwards you feel a little embarrassed, and you wonder whether something is wrong with your memory.

Probably nothing is wrong. Forgetting names while remembering faces is one of the most common memory problems, and psychologists have a good explanation for it. They often describe it with a clever puzzle that is sometimes called the Baker–baker effect. In studies of this kind, people are shown photographs of strangers. Some volunteers are told that the man in the photo is called Mr Baker. Others are told that he is a baker. Later, when they see the same face again, the people who heard about his job remember the word much better than the people who heard his name, even though the word is exactly the same.

Why should the same word be easy to remember in one case and hard in the other? The answer lies in the way memory works. Memory is not like a box where we put things and take them out again. It is more like a web, where each new piece of information is tied to many others. When you learn that a man is a baker, your brain connects him to a whole world of things you already know: the smell of fresh bread, white clothes, flour, early mornings, a warm shop. Each of these connections is a path that can lead you back to the word later. But when you learn that his name is Baker, there is nothing to connect it to. The name is just a sound attached to a face. There is only one thin path, and it is easy to lose.

Faces, on the other hand, are something our brains are very good at. From the first days of life, babies pay special attention to faces. Adults can recognise thousands of them, often after many years. Some parts of the brain seem to be especially involved in this job. So when you meet someone, the face is stored easily, while the name, with its single weak thread, often slips away.

There is another problem, too. When we are introduced to someone, we are often busy. We are thinking about what to say, whether we look nice, or how to shake hands. The name is spoken only once, at the very moment our attention is somewhere else. In many cases, the name was never stored in the first place, so there is nothing to forget.

Fortunately, there are some simple ways to improve. The first is to pay attention at the moment of introduction and to use the name soon afterwards: 'Nice to meet you, Selin.' Saying it aloud gives the memory a second chance. The second is to turn the name into something with meaning, so that it has more connections. If you meet a man called Mr Demir, you might imagine him holding a piece of iron. If you meet a woman called Rose, you might picture a rose in her hair. The picture can be silly; in fact, silly pictures often work best.

Finally, be kind to yourself. Even people with excellent memories forget names. And the person you met in the shop may well have forgotten yours, too.

questions.q: Why is it easier to remember that a man is a baker than that his name is Baker?
options: The job is connected to many things we already know
Jobs are always shorter words than names
People hear about jobs more often than names
The photos of bakers in the studies were clearer
questions.explain: Fırıncı olmak ekmek, un, sabahın erken saatleri gibi zaten bildiğimiz pek çok şeye bağlanır; isim ise sadece bir yüze iliştirilmiş bir sestir. Doğru cevap 'The job is connected to many things we already know'.

questions.q: According to the text, why is a name sometimes never stored at all?
options: Because names are spoken too slowly
Because our attention is on other things when we hear it
Because faces take up all the space in our memory
Because we meet too many people every day
questions.explain: Tanışırken ne diyeceğimizi, nasıl göründüğümüzü düşünürüz; isim dikkatimiz başka yerdeyken bir kez söylenir. Doğru cevap 'Because our attention is on other things when we hear it'.

title: Why You Cannot Tickle Yourself
text:
Try a small experiment. Lift your hand and gently move your fingers along the bottom of your foot, or under your arm. You will probably feel the touch, but you will not laugh, and you will not pull away. Now imagine a friend or a brother doing exactly the same thing. For many people, the result is completely different: they scream, laugh and try to escape. Why is a touch from another person so powerful, while our own touch feels almost like nothing?

Scientists have been interested in this question for a long time, and the answer tells us something important about how the brain works. Our brain is not just waiting for information to arrive from the body. It is constantly making predictions about what is going to happen next. Every time you decide to move, your brain sends a command to your muscles. At the same time, it seems to make a copy of that command and uses it to predict what you will feel. When the feeling arrives, the brain compares it with the prediction. If the two match, the feeling is turned down, like the volume on a radio.

This explains why you cannot surprise yourself with a tickle. Your brain knows exactly where your fingers will go and how hard they will press, so the touch is expected and weak. When someone else tickles you, nothing is predicted. The touch comes as a surprise, and surprise seems to be a large part of what makes tickling so intense.

In the late 1990s, a team at University College London, led by Sarah-Jayne Blakemore, tested this idea with a clever machine. Volunteers held a small handle connected to a robot. When they moved the handle, a soft piece of foam moved across the palm of their other hand. Because they were controlling it, the touch did not feel very ticklish. Then the researchers made the robot wait a fraction of a second before it moved, or move at a slightly different angle. The longer the delay and the bigger the difference, the more ticklish the touch felt. When the movement no longer matched the brain's prediction, the brain no longer turned it down.

This system is very useful in daily life. Imagine how difficult it would be if every movement of your own body felt as strong as a stranger's touch. You would jump every time your arm touched your leg, or your clothes moved against your skin. By turning down the feelings we cause ourselves, the brain leaves more attention for things that come from outside, and these are often the things that matter, such as an insect on your neck or a hand on your shoulder.

Interestingly, some research suggests that the system does not work in the same way for everyone. In certain illnesses, such as some forms of schizophrenia, people may have trouble telling which actions are their own. Some studies have found that these people rate their own touch as more ticklish than other people do. This may help explain why some patients feel that their thoughts or movements are being controlled from outside.

So, although you cannot tickle yourself, you can still learn something from trying. Each time your own fingers fail to make you laugh, your brain is quietly showing you how good it is at predicting the future, at least a fraction of a second ahead.

questions.q: What does the brain do with the copy of a movement command?
options: It sends it to the other hand
It stores it as a long-term memory
It makes the muscles stronger
It uses it to predict what you will feel
questions.explain: Beyin, kaslara gönderdiği komutun bir kopyasını ne hissedeceğimizi önceden kestirmek için kullanır. Doğru cevap 'It uses it to predict what you will feel'.

questions.q: In the robot experiment, when did the touch feel most ticklish?
options: When the volunteers moved the handle very fast
When the robot did not move at all
When there was a longer delay or a bigger difference in angle
When the volunteers closed their eyes

title: The Stone That Spoke Three Languages
text:
In the summer of 1799, a group of French soldiers was repairing an old fort near the town of Rashid, which Europeans called Rosetta, in the Nile Delta of Egypt. Napoleon's army had arrived in Egypt the year before, and it had brought not only soldiers but also scientists, artists and mapmakers. While the men were pulling down an old wall, one of them noticed a large dark stone covered in writing. An officer named Pierre-François Bouchard understood that it might be important, and he sent it to the scholars in Cairo.

The stone was about a metre high and very heavy. Its surface was divided into three parts, and each part was written in a different script. The top part used Egyptian hieroglyphs, the small pictures of birds, eyes, snakes and people that cover the walls of ancient temples. The middle part used another Egyptian script called Demotic, which was used for everyday documents. The bottom part was in ancient Greek, a language that many European scholars could read easily.

This was the exciting part. When the scholars translated the Greek text, they discovered that it was a decree, an official announcement, made by a group of priests in 196 BC in honour of the young king Ptolemy V. At the end, the text said that the decree should be written in three scripts. In other words, the three parts probably said the same thing. If that was true, the Greek could be a key to the hieroglyphs, which nobody had been able to read for almost 1,500 years.

The stone did not stay with the French for long. After the British defeated the French army in Egypt, the stone became British property under an agreement signed in 1801. It was shipped to London and has been in the British Museum since 1802. Copies of the text, however, were sent to scholars all over Europe, and the race to read the hieroglyphs began.

For a long time, many experts believed that every hieroglyph was a symbol for an idea, not a sound. This belief made progress very slow. The English scientist Thomas Young made an important step when he noticed that some hieroglyphs were placed inside oval rings. He suggested that these rings, now called cartouches, held the names of kings, and he worked out some of the signs in the name Ptolemy.

The real breakthrough came from a young Frenchman, Jean-François Champollion. He had been fascinated by Egypt since childhood, and he had learned many languages, including Coptic, a late form of the Egyptian language that was still used in some church services. Champollion compared the names of Ptolemy and Cleopatra in cartouches and found that the shared letters matched the same signs. Slowly, he understood that hieroglyphs were a mixed system: some signs stood for sounds, and others stood for whole words or ideas. His knowledge of Coptic helped him guess how many words were pronounced.

In September 1822, Champollion announced his results in a famous letter to the French Academy. A well-known story says that when he finally understood the system, he ran into his brother's office, shouted that he had done it, and then fainted from excitement. Nobody can be sure that the story is completely true, but it shows how much the discovery meant to him.

Today the Rosetta Stone is one of the most visited objects in the British Museum, and it is often surrounded by crowds taking photos. Its name has also become a common expression. When people call something “a Rosetta Stone”, they mean a key that suddenly makes a difficult problem understandable. Egypt has asked for the stone to be returned, so its story is not finished yet.

questions.q: Why was the Greek part of the stone so useful?
options: It was written by Napoleon’s scientists.
It explained how to pronounce Coptic words.
It listed the names of all the Egyptian kings.
It probably said the same thing as the two Egyptian parts.

questions.q: What did Champollion understand about hieroglyphs?
options: Each sign was only a symbol for an idea.
Some signs stood for sounds and others for words or ideas.
They were the same as the Demotic script.
They could only be read by priests.
