title: The Boys Who Found a Painted Cave
text:
In September 1940, France was in the middle of the Second World War, but in the quiet hills near the village of Montignac, in south-west France, four teenagers were looking for adventure. The oldest, Marcel Ravidat, was eighteen. A few days earlier, he had noticed a hole in the ground where a tree had fallen many years before. According to a popular version of the story, his dog, Robot, had disappeared into the hole while chasing a rabbit. Other versions do not mention the dog at all, but everyone agrees that Marcel came back with his friends to explore.

On 12 September, the boys made the hole wider with knives and sticks and slid down into the darkness. They had only a simple oil lamp. When they lifted it, they saw something they would never forget. Across the walls and the ceiling, there were huge animals painted in red, yellow, brown and black: horses, deer, cattle and enormous bulls, some of them more than five metres long. The animals seemed to run across the rock in the moving light.

The boys understood that they had found something special, and at first they tried to keep it a secret. Soon, however, they told their teacher, who contacted experts. One of them was the priest and scholar Henri Breuil, who was famous for his work on prehistoric art. He visited the cave within days and was amazed. He later described it as one of the most important caves of its kind.

Scientists now believe that the paintings at Lascaux are about 17,000 years old. They were made by hunter-gatherers who lived during the last ice age. The cave contains around 600 paintings and about 1,500 engravings, which are pictures cut into the rock. The artists used natural colours made from minerals and charcoal. They probably blew some colours through hollow bones or tubes, and they used the natural shape of the rock to give the animals a sense of movement and depth.

Why did they paint these animals? Nobody really knows. Some researchers think the pictures were part of hunting rituals. Others think they were connected to stories, seasons or the stars. Interestingly, the reindeer, which people at that time often ate, appears only once or twice on the walls. This suggests that the paintings were not simply a list of the animals people hunted for food.

After the war, Lascaux opened to visitors in 1948, and it became extremely popular. On some days, more than a thousand people walked through the narrow passages. Unfortunately, their breath and body heat changed the air inside. The carbon dioxide, warmth and moisture damaged the paintings, and green mould and white crystals started to grow on the walls. In 1963, the French government closed the cave to the public. Today only a few scientists may enter, and only for short periods.

To let people experience the cave again, France built copies. Lascaux II, a careful copy of the main rooms, opened in 1983, and a larger, more modern copy called Lascaux IV opened in 2016. Visitors walk through cool, dark rooms and see the bulls and horses just as the four boys saw them.

And what happened to the boys? Two of them, Marcel Ravidat and Jacques Marsal, stayed close to the cave for many years, guarding it and showing visitors around. Their discovery, made by chance on an ordinary autumn day, changed what the world knew about the minds of our early ancestors.

questions.q: Why was Lascaux closed to the public in 1963?
options: The French government needed it during the war.
The four boys asked for it to be closed.
Visitors’ breath and body heat were damaging the paintings.
Scientists discovered that the paintings were copies.
questions.explain: Ziyaretçilerin nefesi ve vücut ısısı mağaradaki havayı değiştirdi, resimler zarar gördü ve küf oluştu. Doğru cevap “Visitors’ breath and body heat were damaging the paintings.”

questions.q: What does the small number of reindeer pictures suggest?
options: The paintings were not just pictures of the animals people ate.
Reindeer did not live in France during the ice age.
The artists were afraid of reindeer.
The reindeer pictures were destroyed by visitors.
questions.explain: İnsanlar o dönemde ren geyiğini sık yediği hâlde duvarlarda ren geyiği neredeyse yok; bu da resimlerin yalnızca avlanan hayvanların listesi olmadığını gösteriyor. Doğru cevap “The paintings were not just pictures of the animals people ate.”

title: An Army Under the Fields
text:
In the spring of 1974, during a dry year in northern China, a group of farmers near the city of Xi'an decided to dig a well. Water was scarce, and their crops needed it badly. The men dug for several days through the hard yellow earth. At a depth of a few metres, one of them, Yang Zhifa, hit something hard. It was a piece of baked clay shaped like a human head. Soon the farmers found broken arms, bodies and old bronze arrowheads.

At first, the farmers did not realise what they had found. Some local people had found strange clay pieces in the area before and believed they brought bad luck. This time, however, a local official saw the pieces and contacted archaeologists. When the experts arrived, they quickly understood that the well had reached the edge of one of the greatest archaeological sites in the world.

The pieces belonged to a huge army of life-size clay soldiers. They had been made more than 2,200 years ago for Qin Shi Huang, the first emperor to unite China. He came to power as a young king and, after years of war, joined several rival states into one empire in 221 BC. He also introduced the same money, weights and writing across his lands. Like many rulers, however, he was afraid of death. He started building his tomb when he was still a boy, and the work continued for decades.

The soldiers were placed in long pits in battle order, facing east, as if they were protecting the emperor in the next life. Archaeologists believe there are around 8,000 soldiers, together with hundreds of horses and many wooden chariots. The figures were made in parts, probably in workshops, and then put together. Their faces, hair and clothes differ, and some experts think that no two faces are exactly the same. Some soldiers are archers, some are officers and some are drivers of chariots. They once held real bronze weapons, and many of these weapons are still sharp.

Today the soldiers are the colour of earth, but this was not their original look. They were once painted in bright colours, such as red, green, blue and purple. When the figures are dug out, the paint meets the dry air and often begins to curl and fall off within minutes. For this reason, archaeologists now work very slowly, and large parts of the site have been left untouched until better methods are developed.

The biggest mystery is the emperor's own tomb, which lies under a large hill not far from the pits. It has never been opened. About a hundred years after the emperor's death, the historian Sima Qian wrote that the tomb contained a model of the empire with rivers of mercury, a liquid metal. Many people thought this was just a legend, but modern tests have found unusually high levels of mercury in the soil of the hill. The Chinese government has decided not to open the tomb for now, partly because no one is sure how to protect what lies inside.

The farmers' discovery changed their village. A large museum opened at the site in 1979, and millions of tourists now visit every year. Yang Zhifa, the man who first hit the clay head, later spent years at the museum shop, signing books for visitors. He had gone looking for water and found an army instead.

questions.q: Why do archaeologists dig out the soldiers very slowly?
options: The bright paint can fall off soon after it meets the air.
The government allows only one soldier a year.
The soldiers are too heavy to lift quickly.
The farmers still use the land for their crops.
questions.explain: Heykeller topraktan çıkarıldığında boya kuru havayla karşılaşıp dakikalar içinde kıvrılıp dökülebiliyor. Doğru cevap “The bright paint can fall off soon after it meets the air.”

questions.q: What have modern tests found in the soil of the emperor’s tomb hill?
options: Pieces of painted clay heads
Bronze weapons that are still sharp
The remains of a farmers’ well
Unusually high levels of mercury
questions.explain: Sima Qian mezarda cıva nehirleri olduğunu yazmıştı; modern testler tepenin toprağında olağandışı yüksek cıva düzeyi buldu. Doğru cevap “Unusually high levels of mercury”.

title: The King’s Ship Comes Home
text:
On a summer evening in July 1545, King Henry VIII of England stood on the shore near Portsmouth and watched his fleet sail out to meet a French invasion force. One of his favourite ships was the Mary Rose, a large warship that had served him for more than thirty years. Then, in front of the king, something went terribly wrong. The Mary Rose leaned to one side, water rushed in through the open holes for her guns, and she sank within minutes.

There were around 400 to 500 men on board. Fewer than forty are believed to have survived. Most of the others were trapped under the nets that covered the open decks. These nets were meant to stop enemy sailors from climbing on board, but on that day they stopped the crew from escaping.

Why did the ship sink? Historians still do not agree. Some think a sudden strong wind pushed the ship over while she was turning. Others believe she was carrying too many soldiers and heavy guns, which made her unstable. A French account claimed that French cannons had hit her, but English sources do not mention this. It is possible that several of these causes worked together.

After the disaster, people tried to raise the ship, but they failed. Over time, the Mary Rose disappeared into the mud of the Solent, the narrow sea between Portsmouth and the Isle of Wight. The mud, however, did something useful. It covered one side of the ship and protected it from the sea creatures that normally destroy wood under water. The part that remained above the mud slowly broke apart, but the buried half stayed in surprisingly good condition.

In the 1960s, a local historian and diver named Alexander McKee began to search for the wreck. He and his team worked for years in cold, dark water. In 1971, they finally found parts of the ship. Over the next decade, hundreds of volunteer divers helped to clear the mud and record thousands of objects.

On 11 October 1982, the remains of the ship were lifted from the seabed in a steel frame. The event was shown live on television, and millions of people around the world watched. There was a frightening moment when part of the lifting frame slipped, but the ship reached the surface safely.

The objects found on the ship are perhaps even more valuable than the ship itself. Divers recovered around 19,000 items, including bows and arrows, cannons, cooking pots, musical instruments, wooden plates, shoes, and small combs for removing insects from hair. They also found the skeleton of a dog, which the crew probably kept to catch rats. These everyday things show us how ordinary sailors lived, ate and dressed in Tudor England.

Keeping the old wood was a huge challenge. Wood that has been under water for centuries can fall apart if it dries too quickly. For many years, the ship was sprayed with cold water and then with a special wax-like chemical that slowly replaced the water in the wood. Finally, it was carefully dried with warm air. Since 2016, visitors to the Mary Rose Museum in Portsmouth have been able to see the ship without glass walls, close to the objects that her sailors once used. The ship that sank in front of a king has finally come home.

questions.q: Why did so many men die when the Mary Rose sank?
options: They were trapped under the nets that covered the decks.
They had all been hit by French cannons.
They could not swim in the cold water.
They refused to leave the king’s favourite ship.
questions.explain: Mürettebatın çoğu, düşman denizcilerin gemiye çıkmasını engellemek için güverteleri örten ağların altında kaldı. Doğru cevap “They were trapped under the nets that covered the decks.”

questions.q: How did the mud of the Solent help the ship?
options: It made the ship lighter, so it was easy to raise.
It protected the buried side from sea creatures that destroy wood.
It filled the ship with chemicals that kept the wood dry.
It hid the ship from French divers.
questions.explain: Çamur geminin bir tarafını örttü ve onu suyun altında ahşabı yok eden deniz canlılarından korudu. Doğru cevap “It protected the buried side from sea creatures that destroy wood.”

title: The Ship in the Field
text:
In the 1930s, a wealthy widow named Edith Pretty lived in a large house at Sutton Hoo, in Suffolk, in the east of England. From her windows she could see a group of low, grassy mounds on her land. Local people told stories about hidden gold under them, and Mrs Pretty, who was interested in history, wanted to know what was really there.

In 1938, she hired Basil Brown, a local man who had left school at twelve. He had no university degree, but he had taught himself astronomy, geology and archaeology, and he knew the soil of Suffolk better than most experts. Brown began by opening some of the smaller mounds. He found that thieves had already reached them, probably centuries earlier, but the few objects left behind suggested that the mounds were Anglo-Saxon graves, about 1,400 years old.

In May 1939, Brown started to dig into the largest mound. Soon he found a line of iron rivets, the metal pins that once held wooden boards together. He understood that he was digging into a ship. The wood itself had rotted away completely in the sandy soil, but it had left a perfect shape in the earth, like a footprint. Brown carefully removed the sand and followed the lines of rivets. Slowly, the outline of a ship about 27 metres long appeared. Someone, long ago, had pulled it up from the river and buried it on the hill.

News of the find spread, and professional archaeologists from Cambridge and London arrived. They took control of the work, and Brown was pushed into the background. In the burial room in the middle of the ship, the team found an extraordinary collection of treasure. There was a large gold belt buckle, decorated shoulder pieces made of gold and red stones, silver bowls from the eastern Mediterranean, drinking horns, weapons and coins from France. Perhaps the most famous object was an iron helmet with a face mask, which had broken into hundreds of pieces and was later carefully rebuilt.

There was one strange thing: no body was found. For a while, some people thought the ship was a memorial for someone buried elsewhere. Later chemical tests, however, suggested that a body had probably been there, but the acidic soil had destroyed it. Many historians believe the grave belonged to Rædwald, a king of East Anglia who died around 624, but there is no name written anywhere, so this remains an educated guess.

The excavation finished in the summer of 1939, only weeks before Britain entered the Second World War. A court decided that the treasure belonged to Mrs Pretty. She then made a remarkable decision: she gave the entire collection to the British Museum as a gift to the nation. During the war, the objects were hidden in a London Underground tunnel for safety.

For many years, Basil Brown's name was rarely mentioned in the official story. Today, things have changed. His work is recognised at the site and in the museum, and in 2021 a film called The Dig told the story of Edith Pretty, Basil Brown and the ship in the field. A quiet, self-taught man with a spade had found one of the greatest treasures in British history.

title: The Chemist Whose Name Was Forgotten
text:
For more than two thousand years, people in India and Southeast Asia treated a disease called leprosy with oil pressed from the seeds of the chaulmoogra tree. Leprosy is a slow bacterial infection that damages the skin and the nerves, and for most of history those who caught it were feared and sent away from their families. The oil seemed to help some patients, but using it was miserable. Taken by mouth, it had a terrible taste and made people sick. Rubbed on the skin, it did little. Injected, it was so thick and sticky that it formed painful lumps under the skin and was not properly absorbed.

In 1915 this problem reached a young chemist in Hawaii named Alice Ball. Born in Seattle in 1892, she came from a family of photographers and had earned two degrees in pharmacy and chemistry before moving to the College of Hawaii, now the University of Hawaii. There, she is usually described as the first woman and the first African American to receive a master's degree from the college, and she soon became its first female chemistry teacher. A doctor at a nearby hospital, who was treating patients with leprosy, asked her whether the oil could be changed into a form that the body could accept.

Ball spent about a year on the problem. She separated the oil into its fatty acids and then changed these chemically into compounds called esters. The result kept the healing power of the oil but was thin enough to be injected and could be absorbed by the body. Her method was simple, cheap, and could be used to produce large amounts. For the first time, patients could receive regular treatment without unbearable side effects, and some who had been forced to live in isolated settlements were later allowed to return home.

Alice Ball never saw this success. She became ill, apparently after breathing in chlorine gas during a laboratory demonstration, though the exact cause is uncertain. She went back to Seattle and died in 1916, at the age of only twenty-four. The president of the college, a chemist named Arthur Dean, continued her work and produced the medicine on a large scale. When results were published, her name was largely missing, and the treatment became widely known as the Dean method.

How should we judge this? One view is that Dean behaved unfairly, and perhaps knowingly so. Ball was a young Black woman in a field dominated by white men, and it was easy to let her contribution disappear. A doctor who had worked with her later complained in print that she had not been given credit, which suggests that people at the time knew whose idea it was. On this view, her story is one more example of talented people being written out of history because of their race or sex.

Another view is more cautious. Science is often a group effort, and Dean did spend years developing the process and making it available to hospitals. Credit in laboratories was frequently unclear in that period, and Ball had died before she could publish her results herself. According to this view, the problem was partly a system that rewarded senior people, not simply one man's dishonesty.

Both views probably contain some truth, but they lead to the same conclusion: the idea was hers. Her treatment remained the most effective option for leprosy until antibiotic drugs replaced it in the 1940s. For decades, however, she was almost entirely forgotten. Only in the 1970s and later did researchers rediscover her role. The University of Hawaii placed a plaque in her honour, and in 2000 the state's lieutenant governor declared the twenty-ninth of February Alice Ball Day, a date that comes only once every four years, much like the recognition she has received.

options: It was too expensive for most hospitals
It had no effect on leprosy at all

It was difficult to take: it tasted terrible and was too thick to inject properly

title: A Ruler for the Universe
text:
At the end of the nineteenth century, the Harvard College Observatory faced a pleasant problem: it had too much information. New telescopes fitted with cameras were photographing the night sky on thousands of glass plates, and each plate held the images of countless stars. Someone had to examine them, measure the brightness of each star, and record the results by hand. The director, Edward Pickering, hired a group of women to do this work. They were known as computers, because they computed, and they were paid far less than men doing scientific work, reportedly around twenty-five to thirty cents an hour.

One of them was Henrietta Swan Leavitt, the daughter of a minister, who had studied at what later became Radcliffe College and had developed an interest in astronomy almost by chance in her final year. She began at the observatory as a volunteer in 1895. Illness interrupted her career several times, and she gradually lost much of her hearing, but she returned again and again to the plates.

Her task was to find variable stars, stars whose brightness rises and falls over a regular period of days or weeks. Leavitt was extraordinarily good at it. By laying one plate over another taken on a different night, she could spot the tiny differences that showed a star had changed. In her career she identified well over two thousand such stars, more than anyone before her.

Many of them were in the Small Magellanic Cloud, a fuzzy patch of light visible from the southern half of the world, which we now know is a small galaxy near our own. Because all of these stars were in the same cloud, they were all roughly the same distance from Earth. Leavitt realised that this gave her a fair comparison. If one star looked brighter than another, it really was brighter, not simply closer. When she compared them, she found a striking pattern: in one particular type of variable star, the brighter the star, the longer its period. She published this relationship in 1912, in a short paper that appeared under Pickering's name, with a note saying that she had prepared it.

The importance of her discovery is hard to overstate. Measuring the distance to a star is one of the hardest problems in astronomy. A faint light in the sky might be a weak star nearby or a powerful one very far away. Leavitt's pattern solved this. Measure how long a star takes to pulse, and you know how bright it really is. Compare that with how bright it looks from Earth, and you can calculate how far away it is. These stars became what astronomers call standard candles, a kind of ruler for space.

Within a few years other astronomers were using her ruler. In the 1920s Edwin Hubble found such stars in the Andromeda nebula and showed that it was far outside our own galaxy. This settled a great debate: the universe was not one galaxy, but countless galaxies. Hubble later said that Leavitt deserved a Nobel Prize for her work.

She never received one. She died of cancer in 1921, at fifty-three. A few years later a Swedish mathematician wrote to Harvard, intending to nominate her for the prize, and learned that she had already died. The prize cannot be given after death.

Some historians argue that Leavitt was badly treated: she was underpaid, rarely allowed to choose her own research, and her most important result appeared under a man's name. Others point out that, by the standards of the time, Pickering gave her unusual opportunities and acknowledged her work in print. Perhaps the fairest judgement is that the system around her was narrow, and that her talent was so great it broke through anyway. Today a crater on the Moon carries her name, and astronomers still use her ruler.

options: Because the cloud was very close to Earth
Because they were roughly the same distance away, so differences in brightness were real
Because they could be seen without a telescope
Because they all had exactly the same period

title: The Woman Who Found a Planet Inside Our Planet
text:
Nobody has ever travelled to the centre of the Earth. The deepest hole ever drilled goes down only about twelve kilometres, a tiny scratch compared with the more than six thousand kilometres to the middle of the planet. Yet we know a surprising amount about what lies down there, and one of the most important pieces of that knowledge comes from a Danish scientist who worked with little more than a pencil, a pile of cards, and great patience. Her name was Inge Lehmann.

Lehmann was born in Copenhagen in 1888. She attended an unusual school, run by an aunt of the physicist Niels Bohr, where boys and girls were taught exactly the same subjects. She later said that this early experience made her expect to be treated as an equal, and she was often disappointed when, as an adult, she was not. She studied mathematics in Copenhagen and Cambridge, worked for some years in an insurance office, and only in her thirties moved into the young science of seismology, the study of earthquakes and the waves they send through the Earth.

Those waves are the key to the story. When a large earthquake happens, it sends out vibrations that travel through the whole planet and are recorded by instruments called seismographs all over the world. Different types of waves travel at different speeds, and they bend and bounce when they pass from one kind of material into another, much as light bends when it passes from air into water. By studying when and where waves arrive, scientists can work out what they passed through.

By the 1920s seismologists believed that the Earth had a solid outer layer, a thick rocky middle layer, and a liquid core. The liquid core was thought to create a shadow: on the far side of the planet from an earthquake, there was a zone where certain waves should not appear at all. In 1929 a strong earthquake struck New Zealand, and Lehmann studied the records from stations in Europe. Some waves were appearing inside the shadow zone, where, according to the accepted model, they had no business being.

She could have treated this as a mistake in the instruments. Instead, she kept working on it. Lehmann stored her data on cards, which she famously kept in old cardboard oatmeal boxes, and she compared records from many earthquakes. In 1936 she published a paper with one of the shortest titles in scientific history, simply P with a small mark next to it. In it, she suggested that inside the liquid core there was a second, inner core, with different properties, which reflected the waves back into the shadow zone. Later research confirmed that this inner core is solid, a ball of mostly iron roughly the size of the Moon.

Was her discovery a single moment of genius, or the result of a group effort? Some argue that the credit should be shared: other seismologists had noticed strange waves, and the solid nature of the inner core was only shown decades later by others. Yet it was Lehmann who took the unexplained data seriously and proposed a clear, testable explanation. The usual view, which seems fair, is that she deserves the main credit while standing, as all scientists do, on the work of many others.

Lehmann continued to work long after her official retirement, making further discoveries about the layers of the upper Earth. She received many honours and died in 1993 at the age of one hundred and four. In a famous remark late in life, she suggested that she had spent much of her career competing with men who were less able than she was. She did not say it angrily, but as a plain statement of fact. When we picture the hidden metal heart of our planet today, we are looking at a picture that she was the first to sketch.

options: Some waves appeared in the shadow zone where the accepted model said they should not be
The waves travelled much faster than expected
No waves at all reached the stations in Europe
The earthquake had happened deep inside the core

options: It should go equally to all seismologists of the time
Lehmann deserves the main credit, although she built on others' work

title: A Bit of Scruff on the Chart
text:
In the summer of 1967, a twenty-four-year-old research student at Cambridge University was spending her days doing something that sounds very far from the glamour of astronomy. Jocelyn Bell, as she was then called, was reading paper. A radio telescope that she had helped to build, a field of more than a thousand wooden posts connected by wires, recorded signals from the sky as lines drawn by a pen on long rolls of chart paper. Every few days the telescope produced about thirty metres of it, and her job was to examine every centimetre by eye.

Bell had grown up in Northern Ireland. At her school, girls had at first been expected to study cooking while boys did science, and her parents had to protest before she was allowed into the science class. She did badly in an important exam at the age of eleven, but a gifted physics teacher later showed her that the subject could be exciting, and she went on to study physics at university in Glasgow before coming to Cambridge.

The project she joined was designed to study quasars, distant and very bright objects whose radio signals seem to twinkle as they pass through the stream of particles coming from the Sun. But one day Bell noticed something else, a small mark taking up perhaps a centimetre of paper, which she later described as a bit of scruff. It did not look like the quasars, and it did not look like interference from cars or radios. She noticed that it came back at about the same position in the sky on different days.

To look more closely, she arranged a faster recording. What she saw was astonishing: a series of sharp pulses, separated by almost exactly one and a third seconds. Nothing natural that astronomers knew of could produce such a regular signal. For a short time the team half seriously wondered whether it came from another civilisation, and they gave the source the nickname LGM-1, for little green men. Then, just before Christmas, Bell found a second source in a different part of the sky, pulsing at a different rate. It seemed very unlikely that two groups of aliens would be signalling to Earth from opposite directions at the same time.

The explanation turned out to be almost as strange. The pulses came from neutron stars, the collapsed remains of huge stars that have exploded. A neutron star is perhaps twenty kilometres across but heavier than the Sun, and it spins very rapidly, sending out beams of radio waves like a lighthouse. These objects became known as pulsars, and they have since been used to test some of the most important ideas in physics.

In 1974 the Nobel Prize in Physics was awarded partly for this discovery. It went to Bell's supervisor, Antony Hewish, and to another Cambridge astronomer, Martin Ryle. Bell was not included. Many scientists were angry. One well-known astronomer said publicly that she should have shared the prize, and the case has been discussed ever since as an example of how young researchers, and women in particular, are overlooked.

Bell Burnell herself has taken a different view. She has argued that a student's work is the responsibility of the supervisor, who would have taken the blame if the project had failed, and that prizes for students would lower their value. Some people find this generous; others feel she was being too modest about a real injustice. Both positions have merit, but it is hard to deny that without her careful eye the scruff would have stayed on the paper.

In any case, her career did not suffer for long. She became a respected professor and president of major scientific societies. In 2018 she received a large international prize worth three million dollars, and she gave all of it away to help students from groups that are underrepresented in physics study for their degrees. It was, perhaps, her answer to the question of who deserves the credit.

title: The Scientist Who Refused to Patent
text:
In 1895, in a public hall in Calcutta, an Indian physicist named Jagadish Chandra Bose gave a demonstration that surprised his audience. Using invisible electromagnetic waves, he sent a signal across the room and through walls, and at the other end it caused a bell to ring and a small amount of gunpowder to explode. The waves he used were very short, only a few millimetres long, much shorter than those used by other researchers of the time. More than a century later, waves of this length would be used in mobile phone networks, radar and the instruments that study the early universe.

Bose was born in 1858 in what is now Bangladesh. His father, a government official, made an unusual decision: he sent his son first to a local village school, where he sat with the children of farmers and fishermen, because he believed that a person should know his own language and people before learning English. Bose later studied in Calcutta and then at Cambridge, where he trained in physics and natural science.

When he returned to India and became a professor at Presidency College in Calcutta, he discovered that Indian professors were paid much less than their British colleagues, even for the same work. Bose refused to accept a reduced salary, and for three years he took no salary at all, even though this caused his family real hardship. In the end the college gave way and paid him in full, including the money he had refused. He had no proper laboratory either, so he built most of his instruments himself, often with the help of a local metalworker.

In this difficult situation he produced remarkable work on radio waves, including detectors that were among the most sensitive of their day. Yet he did something that many people today find hard to understand: for most of his career he refused to take out patents on his inventions. He believed that scientific knowledge should be shared freely with the whole world, not owned and sold. He published his results openly, and others were free to build on them. The Italian inventor Guglielmo Marconi, who did patent his radio systems, became rich and famous, and in 1909 he shared the Nobel Prize in Physics. Some historians believe that one of the devices Marconi used was based on a design similar to Bose's, though this remains a matter of debate.

Was Bose wise or naive? Supporters of patents argue that they reward inventors, attract money for research and development, and make sure that a person who has an idea can afford to keep working on it. Without patent protection, they say, a poor inventor in a colonial country was almost certain to lose out to well-funded companies in Europe. On the other hand, Bose's approach reflected an old ideal of science as a common good. Open sharing allows knowledge to spread faster, and it prevents a few people from controlling discoveries that might benefit everyone. Many modern scientists who publish their data openly would recognise his attitude.

In the second half of his life, Bose turned to an entirely different question: do plants respond to the world in ways similar to animals? He built extremely sensitive instruments, including one called the crescograph, which could magnify the growth of a plant thousands of times. He showed that plants react to heat, cold, light and poisons with tiny electrical signals. Some of his wider claims, for example that plants have feelings, went further than his evidence, and other scientists criticised them. But his measurements helped to open a field that is still active today.

Bose founded a research institute in Calcutta in 1917, which still carries his name, and he wrote science fiction in Bengali. Whatever one thinks of his choice about patents, he showed that first-class science could be done in a country that the rulers of the time did not take seriously.

title: Socotra: An Island Apart
text:
Some places feel as if they belong to another planet, and the island of Socotra is often described this way. It lies in the Arabian Sea, about 240 kilometres east of the Horn of Africa and roughly 380 kilometres south of the Arabian Peninsula, and it belongs to Yemen. Seen from the air, it looks like a dry, rocky island with mountains in the centre and white beaches along the coast. On the ground, however, it is full of plants that seem to have been designed by someone with a strange imagination.

The most famous of them is the dragon's blood tree. Its thick branches grow upward and outward until the top of the tree looks like an umbrella turned inside out, or a giant mushroom. This shape is probably not an accident. Scientists believe it helps the tree survive in a dry climate: the dense crown provides shade for the roots and catches moisture from the mist that blows in from the sea. When the bark is cut, the tree produces a dark red resin, which gave it its name. For centuries this resin was traded as a medicine, a dye and a varnish, and some writers have suggested that it was even used on Italian violins, although that claim is difficult to prove.

The reason for Socotra's unusual plants is isolation. The island separated from the mainland millions of years ago, and since then its plants and animals have developed largely on their own. According to many estimates, more than a third of its plant species exist nowhere else on earth. Alongside the dragon's blood tree there is the desert rose, whose fat, bottle-shaped trunk stores water, and the cucumber tree, the only member of its family that grows as a tree. For this reason the island was added to the UNESCO World Heritage list in 2008, and some scientists call it the Galápagos of the Indian Ocean.

Isolation, however, also makes the island vulnerable. In 2015, two powerful cyclones hit Socotra within about a week, something that had not been recorded there before. They destroyed houses and roads and knocked down large numbers of old trees. At the same time, young dragon's blood trees struggle to grow because goats eat the seedlings. Many of the trees standing today are very old, and researchers warn that without protection there may be far fewer of them within a few generations.

How the island should develop is a difficult question. On one side are those who believe that more roads, a larger airport and more tourism would bring jobs, hospitals and schools to a population that has long been poor. Tourism, they argue, could also give local people a reason to protect the trees, since visitors come specifically to see them. On the other side are conservationists, who fear that new roads and hotels could damage the very landscape that makes the island special. Roads built in the past, they point out, have already cut through valleys and made it easier for people to remove rare plants and sand.

Both arguments contain some truth. Protection that ignores the needs of local families is unlikely to last, but development without careful limits could destroy what cannot be replaced. Some small projects try to combine the two, for example by paying local people to grow young trees in fenced gardens where goats cannot reach them. Whether such efforts will be enough remains to be seen. What is clear is that the strange trees of Socotra, which have survived for so long, now depend on the decisions people make in the next few decades.

title: Life at the Top of the World
text:
Longyearbyen, on the Norwegian islands of Svalbard, is one of the northernmost towns in the world. It lies roughly a thousand kilometres from the North Pole, and around two and a half thousand people live there. They have a university, a school, a cinema, a supermarket and several cafés. In many ways it is an ordinary small town. In other ways, it is unlike anywhere else.

Consider the light. From late October to the middle of February, the sun does not rise above the horizon at all, and during the darkest weeks even midday looks like night. In summer the opposite happens: from late April to late August the sun never sets, and people hang heavy curtains on their windows so that they can sleep. Residents celebrate the return of the sun every March with a week-long festival, and when the first light reaches the steps of the old hospital, people gather there to welcome it.

Then there are the polar bears. Several thousand of them live in the wider sea region around Svalbard, and they occasionally wander into the edges of town. For this reason, anyone who leaves the settlement is expected to carry a rifle or to travel with a guide who has one. Signs at the edge of town show a bear inside a red triangle. Yet shooting a bear is allowed only in self-defence, and every such case is investigated by the authorities.

One rule surprises almost every visitor: in a sense, you are not supposed to die in Longyearbyen. The small cemetery stopped accepting new burials around seventy years ago, partly because bodies did not decompose in the frozen ground. In 1998 scientists even took samples from the graves of young miners who had died in the flu pandemic of 1918, hoping to learn more about the virus. Today, people who are seriously ill are usually flown to the Norwegian mainland, and pregnant women are expected to travel there some weeks before giving birth.

Svalbard is also home to a building that might one day help to feed the world. The Global Seed Vault, dug into a mountain near the airport and opened in 2008, stores more than a million samples of seeds from almost every country. The idea is simple: if crops are lost because of war, disease or natural disaster, the stored seeds can be used to grow them again. Seeds have already been taken out once, when a research centre in Syria lost access to its own collection during the war there.

Yet these frozen islands are changing faster than almost any other place on earth. Average temperatures have risen several times more quickly than the global average, and in 2017 meltwater even entered the entrance tunnel of the seed vault, although the seeds themselves were not harmed. Coal mining, which built the town, is coming to an end, and tourism is growing to replace it.

This raises a difficult question. Supporters of tourism argue that it provides jobs, keeps the town alive and helps visitors understand climate change by seeing its effects with their own eyes. Critics reply that every flight and cruise ship adds to the very problem visitors come to observe, and that crowds may disturb wildlife in a fragile environment. Perhaps the answer lies in fewer, longer and more careful visits. Either way, Longyearbyen has become a kind of warning light at the top of the world, showing everyone else what may soon be coming.

Because polar bears often came into the cemetery

Because scientists needed the land for the seed vault

title: From National Shame to Capital of Culture
text:
Few towns have changed their reputation as dramatically as Matera, in the region of Basilicata in southern Italy. Its oldest districts, known as the Sassi, meaning stones, are made of houses, churches and storerooms carved into the side of a deep ravine. Some of the caves may have been used by people for nine thousand years or more, which would make Matera one of the oldest continuously inhabited places in the world. Seen at sunset, when the stone turns gold and the lights come on one by one, the town is breathtaking.

Seventy years ago, however, few people would have used that word. In the 1940s, the writer and painter Carlo Levi described the Sassi in a famous book about his time in southern Italy. He wrote of families living in dark caves without running water or electricity, often sharing the space with their animals, and of children suffering from diseases such as malaria. The book shocked readers across the country, and politicians began to call Matera a national shame.

The government's answer was radical. In the early 1950s a special law was passed, and over the following years most of the inhabitants of the Sassi, around fifteen thousand people, were moved into new apartment blocks on the higher ground above. For many, the new homes meant clean water, electricity and better health. But the move also broke up close communities, and some older residents later remembered the caves with a mixture of pain and longing. The empty Sassi fell into ruin, and for decades they were largely abandoned.

The turning point came slowly. In the 1970s and 1980s, a group of young local people began to argue that the caves were not a source of shame but a unique heritage. Restoration began, and in 1993 the Sassi were added to the UNESCO World Heritage list. Film directors discovered the town as well, because its ancient streets could easily stand in for Jerusalem, and several films about the life of Jesus were shot there. In 2019, Matera was named a European Capital of Culture, and visitors began arriving in large numbers. Today, many former cave homes have become hotels, restaurants and galleries.

Not everyone sees this success in the same way. Supporters point out that tourism saved the Sassi from collapse. Without visitors, they argue, there would have been no money to repair the buildings, and the old town would simply have crumbled. Young people who once had to leave for northern Italy or abroad can now find work at home.

Critics, however, worry that Matera is turning into a beautiful stage set rather than a living town. Rents and house prices have risen, and in parts of the Sassi there are now more beds for tourists than permanent residents. Some fear that the town is selling an attractive version of its past while forgetting the real poverty that people suffered there. There is an irony, they note, in paying a high price to sleep in a cave that people once struggled to escape.

Perhaps both views are right. Matera's story shows that heritage is not only about preserving old stones but also about deciding who those stones are for. The challenge now is to welcome visitors without pushing out the people whose families made the place what it is.

title: The Long Walk to Santiago
text:
Every morning, long before sunrise, people with backpacks and walking sticks step out of hostels across northern Spain and begin to walk west. They come from dozens of countries and are of every age. Some are religious, some are not, and many could not explain exactly why they started. All of them are following the Camino de Santiago, the Way of Saint James, a network of old routes that lead to the city of Santiago de Compostela, not far from the Atlantic coast.

According to tradition, the remains of Saint James, one of the followers of Jesus, were discovered in this corner of Spain in the ninth century. A church was built over the tomb, and soon pilgrims began to arrive from all over Europe. In the Middle Ages, the journey could take months, and it was dangerous: travellers faced robbers, disease, bad weather and rivers without bridges. Along the way, monasteries, hospitals and inns were built to look after them, and many of those buildings, as well as the villages that grew up around them, still stand today.

The most popular route, known as the French Way, begins in a small town on the French side of the Pyrenees and crosses about eight hundred kilometres of Spain. Walking it usually takes around five weeks. Pilgrims carry a kind of passport, called a credential, which they get stamped at hostels, churches and cafés along the way. Anyone who walks at least the last hundred kilometres, or cycles the last two hundred, can receive a certificate in Latin, known as the Compostela, at the pilgrims' office in Santiago. The symbol of the route is a scallop shell, which pilgrims often hang on their backpacks and which appears on signposts, walls and even pavements, pointing the way.

For centuries the Camino was a purely religious journey. By the 1980s, however, only a few thousand people walked it each year. Then the numbers began to rise sharply. The route was named the first European Cultural Route in 1987, and books and films about it attracted new kinds of walkers. In recent years, several hundred thousand people have collected their certificates annually. For many, the walk is a break from busy modern life, a time to think, or a way to deal with grief or a major change.

This success has brought problems as well as benefits. On the final hundred kilometres, especially in summer, the paths can be crowded, and some hostels are full by early afternoon. Walkers who started weeks earlier sometimes complain that the last stage feels more like a tourist trail than a pilgrimage. Local residents in some places also have to deal with rubbish, noise and rising prices.

On the other hand, the Camino has given new life to many rural villages that were slowly emptying as young people moved to the cities. Small bars, bakeries and family-run hostels depend on the walkers, and in some villages pilgrims are almost the only source of income. Supporters also point out that most walkers travel lightly, spend their money locally and leave little behind but footprints.

Which view is more convincing may depend on where you stand, and perhaps on which part of the route you walk. Many experienced pilgrims recommend a simple solution: avoid the busiest months, or choose one of the quieter routes, such as the one along the northern coast. Whatever route they take, most walkers agree on one thing. Arriving in the great square in front of the cathedral, tired, dusty and surrounded by strangers who have become friends, is a moment they never forget.

Walk at least the last hundred kilometres or cycle the last two hundred

Carry a scallop shell on their backpack

title: The Loneliest Island
text:
If you want to visit Tristan da Cunha, you will need patience. There is no airport, because the island is too steep and rocky for a runway. The only way to get there is by ship from Cape Town in South Africa, a journey of about six days across one of the roughest oceans in the world, and ships make the trip only around nine or ten times a year. Tristan lies in the middle of the South Atlantic, roughly 2,400 kilometres from St Helena, its nearest inhabited neighbour, and it is often called the most remote inhabited island on earth.

The island is essentially the top of a volcano, which rises more than two thousand metres above the sea. Its only settlement, Edinburgh of the Seven Seas, sits on a narrow strip of flat land on the north-west coast. About two hundred and fifty people live there, and they share only a handful of surnames, because most of them are descended from a small number of settlers who arrived in the nineteenth century, including a Scottish soldier, sailors whose ships had been wrecked nearby and a few women from St Helena.

Life on Tristan is organised in an unusual way. The land belongs to the whole community, and outsiders are not allowed to buy property or settle permanently. Families grow potatoes in fields outside the village and keep cattle and sheep, with strict limits on how many animals each household may own, so that the grass is shared fairly. The main source of income is fishing for a type of lobster, which is frozen and sold abroad, and the island also earns money by selling its colourful postage stamps to collectors.

In 1961, the island's isolation was tested in a dramatic way. The volcano erupted close to the village, and the entire population was taken off the island and eventually carried by ship to England. They were housed in a former army camp in the south of the country. The islanders were offered modern houses, jobs and comforts that did not exist at home, and many newspapers expected them to stay. Yet most of them disliked the cold, crowded, hurried life they found there, and the majority voted to go back. By 1963 most had returned, and they found their homes largely undamaged.

Their choice raises a question that is still interesting today: is such extreme isolation a burden or a blessing? On the one hand, it creates real difficulties. The island has a small hospital, but serious medical cases may have to wait days for a ship to South Africa, and the internet is slow and expensive. Young people who want further education must leave, and not all of them come back. The small population also means that the community depends heavily on a few key workers, such as the doctor and the teachers.

On the other hand, many islanders describe a sense of safety and belonging that is rare elsewhere. There is almost no crime, everyone knows everyone else, and neighbours help each other with harvests, repairs and emergencies. The pace of life follows the weather and the arrival of ships rather than the clock. For visitors from busy cities, this can seem almost unbelievable.

Perhaps the islanders' decision in the early 1960s is the best answer. They had seen modern life up close, with all its advantages, and they chose to return to their remote rock. Isolation, it seems, is not simply good or bad. Its value depends on what people want from their lives and on what they are willing to give up for it.

options: Because the volcano erupted close to their village
Because the British government closed the island
Because there were no more lobsters to catch
Because they wanted modern houses and jobs in England

options: It is always a burden that people should escape

title: The Journalist and the Rolling Ball
text:
For most of history, writing was a messy business. Quill pens had to be dipped in ink every few words, and even the fountain pens of the early twentieth century leaked, smudged and needed regular refilling. László Bíró, a Hungarian journalist working in Budapest in the 1930s, knew these problems well. He spent his days surrounded by paper, and he was tired of ink stains on his fingers and his documents.

According to the usual story, the solution came to him while he was visiting a printing press. He noticed that the ink used for newspapers dried almost immediately and did not smudge. Unfortunately, it was far too thick to flow through the narrow nib of a fountain pen. Bíró began to wonder whether a different kind of pen could use a thicker ink. His idea was to put a tiny metal ball at the tip. As the pen moved across the paper, the ball would turn, picking up ink from a tube behind it and laying a thin line on the page.

Bíró was not a chemist, so he asked his brother György, who was a dentist with a good knowledge of chemistry, to help him develop a suitable ink. Together, they patented their design in Britain in 1938. The timing, however, was terrible. As a Jewish journalist in Hungary, Bíró faced growing danger as anti-Jewish laws spread across Europe. Shortly afterwards, the brothers left the country and eventually settled in Argentina, where they continued to improve the pen and started a small company.

Their big break came from the sky. During the Second World War, pilots discovered that fountain pens leaked badly at high altitudes, where the air pressure is lower. The ballpoint pen did not have this problem. The British government bought the rights to produce it for its air force, and thousands of pilots and navigators began writing with Bíró's invention. In Britain, the name "biro" is still used for almost any ballpoint pen, and in Argentina, Bíró's birthday is celebrated as a national day for inventors.

So was László Bíró the inventor of the ballpoint pen? Here the story becomes more complicated. Fifty years earlier, in 1888, an American called John Loud had patented a pen with a rolling ball at its tip. Loud wanted a tool for marking rough surfaces such as leather, and his pen was too crude for writing letters. He never sold it, and his patent eventually expired. Other inventors also tried similar designs in the early twentieth century, but none of them managed to solve the problem of ink that either leaked or failed to flow.

One view, then, is that Bíró deserves less credit than he usually receives, because the basic idea already existed. The opposite view is that an idea on paper is not the same as a working product. What mattered, according to this argument, was the combination of the right ball, the right ink and the right way of feeding the ink to the tip, and that combination was largely the work of the Bíró brothers. Both views contain some truth, and historians of technology often say that most inventions are the result of many people building on each other's work.

The final twist belongs to a French businessman, Marcel Bich. In the early 1950s, he bought a licence to use the design and found a way to manufacture pens extremely cheaply, with a transparent plastic body that showed how much ink was left. His company, BIC, went on to sell billions of them. Bíró himself never became especially rich. Still, every time someone signs a form with a cheap plastic pen, they are using a solution that began with a journalist who simply wanted cleaner hands.

options: A conversation with an American inventor
Watching pilots write during the war
Reading about John Loud's patent
Noticing how quickly newspaper ink dried

options: That John Loud never existed
That turning an idea into a working product is what really matters
That Bíró became richer than any other inventor
That Marcel Bich copied his design without permission

title: A Clear View in the Snow
text:
In the winter of 1902, a woman from Alabama called Mary Anderson travelled to New York City. One cold, snowy day, she was riding a streetcar through the city when she noticed something that the other passengers probably took for granted. The driver could hardly see where he was going. Snow kept building up on the front window, and every few minutes he had to stop, open the window and lean out to clear it by hand. Each time, freezing air poured into the car, and the passengers shivered.

Anderson was not an engineer, and she had no special training in mechanics. She was, however, a practical woman who had already managed property and run her own business. When she returned home, she began sketching a simple device. It consisted of a rubber blade on a metal arm, which was attached to the outside of the window. Inside, there was a handle that the driver could turn to move the blade back and forth across the glass. The arm could also be removed when the weather was good, so it would not spoil the appearance of the vehicle.

In November 1903, she received a patent for her "window cleaning device", which protected her idea for seventeen years. She then tried to sell the rights. According to most accounts, she wrote to a manufacturing company in Canada, but the company replied that the device had no commercial value. Other companies showed little interest either. Anderson put the patent away, and it expired in 1920 without having earned her any money.

By that time, the situation on the roads had changed completely. In 1903, cars were still rare and expensive, and most people drove slowly and mainly in fine weather. Within two decades, millions of cars were on the roads, and drivers needed to see clearly in rain and snow. Windscreen wipers soon became standard equipment, and car makers used designs that looked very much like the one Anderson had drawn. It is unclear how much they were directly influenced by her patent, but her basic idea had clearly been right.

She was not the only woman with an idea in this area. In 1917, Charlotte Bridgwood, who ran a film company in New York, patented an automatic wiper driven by rollers instead of a hand lever. Like Anderson, she does not appear to have profited from her invention. It was later engineers who turned these ideas into the electrically powered wipers that now move silently across the windows of almost every car on earth.

How should we judge Anderson's story? One view is that it is a story of unfairness. A woman with a useful idea was ignored by companies run by men, and others later made money from a device very similar to hers. There is probably some truth in this, since women inventors in that period often struggled to be taken seriously. Another view is that Anderson was simply too early. In 1903, there were so few cars that even a brilliant safety device had no real market, and a company could reasonably decide that it was not worth the investment.

Perhaps both views can be true at the same time. Timing matters enormously in the history of technology, but so does who is given the chance to be heard. Mary Anderson died in 1953, by which time wipers were on every car. In 2011, she was added to the National Inventors Hall of Fame in the United States, more than a century after that snowy ride in New York.
