title: Black and White Squares
text:
Today, the small black-and-white squares of a QR code appear almost everywhere: on restaurant tables, train tickets, museum signs and product packaging. You point your phone at one, and a web page opens. Yet this technology was not designed for phones or for the general public. It was created in the early 1990s to solve a rather unglamorous problem in Japanese car factories.

At that time, Denso Wave, a company connected to the Toyota group, produced parts for cars. Workers tracked these parts using ordinary barcodes, the familiar rows of black lines found on supermarket products. Barcodes had a serious limitation: they could hold only around twenty characters of information. As factories grew more complex, workers sometimes had to scan many barcodes on a single box, which was slow and tiring. An engineer named Masahiro Hara was given the task of finding something better.

According to interviews Hara has given, part of his inspiration came from the board game Go, which he played during lunch breaks. In Go, players place black and white stones on a grid, and Hara realised that a pattern of black and white squares in two directions could hold far more information than lines in one direction. The challenge was to make such a pattern readable quickly and from any angle. His team solved this by adding three large squares to three corners of the code. These markers tell the scanner where the code is and which way it is turned. To choose their exact design, the team reportedly studied huge numbers of printed pages to find a pattern that almost never appeared in ordinary printing, so that scanners would not confuse it with anything else.

The result, released in 1994, was called the QR code, which stands for "Quick Response". It could store thousands of numbers, and it could still be read even if part of it was dirty or damaged, because the information was stored more than once. Denso Wave held a patent on the technology, but it made an unusual decision. It announced that it would not use the patent to charge other people for using QR codes. Anyone was free to create and read them.

For many years, the codes remained mostly an industrial tool, although they became popular in Japan in the early 2000s when mobile phones there began to include cameras. In much of the world, they only became truly common after smartphones learned to read them without special apps. The COVID-19 pandemic then gave them an enormous push, as restaurants replaced paper menus with codes that customers could scan without touching anything.

Was the decision to give the technology away a wise one? From a narrow business point of view, Denso Wave may have lost a great deal of money. Charging even a tiny amount for every code would have produced an enormous income. On the other hand, many experts argue that the codes became a world standard precisely because they were free. If companies had needed to pay, they might have chosen a rival system, and the QR code could have remained a small Japanese product. Denso Wave still earns money by selling scanners and related services, so its generosity was not entirely without reward.

The success has also brought new concerns. Because people cannot read a code with their own eyes, criminals sometimes place fake codes over real ones, sending users to dishonest websites. Security experts now advise people to check the address before entering any personal information. Hara himself has said in interviews that he is pleased, and a little surprised, that a tool for counting car parts has found its way into the daily lives of billions of people.

questions.q: Why did Denso Wave need something better than barcodes?
options: Barcodes could hold only a small amount of information
Barcodes could not be printed on boxes
Customers in supermarkets did not like barcodes
Barcodes could only be read by mobile phones
questions.explain: Barkodlar yalnızca yaklaşık yirmi karakter bilgi tutabiliyordu ve işçiler tek kutuda birçok barkod taramak zorunda kalıyordu; doğru cevap "Barcodes could hold only a small amount of information".

questions.q: What do many experts say about Denso Wave's decision not to charge for QR codes?
options: It made the company bankrupt
It was illegal under Japanese law
It helped the codes become a world standard
It made the codes less secure
questions.explain: Birçok uzmana göre kodlar tam da ücretsiz oldukları için dünya standardı hâline geldi; doğru cevap "It helped the codes become a world standard".

title: A Machine for the Family China
text:
Josephine Cochrane did not need to wash dishes herself. She lived in a comfortable house in Shelbyville, a small town in Illinois, and she had servants to do the housework. What she did care about was her china. According to family stories, some of the plates had been in her family for generations, and she loved to use them at the dinner parties she often gave. After these parties, the servants washed the plates by hand, and too often they came back chipped or broken.

At first, the story goes, Cochrane decided to wash the precious plates herself. She soon found the work boring and slow, and she began to wonder why nobody had built a machine to do it. Earlier inventors had in fact tried, but their machines did not work well. Cochrane's situation then changed dramatically. In 1883, her husband died, leaving her with large debts and very little money. The dishwashing machine was no longer just a hobby. It became a possible way to support herself.

Cochrane had no formal training in engineering, but she had a clear idea of what she wanted. She measured her plates, cups and saucers carefully and designed wire compartments shaped to hold each one firmly. These compartments were placed on a wheel inside a copper boiler. When a motor or a hand pump turned the wheel, hot soapy water was sprayed up from below onto the dishes. She worked with a local mechanic, George Butters, to build the machine, and in December 1886 she received a patent for it.

Her first customers were not ordinary families. Most homes at that time did not have enough hot water, and many housewives were not convinced that a machine could clean as well as human hands. Hotels and restaurants, however, washed enormous quantities of dishes every day, and they were interested. At the 1893 World's Columbian Exposition in Chicago, Cochrane's machines were used in several restaurants and won an award for their design and durability. Orders followed, and her company slowly grew. After her death in 1913, it became part of the business that later turned into KitchenAid, a brand still known for kitchen appliances.

For decades, the home dishwasher remained a luxury. It became common in American homes only after the Second World War, when houses had better plumbing and reliable electricity, and it spread to many other countries even later. Today, it is a standard feature of many kitchens.

This raises an interesting question: did machines like the dishwasher really give people more free time? Many people would say yes without hesitation. Washing dishes for a large family by hand can take an hour or more every day, and a machine clearly reduces this. Some historians, however, have argued that household technology did not reduce housework as much as expected. In their view, standards of cleanliness rose as the machines arrived, so people simply washed more things, more often. In addition, the work of loading, unloading and maintaining the machines still fell mostly on women.

Both sides make a reasonable point. A dishwasher certainly saves physical effort, and many families value it highly. Yet the hope that machines would free people from housework entirely has not quite come true. Josephine Cochrane, for her part, probably cared less about such debates. She wanted her grandmother's plates to survive the next dinner party, and in solving that small problem, she started an industry.

questions.q: Why did the dishwasher become more than a hobby for Cochrane?
options: Her servants refused to wash the dishes
A hotel offered her a lot of money
She won an award in Chicago
Her husband died and left her with debts
questions.explain: Kocası 1883'te öldü ve ona büyük borçlar bıraktı; makine böylece geçimini sağlamanın bir yolu oldu. Doğru cevap "Her husband died and left her with debts".

questions.q: What do some historians argue about household machines?
options: That they were too expensive for anyone to buy
That people cleaned more as standards rose, so housework did not fall much
That they were mostly invented by servants
That they made women's work disappear completely
questions.explain: Bazı tarihçilere göre makineler geldikçe temizlik standartları yükseldi ve insanlar daha çok şey yıkadı; doğru cevap "That people cleaned more as standards rose, so housework did not fall much".

title: Tea in a Little Bag
text:
In Turkey, tea is usually prepared in a double teapot called a çaydanlık, with loose leaves brewing slowly above boiling water. In many other countries, however, a cup of tea starts with a small paper bag dropped into a mug. This simple object is now so common that it is easy to forget that it is little more than a century old, and that its origins are surprisingly uncertain.

The most famous version of the story takes place in New York around 1908. A tea merchant named Thomas Sullivan wanted to send samples of his tea to customers. Instead of using expensive tins, he packed small amounts of leaves into little silk bags. According to the legend, some customers did not understand that they were supposed to open the bags. They simply put them into hot water, found that it worked perfectly, and then asked Sullivan for more tea in the same bags. Sullivan is said to have replaced the silk with a cheaper cloth, and the tea bag was born.

It is a charming story, but historians treat it with some caution. Earlier evidence points in a different direction. In 1901, two women from Milwaukee, Roberta Lawson and Mary Molaren, applied for an American patent for a "tea leaf holder". This was a small bag of loosely woven cloth that could be placed in a cup and removed after the tea had brewed. Their design shows that the basic idea existed several years before Sullivan's famous accident, if that accident really happened. As with many everyday objects, the tea bag probably had several parents.

Whatever its beginnings, the tea bag gradually changed. Silk and cotton were replaced by special paper made from plant fibres, which let water through easily but kept the leaves inside. Companies began to produce bags in large numbers using machines, and in the United States they became popular in the first half of the twentieth century. Britain, a nation famous for its love of tea, was much slower. Many British tea drinkers regarded bags as an American shortcut. It was only in the 1950s that a major British company began selling them, and it took several more decades for bags to dominate the market. Today, the great majority of tea in Britain is made with bags.

Not everyone sees this as progress. Tea lovers often complain that bags usually contain very small pieces of leaf, sometimes called "dust" or "fannings", rather than whole leaves. These small pieces release colour and flavour quickly, which is convenient, but critics argue that the taste is flatter and less complex than tea made from loose leaves. More recently, some people have also raised environmental concerns, since certain tea bags contain a small amount of plastic to seal them, which does not break down easily.

Supporters of the tea bag reply that these criticisms miss the point. For millions of busy people, the bag makes it possible to enjoy a decent cup of tea in an office, a hotel room or a train, with no teapot to clean afterwards. Many companies now sell bags that contain larger leaves, and others have switched to plastic-free materials. In other words, the problems are being addressed without giving up the convenience.

Perhaps the fairest conclusion is that the tea bag and the traditional teapot serve different purposes. One offers speed and simplicity; the other offers ritual and depth of flavour. A Turkish family sharing tea from a çaydanlık on a long evening and an office worker dropping a bag into a mug at nine in the morning are both, in their own way, continuing a very old habit.

questions.q: Why do historians treat the Thomas Sullivan story with caution?
options: Because Sullivan never sold tea
Because silk was too expensive in 1908
Because there is evidence of a tea bag patent from several years earlier
Because the story first appeared in a British newspaper
questions.explain: Milwaukee'li iki kadın 1901'de bir "çay yaprağı tutucu" için patent başvurusu yapmıştı; bu, fikrin Sullivan'dan önce var olduğunu gösteriyor. Doğru cevap "Because there is evidence of a tea bag patent from several years earlier".

questions.q: What is the writer's final conclusion about tea bags and teapots?
options: They serve different purposes and both have value
Tea bags should be banned for environmental reasons
Loose-leaf tea will soon disappear
Tea bags are only popular in Britain
questions.explain: Yazar, poşet çayın hız ve kolaylık, demliğin ise ritüel ve lezzet sunduğunu, ikisinin farklı amaçlara hizmet ettiğini söylüyor; doğru cevap "They serve different purposes and both have value".

title: The Animal That Breaks the Rules
text:
Few animals are less attractive than the naked mole-rat. It is about the size of a sausage, with wrinkled pink skin, almost no hair, tiny eyes and two pairs of long front teeth that stick out of its mouth even when its lips are closed. It spends almost its entire life underground in the dry regions of East Africa, in parts of Kenya, Ethiopia and Somalia. For a long time it was regarded as a mere curiosity. Today, however, it is one of the most closely studied animals in medical research, because it seems to break many of the rules that apply to other mammals.

The first surprise is its social life. Naked mole-rats live in colonies that usually contain around seventy or eighty animals, although some have been found with nearly three hundred. Only one female, the queen, produces young, and she mates with just one to three males. All the others work: some dig tunnels with their teeth, some carry food, and the largest defend the colony against snakes. This kind of organisation is common in ants and termites, but it is extremely rare among mammals.

The second surprise is how long they live. A mouse of similar size usually lives for two or three years in a laboratory. A naked mole-rat can live for more than thirty, and one animal reached about thirty-seven. Even more remarkably, its risk of dying does not seem to rise with age in the usual way. In humans, the chance of dying roughly doubles every eight years after middle age. In naked mole-rats, an analysis of thousands of records published in 2018 found that this risk stayed roughly the same throughout adult life. Old queens continue to produce young, and their bones and hearts show few of the usual signs of ageing.

They also rarely develop cancer. For decades, researchers who kept large colonies saw almost no cases, although a small number have since been reported. Several explanations have been proposed. One involves a substance found in their tissues, an unusually large form of a sugar-based molecule, which may stop cells from crowding together and forming tumours. Another suggests that their cells are especially good at repairing damage and at producing proteins without errors.

The third surprise concerns oxygen. In crowded tunnels deep underground, the air can become very poor. In a 2017 experiment, naked mole-rats survived for eighteen minutes in air with no oxygen at all, conditions that kill a mouse in under a minute. During this time, their hearts slowed dramatically and they appeared to switch to burning a different sugar, fructose, which helped their brains keep working until normal air returned.

Not everyone agrees on what all this means for us. Optimists argue that understanding the biology of the mole-rat could one day lead to new treatments for cancer, stroke and the diseases of old age. A large technology company has even funded research on the animal as part of its search for ways to extend human life. Sceptics, however, point out that the naked mole-rat lives a very unusual life: underground, at an almost constant temperature, with a slow metabolism and few enemies. Its long life may depend on this whole way of living, not on a single gene or chemical that could be put into a pill and given to humans.

Both views probably contain some truth. The mole-rat is unlikely to give us a simple cure for ageing, and the hopes of the most enthusiastic supporters may never be met. Yet by studying an animal that solves familiar problems in unfamiliar ways, scientists are learning which questions to ask about our own bodies. Sometimes the ugliest creatures turn out to be the most valuable teachers.

questions.q: What did the 2018 analysis suggest about naked mole-rats?
options: They die much younger than people once believed
Their risk of dying does not clearly increase as they grow older
Only the queen lives longer than thirty years
They become more likely to develop cancer with age
questions.explain: Binlerce kaydın incelendiği 2018 analizi, ölüm riskinin yetişkinlik boyunca aşağı yukarı aynı kaldığını gösterdi: 'Their risk of dying does not clearly increase as they grow older'.

questions.q: What is the sceptics' main argument?
options: Mole-rats are too ugly to attract research money
The 2017 oxygen experiment was badly designed
Mole-rats actually develop cancer as often as mice
Their long life may come from their whole way of living, not one transferable cause
questions.explain: Şüpheciler uzun ömrün yer altındaki sabit sıcaklık, yavaş metabolizma ve az düşman gibi bütün yaşam biçimine bağlı olabileceğini söylüyor: 'Their long life may come from their whole way of living, not one transferable cause'.

title: The Bird That Copies Everything
text:
In 1998, television viewers around the world watched an extraordinary scene. In south-eastern Australia, the naturalist David Attenborough knelt beside a brown bird with a long, elaborate tail. The bird opened its beak and produced, one after another, the calls of other forest birds, the click of a camera, a car alarm and finally the roar of a chainsaw. Almost overnight, the superb lyrebird became famous as the world's greatest mimic.

The scene was real, but it gave many viewers a slightly misleading idea. At least some of the birds in the film had lived close to people, in a wildlife park where such sounds were common. In the wild, the song of a male lyrebird is made mostly of the calls of other native birds, such as kookaburras, whipbirds and parrots, mixed with sounds of its own. Reports of wild birds copying machines do exist, but they are much rarer than the famous clip suggests.

Even without machines, the ability of the lyrebird is astonishing. During the winter breeding season, a male clears a small patch of forest floor or builds a low mound of earth, and performs on it for hours each day. He throws his tail forward over his head, so that its silvery feathers shiver like a curtain, and runs through his collection of imitations, often adding dance steps. The copies are so accurate that experienced bird-watchers can be fooled. Young males spend years learning, and much of their repertoire seems to be passed on from older lyrebirds rather than copied directly from the original species.

Why should a bird invest so much effort in sounding like others? The traditional explanation is that the song is an advertisement. A female choosing a partner cannot see a male's genes, but she can hear how varied and precise his performance is. A male that has mastered a large, perfect collection of sounds is probably healthy, experienced and intelligent, so his song acts as an honest signal of his quality.

Recent research has added a darker possibility. In a study published in 2021, Anastasia Dalziell and her colleagues recorded males during courtship. They found that when a female seemed about to leave, males often produced one very particular sound: an imitation of a whole flock of small birds raising the alarm about a predator, with several species calling at once, together with the sound of beating wings. The researchers suggested that this might trick the female into staying, because she would believe that leaving the safety of the mound was dangerous. If they are right, the lyrebird is not only showing off but also, in a sense, lying.

Not everyone accepts this second interpretation. Some argue that the alarm sequence might simply be part of the male's display, a way of demonstrating his skill with an especially difficult performance, rather than a deliberate attempt to deceive. Females may also be well aware that the sound is fake. More observations will be needed before the question is settled, and the answer may be that both explanations are partly true: a song can impress and manipulate at the same time.

Meanwhile, lyrebirds face serious problems of their own. Huge bushfires in 2019 and 2020 burned large areas of their forest habitat. Scientists have also found that lyrebirds are important engineers of the forest floor. As they search for insects and worms, they turn over enormous amounts of soil and dead leaves every year. This mixes the soil, helps new plants grow and reduces the fuel available for future fires.

The lyrebird, then, is much more than a party trick on television. It is a performer, a possible deceiver and a gardener of the forest. Its true story is less simple than the famous clip, but also far more interesting.

questions.q: According to the text, what is misleading about the famous 1998 scene?
options: The sounds were added to the film later
The bird in the film was not a real lyrebird
Wild lyrebirds mostly copy other birds, not machines
Lyrebirds can only copy sounds in captivity
questions.explain: Metin, vahşi doğadaki erkeklerin şarkısının çoğunlukla diğer yerli kuşların seslerinden oluştuğunu, makine taklidinin ise çok daha nadir olduğunu söylüyor: 'Wild lyrebirds mostly copy other birds, not machines'.

questions.q: What did the 2021 study suggest?
options: Males may imitate a flock's alarm to keep a female from leaving
Females prefer males who copy human machines
Young males learn their songs only from other species
Lyrebirds stop singing after bushfires
questions.explain: Dalziell ve ekibi, dişi ayrılmak üzereyken erkeklerin bir kuş sürüsünün alarm seslerini taklit ettiğini ve bunun dişiyi kalmaya kandırabileceğini öne sürdü: 'Males may imitate a flock's alarm to keep a female from leaving'.

title: Killer or Lifeline? The Strangler Fig
titleTr: Katil mi, can simidi mi? Boğucu incir
text:
In a tropical rainforest, the fiercest competition is not between hunters and their prey but between plants, and the prize is light. Only a small fraction of the sunlight that reaches the top of the forest makes it down to the ground. A young tree that starts life on the dark forest floor may wait decades for an old giant to fall and open a gap. The strangler fig has found a way to skip this long wait. It starts its life at the top.

The story usually begins when a bird, a bat or a monkey eats a ripe fig and later leaves a seed in its droppings, high on the branch of another tree. If the seed lands in a damp spot where dead leaves have collected, it sprouts. At first the little plant grows slowly, living on rainwater and on the nutrients in the rotting leaves around it. Then it sends long, thin roots downward, hanging in the air or creeping along the trunk of its host. When these roots finally reach the soil, sometimes after many years, everything changes. The fig suddenly has access to water and nutrients, and it starts to grow rapidly.

The roots thicken and join wherever they touch, gradually forming a net around the host's trunk. Above, the leaves of the fig spread out and compete with the host's own leaves for light. Below, its roots compete for water. Because the net prevents the trunk from growing wider, the host is slowly squeezed. Over decades, the host may die and rot away, leaving the fig standing on its own, with a hollow centre where the other tree used to be. In some forests, visitors can climb up inside these empty towers of roots.

It is easy to see why the plant got its name, and many writers have described it as a cruel murderer. Yet some botanists argue that this picture is too simple. Not every host dies; some survive alongside the fig for a very long time. A few researchers have even suggested that in storms, a tree wrapped in fig roots may sometimes be better supported than one standing alone. The fig, they say, is not acting with any intention; it is simply a plant using an unusual route to the light.

There is also a much stronger argument in favour of the fig. Fig trees are among the most important food sources in tropical forests. Each fig species depends on its own tiny species of wasp to carry its pollen, and this partnership means that different fig trees produce fruit at different times of the year. As a result, there are almost always some ripe figs somewhere in the forest, even in the seasons when other trees have nothing to offer. One survey counted well over a thousand species of birds and mammals that eat figs. For many monkeys, hornbills and fruit bats, figs are what keeps them alive during the hungry months. For this reason, scientists often describe fig trees as keystone species: remove them, and much of the forest community could collapse.

So is the strangler fig a killer or a lifeline? From the point of view of a single host tree, it can certainly be a deadly enemy. From the point of view of the forest as a whole, it is one of the most generous plants there is, feeding hundreds of species and helping to spread the seeds of many others. Perhaps the real lesson is that human words like murderer or hero fit nature badly. The strangler fig is neither good nor evil. It is simply very good at surviving, and a great many other creatures survive because of it.

questions.q: What changes when the fig's roots reach the soil?
options: The host tree immediately falls down
The fig begins to grow much faster
The fig stops producing fruit
Birds can no longer reach the seeds
questions.explain: Kökler toprağa ulaşınca incir su ve besine erişir ve hızla büyümeye başlar: 'The fig begins to grow much faster'.

questions.q: Why do ecologists call fig trees keystone species?
options: Because their roots hold the soil together during storms
Because they kill the oldest trees and make space for young ones
Because their fruit is available at almost any time and feeds many animals
Because they are the tallest trees in the rainforest
questions.explain: Farklı incir ağaçları yılın farklı zamanlarında meyve verdiği için ormanda neredeyse her zaman olgun incir bulunur ve bin türden fazla hayvanı besler: 'Because their fruit is available at almost any time and feeds many animals'.

title: The Flower That Smells of Death
text:
Every few years, a strange kind of excitement spreads through a botanical garden somewhere in the world. Staff post daily updates online, cameras stream live pictures, and long queues form outside the glasshouse doors. Thousands of people wait for hours, not to admire a beautiful scent, but to experience one of the worst smells in the plant kingdom. The cause of all this attention is the titan arum, a giant plant from the rainforests of Sumatra in Indonesia.

What looks like a single enormous flower is actually a structure made of many flowers. In the centre stands a tall, pale spike that can reach around three metres in height. Around its base is a wide, frilled sheet, green on the outside and a deep, meaty red on the inside. Hidden at the bottom, out of sight, are hundreds of tiny male and female flowers. Botanists usually describe it as the largest unbranched flower structure in the world.

The plant grows from a huge underground storage organ, which in some cases weighs more than a hundred kilograms. For most of its life it does not flower at all. Instead, it produces a single, enormous leaf that can look like a small tree. Only after storing enough energy, usually seven to ten years for the first time, does it finally bloom. Even then, the show is short: the flower is fully open for only a day or two before it collapses.

The smell has been compared to rotting meat, dead fish and very old socks. Chemists who analysed the air around a blooming plant found several of the same substances that are produced by decaying bodies. To spread the smell further, the central spike heats itself up to around the temperature of the human body, so that the warm, stinking air rises into the forest. In the wild, this attracts beetles and flies that normally lay their eggs in dead animals. They crawl down to the hidden flowers, pick up pollen and carry it to the next titan arum, receiving nothing in return.

The plant was first described for science by the Italian botanist Odoardo Beccari, who found it in Sumatra in 1878 and sent seeds to Europe. In 1889 a plant flowered for the first time outside its homeland, at Kew Gardens near London. Since then it has bloomed in many gardens around the world, and each event draws crowds.

Some critics see these crowds as little more than entertainment, a chance to take a photograph and pull a face. They point out that the titan arum is endangered in the wild, where its forests are being cut down for farmland, and that a queue in Europe or America does little to help it. Supporters of botanical gardens disagree. They argue that the excitement brings in visitors and money, and that it makes people curious about tropical forests they might otherwise ignore. Gardens also share pollen with each other so that new seeds can be produced, keeping a living reserve of the species in case wild populations disappear. However, a recent study suggested that many of the plants in gardens are closely related, which may limit the value of this reserve.

The fairest judgement may be that the spectacle is useful but not enough. A smelly flower can open people's eyes, but its long-term survival will depend on protecting the rainforest it came from. Until then, the titan arum will go on doing what it has always done: blooming rarely, smelling terrible and attracting visitors, both insect and human, from far away.

questions.q: Why does the central spike of the titan arum heat itself up?
options: To protect the flowers from cold nights
To keep beetles from eating the pollen
To make the flower open more quickly
To help the bad smell rise and spread further
questions.explain: Merkezdeki başak kendini insan vücudu sıcaklığına kadar ısıtır; böylece sıcak ve kötü kokulu hava yükselip ormana yayılır: 'To help the bad smell rise and spread further'.

questions.q: What is the writer's final view on the crowds in botanical gardens?
options: They are useful but cannot replace protection of the rainforest
They harm the plants and should be stopped
They have already saved the species from extinction
They are the only way to produce new seeds
questions.explain: Yazar gösterinin faydalı ama yeterli olmadığını, türün geleceğinin yağmur ormanının korunmasına bağlı olduğunu söylüyor: 'They are useful but cannot replace protection of the rainforest'.

title: The Loudest Snap in the Sea
text:
During the Second World War, crews listening to underwater sound in the Pacific Ocean were puzzled by a constant crackling noise, rather like fat frying in a pan. It was so loud in some places that it made it harder to hear enemy ships. The source turned out to be not a secret weapon but millions of tiny animals: snapping shrimp, also known as pistol shrimp. Each one is only a few centimetres long, yet together they are among the noisiest creatures in the ocean.

A pistol shrimp has one ordinary claw and one enormous one, which can be almost half the length of its body. The large claw works like the hammer of a gun. The shrimp opens it, locks it in place, and then releases it so that it closes with extraordinary speed. For a long time, scientists assumed that the loud snap came from the two parts of the claw hitting each other. In 2000, however, a team of researchers in the Netherlands and Germany used high-speed cameras to show that this was wrong.

What actually happens is even stranger. When the claw closes, it shoots out a jet of water so fast that the pressure behind it drops sharply, and a bubble forms in the water. A moment later, the bubble collapses violently. It is this collapse, not the claw itself, that produces the sound, which can be louder than a gunshot at close range. The collapse also produces a very brief flash of light, too weak to see with the naked eye, and the temperature inside the bubble may reach several thousand degrees for a tiny fraction of a second. The shock is strong enough to stun or kill small fish and worms, which the shrimp then drags back to its burrow.

Some pistol shrimp have formed a remarkable partnership with small fish called gobies. The shrimp, whose eyesight is poor, digs and maintains a burrow in the sand, which both animals share. The goby, which sees well, stays at the entrance and acts as a guard. When the shrimp comes out, it keeps one of its antennae in contact with the fish. If danger appears, the goby flicks its tail, and both disappear into the burrow. Each partner provides what the other lacks.

In recent years, the shrimp's noise has become the subject of a new debate. Some scientists are concerned that it may be increasing. Studies have found that snapping shrimp snap more often in warmer water, which suggests that as the oceans heat up, reefs may become noisier. This could make it more difficult for fish and other animals that rely on sound to communicate, and it could also interfere with underwater equipment used by people.

Other researchers emphasise a more positive side. A healthy reef is a noisy place, and much of its noise comes from snapping shrimp. Experiments have shown that young fish drifting in the open sea are attracted to the sound of a healthy reef and use it to find a place to settle. A silent reef, on the other hand, is often a damaged one. From this point of view, the crackle of the shrimp is not pollution but a sign of life, and scientists have begun to record it as a way of measuring the health of reefs.

Both views can be true at once. The same sound that guides young fish home may, in a hotter future, become loud enough to cause problems. What is certain is that this small animal, armed with nothing more than a claw and a bubble, has shaped the sound of the sea in ways that people are only beginning to understand.

questions.q: What did the high-speed cameras show about the snap?
options: The two parts of the claw hit each other very hard
The sound is made by the shrimp's tail
The shrimp snaps only when gobies are nearby
The sound comes from a collapsing bubble, not from the claw itself
questions.explain: Kameralar sesin pençenin iki parçasının çarpışmasından değil, oluşan baloncuğun şiddetle çökmesinden kaynaklandığını gösterdi: 'The sound comes from a collapsing bubble, not from the claw itself'.

questions.q: Why do some researchers see the shrimp's noise as a good sign?
options: Because it frightens away dangerous predators
Because young fish use the sound of a healthy reef to find a home
Because it helps submarines hide from enemy ships
Because it makes the water warmer
questions.explain: Açık denizdeki yavru balıklar sağlıklı bir resifin sesine yönelir ve yerleşecek yeri bu sesle bulur; sessiz resif çoğu zaman hasarlıdır: 'Because young fish use the sound of a healthy reef to find a home'.

title: Mending with Gold
text:
Imagine dropping a favourite bowl and watching it break into five pieces. Most of us would sweep up the pieces and throw them away, or perhaps glue them together and hope nobody notices the cracks. In Japan, however, there is a craft that does exactly the opposite. Kintsugi, which means roughly ‘golden joinery’, repairs broken pottery with lacquer mixed with powdered gold, so that the lines of damage shine instead of disappearing.

The origins of kintsugi are not fully documented, but a story often told goes back to the fifteenth century. According to this account, the shogun Ashikaga Yoshimasa sent a precious Chinese bowl back to China for repair after it cracked. It returned held together with ugly metal staples, and Japanese craftsmen, disappointed, looked for a more beautiful solution. Whether or not the story is accurate, by the seventeenth century gold repairs were valued so highly that some collectors were said to have broken pieces deliberately in order to have them mended.

The real technique is slow and demanding. It relies on urushi, a natural lacquer made from the sap of a tree that grows in East Asia. Urushi is an excellent glue once it hardens, but it does not dry in the usual sense; it cures in warm, humid conditions, and each layer can take days or weeks. The craftsperson first joins the pieces, then fills small gaps with a paste of lacquer and powdered stone, sands the surface smooth, and applies further thin layers. Only at the end is fine gold powder dusted onto the final coat. A careful repair may take a month or more, and the fresh lacquer can cause a painful skin rash, so beginners are usually advised to wear gloves.

In recent years, kintsugi has become fashionable far beyond Japan. It appears in self-help books, design magazines and motivational talks, usually as a metaphor: our wounds and failures, the argument goes, need not be hidden; they can become the most beautiful part of who we are. Supporters connect this idea to Japanese aesthetics that value imperfection and the marks left by time and use. For them, kintsugi offers a gentle alternative to a culture that encourages us to replace things the moment they break.

Not everyone is comfortable with this popularity, however. Some craftspeople and scholars point out that the philosophical meaning is partly a modern Western addition, and that historical owners may simply have wanted to keep valuable objects in use. They also worry about cheap kits sold online, which use modern glue and gold-coloured paint and promise results in an afternoon. Such kits may be fun, critics say, but calling them kintsugi turns a skilled tradition into a quick decoration and hides the patience that is its real lesson.

Both sides have a point. It is probably true that the metaphor has been stretched, and that a broken bowl does not automatically teach us about personal growth. Yet ideas often travel and change, and the popularity of kintsugi has sent many people to workshops where they discover how much time real repair demands. Perhaps the most honest conclusion lies in the craft itself: a mended bowl is neither as good as new nor simply damaged. It is something different, carrying a visible record of what happened to it, and that may be reason enough to keep it.

questions.q: Why does real kintsugi take so long?
options: Gold powder is very hard to find in Japan
The pieces must first be sent to China
Craftspeople work on it only in winter
Each layer of urushi lacquer needs days or weeks to cure
questions.explain: Urushi verniği her katta günler ya da haftalar içinde sertleşir, bu yüzden onarım bir ay veya daha fazla sürebilir; doğru cevap 'Each layer of urushi lacquer needs days or weeks to cure'.

questions.q: What is the critics' main concern about kintsugi's popularity?
options: That Japanese pottery has become too expensive
That people now break bowls on purpose
That quick kits and easy metaphors hide the skill and patience of the real craft
That gold repairs are dangerous to eat from
questions.explain: Eleştirmenler, birkaç saatte sonuç vaat eden ucuz setlerin ve kolay mecazların gerçek zanaatin gerektirdiği ustalığı ve sabrı gizlediğini düşünüyor; doğru cevap 'That quick kits and easy metaphors hide the skill and patience of the real craft'.

title: The Bank That Keeps Cheese
text:
In a quiet industrial area of northern Italy, behind heavy doors, stands a strange kind of bank vault. There are no piles of banknotes and no gold bars. Instead, tall shelves rise towards the ceiling, carrying tens of thousands of large golden wheels of cheese. Robots move along the rows, lifting each wheel, brushing it and turning it over. This is one of the warehouses where a regional bank has, for decades, accepted Parmigiano Reggiano as security for loans.

To understand why a bank would hold cheese, it helps to understand how the cheese is made. Parmigiano Reggiano can only be produced in a small area around the cities of Parma, Reggio Emilia, Modena and parts of Bologna and Mantua. Each morning, milk from local cows is heated in large copper vats, the curd is cut into tiny grains, and the mass is lifted out in a cloth and pressed into a mould. After soaking in salty water for several weeks, each wheel, weighing around forty kilos, is placed on a shelf to age. The rules require at least twelve months, and many wheels are kept for twenty-four months or longer before an expert taps them with a small hammer, listening for hidden holes or cracks.

This long wait creates a financial problem. A dairy must pay farmers and workers today for a product it cannot sell for two years. Since the 1950s, the bank, Credem, has offered a solution: producers can store wheels in its climate-controlled warehouses and borrow money against their value. The bank takes care of the cheese while it ages, and if a producer cannot repay the loan, the bank can sell the wheels. Because good cheese usually gains value as it matures, this arrangement is considered relatively safe. Reports suggest that the vaults have occasionally attracted thieves, which says something about how valuable the wheels are.

The cheese is protected not only by vaults but also by law. In the European Union, Parmigiano Reggiano has a protected designation of origin, which means that only cheese made in the official area according to the official rules may carry the name. A 2008 ruling by the European Court of Justice went further, deciding that in Europe even the word ‘Parmesan’ is closely tied to the protected name. Supporters of these rules say they defend small producers, local jobs and a recipe refined over many centuries. Without protection, they argue, factories anywhere could sell cheap imitations and slowly destroy the market for the real product.

Outside Europe, the view is often different. In the United States and several other countries, ‘parmesan’ has long been used as a general word for a hard, grating cheese, and many producers there have made it for generations. They argue that names which have entered everyday language should be free for everyone to use, and that strict rules mainly protect the profits of established regions. Trade negotiations between the European Union and other countries frequently include long arguments over such food names.

The truth probably lies somewhere in between. Protected names clearly help consumers who want to know exactly what they are buying, and they have kept a demanding traditional method economically possible. At the same time, a name used for a century in another country cannot easily be taken back. What seems certain is that few foods are as carefully guarded, both legally and physically, as these heavy golden wheels resting in the dark, slowly becoming more valuable.

questions.q: Why is cheese a useful guarantee for the bank's loans?
options: Because cheese never needs any care
Because Italian law forces producers to repay
Because the bank eats the cheese if the loan is not repaid
Because good cheese usually gains value while it ages, so it can be sold if needed

questions.q: What do producers in the United States and other countries argue about the name 'parmesan'?
options: That it is a general word that everyone should be free to use
That it should only be used for Italian cheese
That it should be replaced with a new name
That the European rules make their cheese taste better

title: The Tiny Grain Behind Injera
text:
At an Ethiopian meal, there are usually no individual plates. Instead, a large round tray arrives at the table, covered with a soft, grey-brown flatbread full of tiny holes. On top of it, the cook places spoonfuls of stews: spicy red lentils, chicken in a deep red sauce, cabbage, beans. Diners tear off pieces of extra bread with their right hand and use them to pick up the food. When the stews are finished, the bread underneath, soaked in sauce, is often considered the best part. This bread is injera, and it is made from a grain that most of the world had never heard of until recently: teff.

Teff is astonishingly small. A single grain is hardly bigger than a full stop on this page, and some sources claim that around one hundred and fifty grains weigh about as much as one grain of wheat. It has been grown in the highlands of Ethiopia and Eritrea for thousands of years, and it remains one of the most important crops in the region. Teff is well suited to local conditions: it tolerates both drought and waterlogged soil better than many other cereals, and because the seeds are so small, a handful is enough to plant a whole field.

Making injera takes patience. Teff flour is mixed with water and left to rest for two or three days, during which wild yeasts and bacteria give the batter a slightly sour taste. The batter is then poured in a circle onto a large, hot clay plate and covered. It cooks on one side only; the bubbles that rise through it create the characteristic holes, which help the bread absorb sauce. Eating together from one plate has social meaning, too. In a gesture known as gursha, a person may place a carefully wrapped mouthful directly into a friend's or guest's mouth as a sign of respect and affection.

In the early twenty-first century, teff suddenly became fashionable abroad. It contains no gluten, so people who cannot digest wheat began looking for it, and health magazines praised its iron, fibre and protein. Some commentators predicted that it would follow quinoa, the Andean grain whose global success had made it far more expensive in its countries of origin. Partly to avoid that risk, the Ethiopian government restricted exports of raw teff from around 2006, and only later began to allow limited exports under certain conditions.

The debate over this policy reveals a real dilemma. Supporters of the restrictions argued that teff is a staple for millions of Ethiopians, many of whom spend a large share of their income on food. If foreign demand pushed prices up, they said, poor families in cities might be unable to afford their daily bread. On the other side, some economists and farmers' groups claimed that the ban kept farmers' incomes low and prevented Ethiopia from benefiting from a valuable international market, while other countries began growing teff themselves and selling it abroad.

Neither position is obviously wrong. Studies of quinoa have suggested that its effect on local consumers was more complicated than early reports claimed, since many farmers also became richer. Yet a government responsible for feeding a large population can reasonably prefer caution. For now, the next time you see a bag of teff flour in a health-food shop, it may be worth remembering that, for many families, it is not a superfood but simply dinner, shared from one plate.

questions.q: Why did the Ethiopian government restrict teff exports?
options: Because teff was no longer grown in the highlands
Because other countries refused to buy it
Partly to prevent rising prices from harming poor local consumers
Because injera can only be made inside Ethiopia
questions.explain: Hükümet, quinoa örneğindeki gibi dış talebin fiyatları yükseltip yoksul aileleri zor durumda bırakması riskinden kaçınmak istedi; doğru cevap 'Partly to prevent rising prices from harming poor local consumers'.

questions.q: What creates the holes in injera?
options: Bubbles that rise through the batter while it cooks on one side
A special tool used to press the bread
Pieces of seeds that fall out
The cook's fingers
questions.explain: Hamur tek tarafı pişerken içinden yükselen kabarcıklar deliklerini oluşturur; doğru cevap 'Bubbles that rise through the batter while it cooks on one side'.

title: The Secret in the Cooking Pot
text:
Every morning in towns across Mexico and Central America, people queue at small shops for warm tortillas, wrapped in paper or cloth. The tortilla looks like the simplest food imaginable, little more than flattened corn dough cooked on a hot plate. Yet behind it lies a technique so effective that, when the rest of the world ignored it, the results were tragic. The technique is called nixtamalisation, from a word in Nahuatl, the language of the Aztecs.

The process is not complicated. Dried maize kernels are cooked and then soaked, usually overnight, in water mixed with an alkaline substance, traditionally slaked lime or wood ash. In the morning, the softened kernels are rinsed to remove their tough outer skins and ground into a moist dough known as masa. Archaeological evidence suggests that people in Mesoamerica were using some version of this method around three thousand years ago, and possibly earlier.

The benefits are remarkable. Treated maize is much easier to grind, and the dough holds together well, which makes thin tortillas possible. It also tastes and smells different, with the warm, slightly earthy flavour that many people associate with Mexican cooking. Most importantly, the alkaline bath changes the chemistry of the grain. Maize contains niacin, one of the B vitamins, but in a form that the human body cannot easily absorb. Nixtamalisation releases much of it. The lime also adds calcium to the dough, and the process may reduce the levels of certain harmful substances produced by moulds.

When European explorers brought maize back across the Atlantic in the sixteenth century, they brought the plant but not the method. Maize grew well and produced large harvests, so it spread quickly through southern Europe, especially among poor farmers in northern Italy and Spain, who often ate it as polenta or porridge almost every day. Over time, a terrible illness appeared in these regions. Sufferers developed rough, dark patches on skin exposed to the sun, followed by digestive problems and, in severe cases, confusion and death. Italians called it pellagra, meaning ‘rough skin’.

For a long time, doctors argued about the cause. Some believed that spoiled maize carried a poison; others suspected an infection. In the early twentieth century, pellagra also struck the southern United States, where many poor families lived mainly on cornmeal. The American doctor Joseph Goldberger studied the problem in prisons and orphanages and concluded that it was linked to a poor diet rather than to germs. He even took part in a famous experiment in which volunteers deliberately exposed themselves to material from patients in order to show that the disease was not contagious. Only in the 1930s did researchers confirm that a lack of niacin was the key factor.

The irony is hard to miss. In Mexico and Central America, where people had eaten maize for thousands of years, pellagra was relatively rare, partly because of nixtamalisation and partly because maize was usually eaten with beans and other foods. The knowledge needed to prevent the disease had existed all along, in the kitchens of ordinary families. Historians sometimes use this story as a warning: when a food travels without the culture that grew up around it, something important may be lost. Today, many countries add vitamins to flour, but the humble tortilla remains a reminder that traditional cooking can contain real scientific wisdom.

questions.q: Why did pellagra appear in southern Europe after maize arrived?
options: European maize contained a poison that Mexican maize did not have
People ate maize as a main food without the nixtamalisation method
Farmers ate too many beans with their maize
The sun in Italy was stronger than in Mexico
questions.explain: Avrupalılar bitkiyi getirdi ama yöntemi getirmedi; yoksul çiftçiler mısırı nikstamalizasyon olmadan neredeyse her gün yediler. Doğru cevap 'People ate maize as a main food without the nixtamalisation method'.

questions.q: What did Joseph Goldberger try to show?
options: That tortillas cause skin problems
That pellagra was carried by germs from patient to patient
That pellagra was linked to diet and was not contagious
That lime was dangerous to eat
questions.explain: Goldberger hastalığın mikropla değil, yetersiz beslenmeyle bağlantılı olduğunu ve bulaşıcı olmadığını göstermeye çalıştı; doğru cevap 'That pellagra was linked to diet and was not contagious'.

title: Paper That Lasts a Thousand Years
text:
In a cold workshop in the mountains of central Japan, a papermaker stands at a wooden tank filled with cloudy water. She lowers a bamboo screen into it, lifts it, and rocks it gently backwards and forwards, so that the fibres floating in the water settle into a thin, even layer. She repeats the movement again and again, building the sheet slowly. When she finally removes the screen, a delicate wet sheet of washi, Japanese handmade paper, lies on top of the pile.

Washi is usually made from the inner bark of the kozo plant, a kind of mulberry, although two other shrubs are also used. The bark is harvested in winter, steamed, peeled and soaked in cold river water. It is then boiled with an alkaline solution, and workers pick out every tiny piece of dark bark or dirt by hand, a slow job often done in icy water. Next, the fibres are beaten until they separate, and they are mixed with water and a sticky substance taken from the root of a plant related to the hibiscus. This substance slows the movement of the fibres in the tank, giving the papermaker time to form a sheet in which long fibres lie in many directions.

Those long, crossing fibres explain why washi is famous for its strength. Ordinary machine-made paper is usually made from short wood fibres and treated with chemicals that can make it turn yellow and brittle over time. Good washi, by contrast, can be thin enough to see through and yet hard to tear. Documents written on it centuries ago survive in Japanese temples. For this reason, conservators in major museums and libraries around the world use thin washi to repair torn books, maps and works of art. In 2014, UNESCO added three local traditions of washi making to its list of intangible cultural heritage.

In daily life, washi once had countless uses. It covered the sliding screens of traditional houses, letting in soft light while giving privacy. It was used for lanterns, umbrellas, fans and even clothing. Yet the craft has declined sharply. In the early twentieth century, tens of thousands of households in Japan made paper by hand; today, only a few hundred workshops remain, and many papermakers are elderly. Growing kozo is hard work, and some workshops now depend partly on imported bark.

How should a society respond to such a decline? One view holds that traditional crafts are a public treasure, like an old temple, and deserve financial support, training programmes for young people and special protection. Without such help, supporters argue, knowledge built up over more than a thousand years could disappear within a generation. Another view is more cautious. Crafts survive, these critics say, when people actually want their products; money from the state may keep a few workshops open, but it cannot create real demand, and it risks turning a living craft into a museum display.

In practice, the most successful workshops seem to combine both approaches. They accept public support, but they also look for new markets: lamps and wallpaper for architects, paper for artists abroad, and the highly specialised tissue that conservators need. Perhaps the future of washi depends on this balance between protection and change. A paper that has lasted a thousand years has already shown that it can adapt; the question is whether enough people will continue to stand at the cold tank and make it.

questions.q: Why do conservators around the world use washi?
options: Because it is cheaper than machine-made paper
Because it turns yellow quickly
Because UNESCO requires museums to use it
Because its long, crossing fibres make it thin but strong and long-lasting
questions.explain: Uzun ve çapraz lifleri sayesinde washi ince olduğu hâlde güçlü ve dayanıklıdır, bu yüzden restorasyonda kullanılır; doğru cevap 'Because its long, crossing fibres make it thin but strong and long-lasting'.

questions.q: What do the more cautious critics argue?
options: That washi should be made only by machines
That kozo should not be imported
That state money cannot create real demand and may turn the craft into a museum display
That young people should not learn papermaking
questions.explain: Eleştirmenlere göre devlet desteği birkaç atölyeyi açık tutabilir ama gerçek talep yaratamaz ve zanaati bir müze sergisine dönüştürebilir; doğru cevap 'That state money cannot create real demand and may turn the craft into a museum display'.

title: A Night of Noise in Paris
text:
On the evening of 29 May 1913, the fashionable audience of Paris gathered in the brand-new Théâtre des Champs-Élysées for the premiere of a ballet called The Rite of Spring. The music was by a young Russian composer, Igor Stravinsky; the dances had been created by Vaslav Nijinsky, the most celebrated male dancer of his age; and the whole production belonged to the Ballets Russes, the company run by the ambitious Sergei Diaghilev. Within minutes, the theatre was in uproar, and the night would become one of the most famous scandals in the history of the arts.

The trouble seems to have started almost at once. The piece opens with a high, strange melody played on the bassoon, an instrument usually heard much lower. Some listeners began to laugh. When the curtain went up, they saw dancers dressed in heavy folk costumes, stamping on the floor with their toes turned inwards and jumping in ways that had nothing in common with the elegant lines of classical ballet. The story, set in ancient Russia, ends with a young woman dancing herself to death as a sacrifice to the god of spring. The music matched this violence: it was full of sudden accents, clashing harmonies and rhythms that changed so often that the dancers had to count with great care.

Accounts of what happened next differ greatly. According to some witnesses, people whistled, shouted and argued, and fights broke out between supporters and opponents of the work. Nijinsky is said to have stood on a chair at the side of the stage, shouting the counts to the dancers, who could no longer hear the orchestra. Stravinsky later wrote that he left his seat in anger and watched from the side of the stage. A popular version of the story adds that vegetables were thrown, that the police were called and that dozens of people were removed from the hall.

Many historians now believe that this colourful version is exaggerated. Most of the dramatic reports were written years later, sometimes by people who wanted to make their own role in the evening seem more important. Newspapers of the time described loud protests and laughter, but they appear to mention no arrests. The performance was not stopped; it continued to the end, and the ballet was performed several more times that season without similar trouble. Some scholars also suggest that part of the noise was expected, or even encouraged. Diaghilev understood that a scandal could sell tickets, and rival groups in the audience may have arrived ready to make their feelings known.

So was it really a riot? The answer depends partly on what we mean by the word. If a riot means serious violence, the evidence is weak. If it means an audience so divided and noisy that the performers could hardly continue, then the word is not entirely unfair. What seems clear is that the evening touched a nerve. For the conservative part of Parisian society, the work seemed to attack the very idea of beauty. For younger artists, it was thrilling proof that music and dance could express raw, primitive energy instead of polite charm.

The later history of The Rite of Spring suggests that the second group understood something important. When the music was played in a Paris concert hall the following year, without dancers, it was reportedly received with enthusiasm, and Stravinsky was carried out on the shoulders of admirers. Over the following decades, the music influenced composers across the world, and its rhythmic power can still be heard in film music today. Nijinsky's original dances, by contrast, were almost forgotten and were only rebuilt, from notes, drawings and memories, in the 1980s.

Perhaps the lesson of 1913 is not that audiences are foolish when they reject something new. Their shock was a real response to something genuinely different. The lesson may rather be that the first reaction to a work of art is rarely the final one, and that history tends to remember the evening's noise long after the arguments behind it have been settled.

questions.q: Why do many historians think the popular version of the evening is exaggerated?
options: Stravinsky himself said that nothing unusual happened.
Most dramatic reports were written years later, and the performance was not stopped.
The police kept detailed records showing no one was removed.
The ballet was never performed again after that night.
questions.explain: Metne göre abartılı anlatımların çoğu yıllar sonra yazıldı, dönemin gazeteleri tutuklama anmıyor ve gösteri sonuna kadar sürdü: "Most dramatic reports were written years later, and the performance was not stopped."

questions.q: What is the writer's main conclusion?
options: The first reaction to a new work of art is rarely the final judgement.
Audiences that reject new art are usually foolish.
Diaghilev planned the whole scandal to become rich.
The music was successful only because of Nijinsky's dances.
questions.explain: Yazar son paragrafta asıl dersin, bir sanat eserine verilen ilk tepkinin nadiren son tepki olduğu olabileceğini söylüyor: "The first reaction to a new work of art is rarely the final judgement."

title: The Day the Films Began to Talk
text:
In October 1927, audiences in New York watched the actor Al Jolson, in the middle of a film called The Jazz Singer, turn towards the camera and say: "Wait a minute, wait a minute, you ain't heard nothing yet!" For many people in the cinema, it was the first time they had heard an actor's voice coming naturally from a screen, as if he were speaking to them directly. The film was mostly silent, with written titles and music, but its few minutes of synchronised speech and song were enough to make it a sensation. Within a few years, the silent film, which had developed into a sophisticated art form, had almost disappeared.

It is worth remembering that silent cinema had never been truly silent. Films were usually shown with live music, from a single piano in a small town to a full orchestra in a grand city theatre. Some cinemas employed people to produce sound effects, and in Japan skilled narrators, known as benshi, stood beside the screen explaining and performing the story. What was missing was recorded, synchronised sound: the ability to hear exactly the right words at exactly the moment the actor's lips moved.

Engineers had been trying to achieve this for decades, but the early systems were unreliable. The Jazz Singer was produced by Warner Bros., then a relatively small studio that took a risk on a technology called Vitaphone, in which the sound was recorded on large discs played alongside the film. Later systems put the sound directly onto the film itself, which made it much easier to keep pictures and voices together. Once audiences had heard voices on screen, the larger studios could not afford to stay behind, and by the early 1930s almost all films produced in Hollywood had sound.

The change created clear winners and losers. Studios and cinema owners had to spend enormous amounts of money on new equipment, and many musicians who had played in cinemas lost their jobs. Some stars of the silent era found that their voices did not suit the microphone, or that their foreign accents limited the roles they could play, and their careers declined. Actors trained in the theatre, who knew how to deliver lines, suddenly became valuable. The story is often simplified, but it is broadly true that the arrival of sound reshaped the industry from top to bottom.

Critics at the time were divided about whether this was progress. Some argued that sound would destroy what made cinema special. Silent film, they said, had developed a universal language of images, gesture and editing which could be understood anywhere in the world without translation. Early sound films, by contrast, were often static. The heavy, noisy cameras had to be placed in soundproof boxes, actors had to stay close to hidden microphones, and many films looked like recorded stage plays. Charlie Chaplin was among the doubters, and he continued to make films without spoken dialogue well into the 1930s.

Others saw sound as a natural step forward. Dialogue allowed more complex characters and stories; music could be precisely tied to the action; and entirely new forms, such as the screen musical and the fast-talking comedy, became possible. Within a few years, technical improvements freed the camera again, and directors learned to use sound creatively rather than simply recording speech.

Looking back, both sides seem to have been partly right. Something real was lost in the late 1920s: an international art of images, and a style of acting that relied on the face and body alone. Yet sound film gradually developed its own richness, and the best directors combined the visual skill of the silent period with the new possibilities of the voice. Jolson's famous line turned out to be accurate in a way he could hardly have imagined. Audiences had indeed not heard anything yet, and the arguments about what technology adds to art, and what it takes away, have continued with every new invention since.

questions.q: According to the text, what did silent cinema lack?
options: Any kind of music or sound in the cinema.
Stories that audiences could follow without help.
Actors who were famous outside their own country.
Recorded sound that matched the pictures exactly.
questions.explain: Metne göre sessiz sinema hiç tam sessiz değildi; eksik olan, oyuncunun dudakları kıpırdadığı anda doğru sözlerin duyulmasını sağlayan kayıtlı, eşzamanlı sesti: "Recorded sound that matched the pictures exactly."

questions.q: Why did some critics think sound would harm cinema?
options: They believed audiences would stop buying tickets.
Sound equipment often caught fire in early cinemas.
Silent film had a language of images that worked everywhere without translation.
Sound films were too short to tell a complete story.
questions.explain: Bazı eleştirmenlere göre sessiz film, çeviriye gerek olmadan her yerde anlaşılan evrensel bir görüntü dili geliştirmişti: "Silent film had a language of images that worked everywhere without translation."

title: Is It Art If an Artist Chooses It?
text:
In April 1917, a new art society in New York announced an exhibition with a simple and generous rule: any artist who paid a small fee could show their work, and there would be no judges and no prizes. Over a thousand artists took part. One object, however, never appeared in the exhibition. It was an ordinary porcelain urinal, bought from a shop that sold bathroom fittings, turned on its back and signed with a false name, "R. Mutt", and the date. Its title was Fountain. The society's directors argued about it and finally decided that it was not art, and it was kept out of sight. Today it is often described as one of the most influential works of the twentieth century.

The man usually credited with Fountain is Marcel Duchamp, a French artist who had moved to New York a few years earlier. Duchamp had already become famous, or rather notorious, for a painting of a figure walking down a staircase, which had shocked visitors to an exhibition in New York in 1913. By 1917, however, he had grown tired of painting that only pleased the eye. He had begun to present what he called "readymades": ordinary manufactured objects, such as a bicycle wheel or a snow shovel, which he selected, sometimes changed slightly, and presented as art.

Duchamp was himself one of the directors of the society that rejected Fountain, and he resigned in protest. Shortly afterwards, a small magazine published a photograph of the object, taken by the well-known photographer Alfred Stieglitz, together with an unsigned defence. The text argued that it did not matter whether Mr Mutt had made the object himself. What mattered was that he had chosen it and, by giving it a new title and a new point of view, had made its practical use disappear. The original object was soon lost, and the versions found in museums today are copies that Duchamp approved decades later.

Supporters of Fountain argue that it changed the central question of art. For centuries, artists had been judged largely by their skill with their hands. Duchamp suggested that the essential act of the artist might be the idea and the choice, not the making. Much of the conceptual art of the later twentieth century, in which the idea matters more than the finished object, would be hard to imagine without this step. In 2004, a survey of several hundred experts in the British art world reportedly named Fountain the most influential modern artwork.

Critics, however, remain unconvinced. If anything can become art simply because an artist chooses it and a gallery displays it, they ask, what is left of the difference between art and everything else? Some see Fountain as a clever joke which has been taken far too seriously, and they complain that it opened the door to work that requires little skill and offers little pleasure to ordinary viewers. Others point out, more gently, that Duchamp himself may have intended a provocation rather than a new rule for all future artists.

There is also a historical puzzle. In a letter to his sister written at the time, Duchamp mentioned that a female friend had sent in a urinal under a male name. Some researchers have suggested that this friend was the German-born poet and artist Elsa von Freytag-Loringhoven, and that she, not Duchamp, had the original idea. Others reply that the letter can be read in different ways and that the evidence is not strong enough to change the traditional view. The debate has not been settled.

Perhaps the most honest conclusion is that Fountain at least succeeds as a question. One does not have to like it, or to accept that it is beautiful, to recognise that it forced people to think about who decides what art is, and why. More than a century after it disappeared from that exhibition in New York, a bathroom fitting is still starting arguments, which may be exactly what its maker, whoever that was, wanted.

questions.q: What, according to supporters, was Duchamp's most important idea?
options: That choosing an object and giving it a new meaning can be the artist's main act.
That artists should be judged only by their skill with their hands.
That exhibitions should always have judges and prizes.
That bathroom objects are more beautiful than paintings.
questions.explain: Destekçilere göre Duchamp, sanatçının asıl eyleminin üretmek değil fikir ve seçim olabileceğini öne sürdü: "That choosing an object and giving it a new meaning can be the artist's main act."

questions.q: What is the "historical puzzle" mentioned in the text?
options: Nobody knows where the original object is kept today.
Duchamp may not have been the person who had the original idea.
Stieglitz may have taken the photograph of a different object.
The exhibition may never have taken place in 1917.
questions.explain: Duchamp'ın kız kardeşine yazdığı mektup nedeniyle bazı araştırmacılar fikrin aslında Elsa von Freytag-Loringhoven'a ait olabileceğini düşünüyor: "Duchamp may not have been the person who had the original idea."

title: The Wall That Was Not There
text:
On the evening of 6 May 1954, on a windy running track in Oxford, a 25-year-old medical student named Roger Bannister ran one mile, about 1,609 metres, in 3 minutes 59.4 seconds. He became the first person officially recorded running the distance in under four minutes. When the announcer began to read out the time with the words "three minutes", the rest of the sentence was lost in the roar of the crowd. Within weeks, the achievement had become a symbol: proof, it was said, that human beings can break barriers that once seemed impossible.

The four-minute mile had been a target for years. In the 1940s, two Swedish runners, Gunder Hägg and Arne Andersson, had pushed the record down to 4 minutes 1.4 seconds, and there it stopped for nearly a decade. Some commentators began to suggest that four minutes might be close to the natural limit of the human body. Popular stories, repeated many times since, claim that doctors had warned that a runner who tried it might seriously harm himself. Historians have found little evidence that experts really said this, but the idea of a wall was certainly part of how the public saw the challenge.

Bannister's approach was unusual for his time. He was not a full-time athlete; he reportedly trained for about an hour a day, often at lunchtime, around his studies at a London hospital. But he thought carefully about his preparation, using his medical knowledge to study breathing and tiredness, and he relied on interval training, in which a runner repeats short, fast runs with brief rests between them. On the day of the record, he was helped by two friends, Chris Brasher and Chris Chataway, who acted as pacemakers. They ran in front of him for most of the race, setting a steady speed, so that he could save his strength for the final lap.

What happened next is the most famous part of the story. Only 46 days later, the Australian John Landy ran even faster, and within a few years many other runners had broken four minutes. For decades, motivational speakers have used this as a lesson about the mind. Once people saw that the barrier could be broken, the argument goes, they believed they could do it too, and so they did. According to this view, the barrier had always been mainly psychological.

The explanation is attractive, but it may be too simple. Landy, for example, had already been running times very close to four minutes before Bannister's race, and many observers expected someone to break the mark soon. The Second World War had interrupted international sport, and by the early 1950s training methods, diet and tracks were all improving. Interval training was spreading. In other words, the physical conditions for a sub-four-minute mile were coming together, and the first runner to cross the line was, in part, benefiting from a general trend.

Even so, it would be a mistake to dismiss the role of belief entirely. Athletes do not train in isolation from what they think is possible. Their targets, their effort in the painful final stages of a race, and the risks they are willing to take are all shaped by expectation, and seeing a rival succeed can make an athlete push a little harder. A balanced view, then, might be that belief did not create the necessary fitness, but it may have influenced how quickly that fitness was turned into results.

Bannister himself retired from competitive running later that year and became a distinguished doctor specialising in the brain and nervous system. He tended to speak of the record modestly, and he is reported to have considered his medical work a greater achievement. Today the mile record stands below 3 minutes 44 seconds, and running under four minutes is no longer exceptional for top runners. Yet the race on that windy evening in Oxford is still remembered, not only as a sporting moment, but as a story we keep telling ourselves about the limits we imagine and the limits that are real.

questions.q: What is the popular lesson that motivational speakers take from the story?
options: That medical students make the best runners.
That pacemakers are more important than the runner.
That the barrier was mainly in people's minds.
That records should only be attempted in windy weather.
questions.explain: Motivasyon konuşmacılarına göre engel kırılabileceği görülünce insanlar kendilerinin de başarabileceğine inandı; yani engel esas olarak zihindeydi: "That the barrier was mainly in people's minds."

questions.q: Which view does the writer finally present as balanced?
options: Belief was the only reason so many runners broke four minutes.
Bannister's record had nothing to do with the runners who followed.
