title: Four Minutes and Thirty-Three Seconds
text:
On 29 August 1952, in a wooden concert hall surrounded by trees near Woodstock, in New York State, the pianist David Tudor walked onto the stage, sat down at the piano and closed the lid over the keys. He looked at a stopwatch. After a while he opened the lid, then closed it again. He did this three times, marking the three parts of the piece. For the whole performance, which lasted four minutes and thirty-three seconds, he did not play a single note. Then he stood up and bowed. Some listeners were puzzled; others were angry. The piece was 4′33″ by the American composer John Cage, and it remains one of the most debated works in the history of music.

It would be easy to describe the piece as silence, but Cage himself rejected that description. His point was that true silence does not exist. During the first performance, he later recalled, listeners could hear the wind in the trees outside during the first part, raindrops on the roof during the second, and, during the third, the audience themselves, talking and walking out. These sounds, Cage argued, were the music. The work was not an absence of sound but a frame: a fixed period of time in which the audience was invited to listen to whatever happened.

Cage's ideas grew from several sources. He had studied Zen Buddhism, which encouraged him to accept things as they are rather than to impose his own taste on them. He had also been impressed by the white paintings of his friend Robert Rauschenberg, plain surfaces that changed with the light and shadows in the room. And he had visited a special soundproof room at Harvard University, expecting to hear nothing at all. Instead, he reported hearing two sounds, one high and one low. He was told, according to his own account, that these were his nervous system and his blood moving around his body. The experience convinced him that as long as we are alive, there will be sound.

Admirers see 4′33″ as a profound work that changed how many people think about listening. Instead of directing our attention to sounds a composer has carefully chosen, it asks us to notice the everyday sounds we normally ignore as noise: traffic, a cough, the hum of a machine. Many composers, sound artists and teachers have used the piece to encourage what might be called active listening. In this view, Cage did not remove music; he widened its boundaries until they included the whole world.

Sceptics are less impressed. They argue that if a piece contains no sounds chosen by the composer, it is hard to say what the composer has actually contributed, apart from a title and an idea. Some see it as a philosophical statement or a piece of theatre rather than music. Others suspect that its fame depends on the shock of a joke, and that once the joke is understood there is little reason to experience it again. Cage, interestingly, took the piece very seriously and later described it as his most important work.

Both sides may have a point. It is fair to ask whether a work without composed sounds belongs in the same category as a symphony. Yet it is also hard to deny that 4′33″ has been unusually effective at what it sets out to do. Anyone who sits through a performance tends to become intensely aware of small sounds they would otherwise ignore, and many people remember the experience for years.

Since 1952, the piece has been performed by orchestras and rock musicians, and it has even been broadcast on national radio, where engineers reportedly had to switch off the systems that automatically detect when a station has gone quiet. Each performance is different, because each room, audience and moment is different. In that sense, Cage created a work that can never be performed the same way twice, and that is completed, every time, by the people who listen.

options: The silence of the piano and the empty stage.
The sounds that happened in the room and outside during the performance.
The movements of the pianist opening and closing the lid.
A melody that the audience was expected to imagine.

title: Tired of Choosing
text:
By the time most of us arrive at work, we have already made dozens of decisions: what to wear, what to eat for breakfast, whether to take the bus or walk, which email to answer first. Most of these choices seem trivial, and we hardly notice making them. Yet a popular idea in psychology suggests that they may have a hidden cost. According to this idea, known as decision fatigue, every choice we make uses up a little of our mental energy, and as the day goes on, the quality of our decisions declines.

The idea became famous largely because of a study published in 2011. Researchers looked at more than a thousand decisions made by judges in Israel, who were deciding whether prisoners should be released early. The results were striking. At the start of the day, and again just after the judges had taken a food break, they made favourable decisions in about 65 percent of cases. As each session went on, this figure dropped steadily, falling close to zero just before the next break. The researchers suggested that tired judges were taking the easier, safer option: leaving things as they were and keeping the prisoner where he was.

Stories like this spread quickly, and they seemed to fit our everyday experience. Who has not stood in a supermarket at the end of a long day, unable to choose between two kinds of pasta? Some well-known business leaders have said that they wear the same type of clothes every day so that they do not have to waste energy on small decisions. Magazine articles began telling readers to make their most important choices in the morning.

However, the picture has become more complicated. Other researchers looked again at the judges' study and pointed out a possible problem. The order of cases may not have been random. Prisoners without a lawyer, for example, may have been more likely to appear at the end of a session, and their cases may have been weaker for reasons that had nothing to do with tiredness. Some critics argued that the drop was simply too large to be explained by mental fatigue alone. At the same time, the wider theory behind decision fatigue, which claimed that self-control is like a muscle that gets tired with use, has run into difficulties. Several large attempts to repeat the original experiments, involving many laboratories, found much weaker effects than expected, or none at all.

Does this mean that decision fatigue is a myth? Not necessarily. Few people would deny that long, demanding days can leave us feeling drained, and that a tired mind may prefer shortcuts. Some newer research suggests that what we believe about our own energy matters too: people who think willpower is limited may tire more quickly than people who do not. In other words, the effect may be real, but smaller and more dependent on the person and the situation than the early studies suggested.

So what can we take from this debate? Perhaps the most sensible lesson is a modest one. It probably does no harm to make important decisions when we are rested and fed, or to reduce the number of small choices we face through simple routines. But we should be careful about building our lives around a single famous study. In psychology, as in other sciences, a striking result is the beginning of a conversation, not the end of it.

Prisoners with lawyers always appeared last

title: The Stranger Behind the Door
text:
Imagine you are walking across a university campus when a stranger with a map stops you and asks for directions. You start explaining the way. A few seconds later, two workers carrying a large wooden door walk rudely between you. When they have passed, you carry on talking. Would you notice if the person in front of you was now a completely different man, wearing different clothes and speaking with a different voice?

Most of us are confident that we would. Yet when the psychologists Daniel Simons and Daniel Levin carried out this experiment in 1998, roughly half of the people they stopped failed to notice the switch. While the door blocked their view, the first researcher had taken hold of it and walked away, and another, who had been carrying the door, stayed behind to continue the conversation. Many of the people who missed the change simply went on giving directions, and when they were told afterwards what had happened, they were often astonished.

This phenomenon is known as change blindness, and it has been shown in many different forms. In laboratory studies, people look at two versions of a photograph that flash one after another, with a brief blank screen in between. One version may be missing a large object, such as the engine of a plane or a building in the background. People can stare at the pair for many seconds, sometimes for a minute or more, before they spot the difference. Once they have seen it, however, it seems so obvious that they can hardly believe they missed it.

Why should our eyes, which seem to give us such a rich and detailed picture of the world, let us down so badly? The answer seems to be that we see much less than we think. At any moment, we only examine a small part of the scene in detail, the part we are paying attention to. The rest is filled in by the brain, using general knowledge and expectations. Some researchers argue that we do not need to store a complete picture of our surroundings, because the world itself acts as a kind of external memory. If we want to know what is on the table, we can simply look again. Most of the time, this strategy works perfectly well, and it saves the brain a great deal of effort.

There is an interesting debate about what change blindness really reveals. One view is that it shows how little we actually take in: we may believe we have a detailed picture, but in reality we have only a rough outline. Another view is more cautious. Perhaps we do store quite a lot of information, but we fail to compare the old scene with the new one, so the change goes unnoticed even though both versions were recorded. Some experiments support this second view, showing that people can sometimes recognise the changed item later when they are asked directly. The truth may lie somewhere in between.

Whatever the explanation, the findings have practical consequences. Drivers may fail to notice a cyclist who appears while they glance at a mirror. Witnesses to a crime may be completely sure about details that they never properly saw. Film editors have long known that audiences rarely notice when a cup or a jacket changes position between shots. Change blindness reminds us that feeling certain about what we have seen is not the same as having seen it.

options: They turned off the lights for a moment
They asked people to close their eyes
They showed people two photographs
They used a door to block the view while the people changed places

title: Why the Years Seem to Fly
text:
Ask a group of older people whether time seems to pass more quickly now than it did when they were children, and most of them will say yes. A summer holiday at the age of eight felt endless; a whole year at the age of fifty can seem to disappear in a moment. The feeling is so widespread that it is often treated as a simple fact of life. But why should the same number of days feel so different at different ages? Several explanations have been offered, and each seems to capture a part of the truth.

The oldest and simplest is a matter of proportion. For a five-year-old child, one year is a fifth of their whole life. For a fifty-year-old, it is only a fiftieth. According to this view, we judge each new period of time against all the time we have already lived, so each year inevitably feels smaller than the one before. The idea is neat and easy to remember, but many researchers find it unsatisfying. It describes the feeling without really explaining how the brain produces it.

A second explanation focuses on memory and novelty. When we are young, almost everything is new: the first day at school, the first trip to the sea, the first friendship and the first heartbreak. Our brains record these experiences in rich detail. When we later look back on that period, it is packed with memories, and so it seems long. In adulthood, many days follow the same pattern. We take the same route to work, sit at the same desk and eat similar meals. Because these routine days create few distinct memories, a whole month can shrink to almost nothing when we look back on it.

This explanation also helps to explain a strange contradiction that many people have noticed. A holiday in a new place often seems to pass very quickly while it is happening, yet afterwards it feels as if we were away for a long time. A dull week at home, by contrast, can drag on endlessly, but in memory it leaves hardly a trace. It seems that we judge time in two different ways: while we are living through it, and when we remember it later. The two judgements do not always agree.

A third, more recent idea concerns the speed at which the brain processes information. One engineer in the United States has argued that, as we age, the signals in our brain travel more slowly, and we take in fewer separate images each second. As a result, the mind registers fewer moments in the same period of real time, and time appears to speed up. This theory is interesting, but it is harder to test, and it remains a matter of discussion.

Whichever explanation is closest to the truth, the second one offers some practical hope. If routine makes time shrink, then novelty may make it grow. Learning a new skill, visiting an unfamiliar town, meeting new people or even taking a different road home can give the brain fresh material to record. None of this will add real days to our lives, but it may make the days we have feel fuller and longer when we look back on them.

Perhaps that is the real lesson. We cannot slow down the clock, but we can change what we put into the time it measures.

Children's brains process information more slowly

title: Remembering Without Remembering
text:
If you learned to ride a bicycle as a child, you can probably still do it today, even if you have not touched a bike for twenty years. You might wobble for a moment, but your body seems to remember what to do. Now try to explain exactly how you keep your balance. Which muscles do you tighten, and how do you turn the handlebars when the bike begins to lean? Most people find this surprisingly difficult. They know how to ride, but they cannot say what they know.

Psychologists use this example to show that memory is not a single thing. Some memories can be put into words. You can say what you had for dinner yesterday, or name the capital of France. These are often called declarative memories, because they can be declared, or stated. Other memories show themselves only in what we do. Riding a bike, typing without looking at the keyboard, tying shoelaces or playing a familiar tune on the piano all depend on what is known as procedural memory: knowing how, rather than knowing that.

Some of the strongest evidence for this distinction comes from people who have lost the ability to form new declarative memories. The most famous case is a man known for many years only by his initials, H.M. In 1953, when he was in his late twenties, he had an operation on his brain to treat severe epilepsy. The operation reduced his attacks, but it left him unable to form new long-term memories of facts and events. He could chat with a visitor, but if the visitor left the room for a few minutes, he would greet them as a stranger on their return.

Yet in the early 1960s, the psychologist Brenda Milner discovered something remarkable. She asked H.M. to trace the outline of a star while seeing his hand only in a mirror, a task that is awkward for anyone at first. Over three days of practice, he became steadily better at it, just like any other learner. But each day, he insisted that he had never done the task before. His hand had learned; his conscious memory had not. A similar story is told about Clive Wearing, a British musician who lost most of his memory after a serious brain infection in 1985. He could not remember events from a few minutes earlier, yet he could still read music and play the piano with skill.

Cases like these suggest that different kinds of memory depend, at least partly, on different systems in the brain. Areas deep inside the brain, along with the cerebellum at the back of the head, appear to play a major role in learning skills, while a structure called the hippocampus is essential for forming new memories of facts and events. Of course, in healthy people the systems usually work together. A beginner driver thinks consciously about every step; an experienced driver does most of it automatically, leaving attention free for the road.

The term 'muscle memory', which people often use for these skills, is therefore a little misleading. The memory is not really stored in the muscles but in the brain, in circuits that have been shaped by repetition. This has a practical side. Because procedural memories are built slowly through practice, they also change slowly. Bad habits in sport or music can be very difficult to correct, since the old pattern runs automatically before we have time to think. Teachers often say that it is easier to learn a skill correctly the first time than to unlearn a mistake. Our hands, it seems, have long memories of their own.

options: He could not improve at the task at all
He refused to take part after the first day

title: How Your Body Says 'Enough'
text:
Most people eat several times a day without thinking much about why they start or stop. We feel hungry, we eat, and at some point we feel full. Behind this simple experience, however, lies a complex conversation between the stomach, the intestines, fat tissue and the brain, carried out through nerves and chemical messengers called hormones. Understanding this conversation helps to explain some familiar puzzles, such as why we always seem to have room for dessert.

Let us begin with hunger. When the stomach has been empty for some time, cells in its walls release a hormone called ghrelin. Ghrelin travels through the blood to the brain, where it acts on a small region called the hypothalamus, which is involved in controlling many basic needs. Levels of ghrelin tend to rise before our usual mealtimes and fall after we eat. Interestingly, the rise seems to follow our habits: if you always eat lunch at one o'clock, your body learns to expect it, and hunger may arrive on schedule, even if you had a large breakfast.

Feeling full is a slower and more complicated process. As food enters the stomach, its walls stretch, and nerves send this information to the brain. As the food moves further along, other hormones are released which signal that nutrients are arriving. These signals take time to build up, which is why many experts suggest that it can take around twenty minutes for the feeling of fullness to develop properly. People who eat very quickly may therefore finish a large meal before their brain has received the message that they have had enough.

Over longer periods, another hormone plays a role. Fat tissue produces leptin, and the amount it releases depends roughly on how much fat the body has stored. Leptin tells the brain about the body's long-term energy reserves. When it was discovered in the 1990s, many people hoped it might offer a simple treatment for obesity. Unfortunately, things proved less straightforward. Many people with obesity already have high levels of leptin, but their brains seem to respond to it less strongly, a condition sometimes described as leptin resistance.

What about the room for dessert? Here the answer lies less in hormones than in variety. Researchers have shown that the pleasure we get from a particular food tends to fall as we eat more of it, while our interest in other foods stays much the same. This effect, known as sensory-specific satiety, means that after a large plate of pasta we may feel unable to eat another bite of pasta, but a sweet cake still seems attractive. From an evolutionary point of view, this may have encouraged our ancestors to eat a wide range of foods and so obtain a wider range of nutrients.

Some scientists argue that modern life has confused these ancient systems. Food is now available at almost any time, often in forms that are high in energy but low in fibre, and portions have grown larger. Others point out that eating is shaped as much by culture, emotion and social habits as by biology, and that blaming hormones alone is too simple. Both views probably contain some truth. Our bodies are equipped with sensitive signals of hunger and fullness, but whether we listen to them depends a great deal on the way we live and eat.

title: Biscuits with Ears off Kaş
text:
In the summer of 1982, a young sponge diver named Mehmet Çakır was working off Uluburun, a rocky point a few kilometres east of Kaş, on Turkey's Mediterranean coast. At a depth of around 50 metres he noticed some strange flat objects lying on the seabed, and when he returned to the surface he described them as “metal biscuits with ears”. Archaeologists from Bodrum had been asking sponge divers to report anything unusual they saw, so the description was passed on. The experts immediately recognised what the “biscuits” must be: copper ingots, the standard bars in which metal was traded in the Bronze Age, shaped a little like a stretched animal skin with four handles.

Excavations started in 1984 under the American archaeologist George Bass and were later led by the Turkish archaeologist Cemal Pulak. The work was demanding and dangerous. Because of the depth, each diver could spend only around twenty minutes on the bottom, twice a day, and the team eventually completed more than 22,000 dives over eleven seasons. Every object was drawn, photographed and mapped before it was lifted, so that the position of the cargo could later be studied as carefully as the cargo itself.

What they found turned out to be one of the richest ancient wrecks ever discovered. Tree rings in pieces of wood on board suggest that the ship sank around 1300 BC, more than three thousand years ago. It carried about ten tons of copper and roughly one ton of tin, close to the ten-to-one mixture needed to make bronze, the most important material of the age. There were also blue glass ingots, logs of African ebony, elephant and hippopotamus teeth, amber from the Baltic region, jars of resin and jewellery from several cultures. One small gold object carried the name of Nefertiti, the famous Egyptian queen. Perhaps the most surprising find was a tiny wooden writing board that folded like a book, which is among the oldest of its kind ever found.

The question that still divides experts is simple to ask but hard to answer: whose ship was it, and why was it travelling? According to one view, it was a merchant ship, probably from the coast of what is now Syria or Lebanon, sailing in a circle around the eastern Mediterranean to buy and sell goods wherever it could make a profit. Supporters of this idea point to the mixture of everyday objects from many places, such as tools, weights and pottery, which suggests a crew used to dealing with different markets.

Others argue that a cargo of this size and value was far too large for ordinary traders. In the Late Bronze Age, kings often exchanged expensive gifts, and letters found in Egypt describe rulers sending each other shipments of copper, gold and glass. From this point of view, the ship may have been carrying a royal gift from one palace to another, perhaps towards the Aegean world, with merchants travelling on board as well. A few personal belongings from Mycenaean Greece have even led some researchers to suggest that important Greek travellers were present.

Weighing these views, many specialists now accept that the line between trade and diplomacy was not very sharp at that time; a ship could carry a royal shipment and private goods at the same time. Whatever the answer, the Uluburun wreck has changed our picture of the Bronze Age, showing a connected world in which copper from Cyprus, resin from Syria and amber from northern Europe could meet in a single ship. Visitors can see the finds, and a full-size copy of the ship, in the Bodrum Museum of Underwater Archaeology, only a few hours' drive from the place where a sponge diver first saw the strange metal biscuits.

Gold jewellery from Egypt

Parts of the ship’s anchor

title: The Word on the Post
text:
In July 1587, around 115 English men, women and children arrived on Roanoke Island, off the coast of what is now North Carolina. They had been sent by Sir Walter Raleigh to build a permanent English settlement in North America, and their governor was an artist named John White, who had visited the area two years earlier. A few weeks after their arrival, White's daughter Eleanor gave birth to a girl, Virginia Dare, who is often described as the first child born to English parents in the Americas.

The colonists soon realised that they were short of food and supplies, and they persuaded White to sail back to England to collect help. He left at the end of August, expecting to return within a few months. Instead, he arrived home just as war with Spain was beginning, and almost every large ship was needed to defend England against the Spanish Armada. It took him three years to find a way back.

When White finally reached Roanoke in August 1590, around the time of his granddaughter's third birthday, he found the settlement empty. The houses had been taken down, and a strong wooden fence had been built around the site, which suggested that the colonists had left in an organised way rather than in panic. On one of the fence posts someone had carved the word CROATOAN, and the letters CRO had been cut into a nearby tree. Before leaving, White had agreed with the colonists that if they moved, they would carve the name of the place they were going to, adding a cross if they were in danger. There was no cross.

Croatoan was the name of an island about 80 kilometres to the south, today part of Hatteras Island, where a friendly Native American people of the same name lived. White wanted to go there at once, but a storm was rising, the ships had lost their anchors, and the sailors refused to stay. White sailed home and never saw his family again. The fate of the colonists has been argued about ever since, and two main explanations have developed.

The first and more hopeful view is that the colonists did exactly what the message said: they went to Croatoan and gradually became part of the local community. Supporters point out that, more than a century later, an English traveller reported that some Hatteras people had grey eyes and said that their ancestors could read books. In recent years, archaeologists working on Hatteras Island have found European objects from roughly the right period, including part of a sword and a piece of a writing slate.

The second view suggests that at least some of the colonists moved inland, towards the north-west. In 2012, researchers at the British Museum examined one of John White's own maps and found a small patch of paper covering a symbol that might mark a fort, roughly 80 kilometres inland. Excavations at that location, known as Site X, have produced English pottery, although critics say it could belong to later settlers.

Weighing the evidence, neither explanation is fully convincing on its own. Objects can be traded, carried or lost, so finding English items in a Native American village does not prove that English people lived there, and stories recorded a century later may not be reliable. It is perhaps most likely that the colonists split into smaller groups, some joining their Croatoan friends, some moving inland, and some dying from disease, hunger or conflict. Until a clear piece of evidence appears, such as a grave or a dated inscription, the single word on the fence post remains the last message from the lost colony.

questions.q: Why was the missing cross important?
options: It showed that White had forgotten the agreement.
It suggested that the colonists were not in danger when they left.
It proved that the Spanish had attacked the settlement.
It meant that the colonists had gone back to England.

options: The colonists all moved to Site X.
The colonists were all killed in a storm.
The colonists probably split into smaller groups with different fates.
The English traveller’s report proves the first view.

title: The King Under the Car Park
text:
On 22 August 1485, King Richard III of England was killed at the Battle of Bosworth, the last English king to die in battle. His enemy, Henry Tudor, became King Henry VII, and the Tudor family ruled England for more than a century. Richard's body was reportedly shown in public in the nearby town of Leicester and then buried without much ceremony in the church of the Greyfriars, a community of monks. About fifty years later, when Henry VIII closed the monasteries, the church was pulled down, and over the centuries the exact place of the grave was forgotten. One popular story even claimed that the king's bones had been thrown into a river.

For a long time, Richard was remembered mainly through the play by William Shakespeare, written about a century after his death. In it, Richard is a cruel man with a bent back who murders his way to the throne, including, it is suggested, his two young nephews, the so-called Princes in the Tower. Some historians, however, have long argued that this picture was largely Tudor propaganda, created to make the new royal family look legitimate.

One of Richard's admirers, a writer named Philippa Langley, became convinced that the grave could still be found. Using old maps and records, researchers concluded that the church had probably stood under what was now a council car park. Langley spent years raising money and persuading the University of Leicester to dig. In August 2012, on the very first day of the excavation, the team found human leg bones. Over the following days they uncovered a skeleton with a severely curved spine and several serious injuries to the skull, consistent with a violent death in battle.

The skeleton alone could not prove who it was, so scientists combined several kinds of evidence. Radiocarbon dating placed the death in the right period, and the injuries fitted accounts of the battle. Most importantly, researchers traced two living relatives through the female line of Richard's family, one of whom was a Canadian-born furniture maker named Michael Ibsen. Their mitochondrial DNA, which passes almost unchanged from mother to child, matched the DNA from the bones. In February 2013, the university announced that, beyond reasonable doubt, the skeleton was Richard III. In 2015 he was reburied in Leicester Cathedral, in a ceremony watched by thousands.

The discovery settled one question but revived another: what kind of man was he? Supporters of Richard argue that the find helps to correct the Shakespearean picture. The curved spine was caused by scoliosis, which developed in his teenage years; he was not born with it, and his condition would probably not have been obvious when he was dressed. They also point out that he introduced some fair legal reforms during his short reign, such as helping poorer people to get bail.

Critics reply that the bones say nothing about his character. A curved spine does not tell us whether he ordered the deaths of his nephews, and the fact that the boys disappeared while under his protection remains, in their view, strong evidence against him. On balance, the discovery seems to have made Richard more human without fully clearing his name. It has shown that some parts of the Tudor story were exaggerated, but the central mystery of the Princes in the Tower is still unsolved, and it may never be fully answered by science.

questions.q: How did scientists finally confirm that the skeleton was Richard III?
options: They found his name written on the grave.
They compared DNA from the bones with DNA from living relatives.
They found a crown next to the skeleton.
They used a portrait painted by Shakespeare.
questions.explain: Araştırmacılar Richard’ın ailesinin kadın soyundan iki yaşayan akraba buldu; onların mitokondriyal DNA’sı kemiklerdeki DNA ile eşleşti. Doğru cevap “They compared DNA from the bones with DNA from living relatives.”

questions.q: According to the critics, what does the discovery NOT tell us?
options: Whether Richard ordered the deaths of his nephews
How Richard died in battle
Where the Greyfriars church stood
When Richard’s spine became curved
questions.explain: Eleştirmenlere göre kemikler karakter hakkında bir şey söylemez; eğri bir omurga, Richard’ın yeğenlerinin ölümünü emredip etmediğini göstermez. Doğru cevap “Whether Richard ordered the deaths of his nephews”.

title: Going Strong for the Top
text:
On the morning of 8 June 1924, the geologist Noel Odell was climbing alone on the north side of Mount Everest when the clouds briefly cleared. High above him, on the long north-east ridge, he saw two small black figures moving steadily upwards, and he later wrote that they appeared to be “going strong for the top”. They were George Mallory, aged 37, the best-known British climber of his day, and Andrew “Sandy” Irvine, a 22-year-old engineering student who was in charge of the expedition's oxygen equipment. Then the clouds closed again, and neither man was ever seen alive.

Whether they reached the summit before they died has become one of the great puzzles of mountaineering. If they did, they were the first people to stand on the highest point on Earth, 29 years before Edmund Hillary and Tenzing Norgay reached it in 1953. Mallory had famously answered a journalist who asked why he wanted to climb Everest with the words “Because it's there”, although some historians doubt that he really said it.

For seventy-five years there was little evidence. An ice axe that probably belonged to Irvine was found in 1933, and a Chinese climber later reported seeing the body of an “English dead” high on the mountain, but he was killed in an avalanche before he could give details. Then, on 1 May 1999, an American expedition searching for the climbers found a body lying face down on a slope at about 8,150 metres. The name tag on the clothing read G. Mallory. His leg was broken, and a rope injury around his waist suggested that the two men had been tied together when he fell.

Supporters of the summit theory draw attention to several details. Mallory had carried a photograph of his wife, Ruth, which he had promised to leave on the summit, and it was not found on his body. His snow goggles were in his pocket, which could mean that he was coming down in the evening, after a long day, when goggles were no longer needed. Moreover, Odell's sighting, they argue, placed the climbers higher and later in the day than a cautious team would be if it had already turned back.

Sceptics consider these clues far too weak. The photograph could simply have been lost, and the goggles might have been removed for many reasons. The biggest obstacle is a steep wall of rock on the ridge known as the Second Step, about thirty metres high. When Chinese climbers succeeded in 1960, one of them had to stand on another's shoulders, and a ladder has been fixed there since 1975. It was not until 2007 that a modern climber, Conrad Anker, the man who had found Mallory's body, climbed it without the ladder, and even he found it extremely hard. Whether two men in wool and leather, carrying heavy early oxygen sets, could have done the same is open to serious doubt.

A new piece of the puzzle appeared in 2024, when a film team on the Central Rongbuk Glacier found the remains of a boot with a sock that was reported to carry the name A. C. Irvine. The find suggests that Irvine's body fell a long way down the mountain, and it has renewed hopes that the climbers' small camera might one day be found. Experts believe that, if the film inside has survived the cold, it could still be developed.

On balance, most mountaineering historians think that Mallory and Irvine probably did not reach the summit, mainly because of the difficulty of the Second Step. Yet the possibility cannot be ruled out, and that uncertainty is part of the story's lasting power. Without a photograph from the top, the question will remain open, and two small figures will keep climbing through the clouds in our imagination.

questions.q: Why do some people think the missing photograph of Ruth is important?
options: It was found next to Irvine’s boot in 2024.
It showed the route that Mallory planned to take.
Mallory had promised to leave it on the summit.
Ruth had asked Odell to carry it to the top.
questions.explain: Mallory karısı Ruth’un fotoğrafını zirveye bırakacağına söz vermişti ve fotoğraf cesedinin üzerinde bulunmadı; zirve kuramını savunanlar bunu önemli bir ipucu sayıyor. Doğru cevap “Mallory had promised to leave it on the summit.”

questions.q: What is the main reason most historians doubt that the two men reached the summit?
options: Odell never saw them on the ridge.
Their oxygen equipment did not work at all.
The Second Step would have been extremely difficult for them to climb.
Mallory’s body was found too close to the base camp.
questions.explain: Tarihçilerin çoğu, özellikle İkinci Basamak’ın o dönemin donanımıyla tırmanılmasının çok zor olacağı için zirveye ulaşmadıklarını düşünüyor. Doğru cevap “The Second Step would have been extremely difficult for them to climb.”

title: The Last Flight of Amelia Earhart
text:
By 1937, Amelia Earhart was one of the most famous people in the United States. Five years earlier she had become the first woman to fly alone across the Atlantic Ocean, and she used her fame to encourage women to enter fields that were then dominated by men. Now, at the age of 39, she wanted to become the first woman to fly around the world close to the equator, a journey of around 47,000 kilometres. Her navigator was Fred Noonan, an experienced man who had helped to plan airline routes across the Pacific.

By the end of June, after stops in South America, Africa and Asia, they had reached Lae, in New Guinea, with about 35,000 kilometres behind them. The most difficult part of the trip was still ahead: a flight of about 4,000 kilometres across the Pacific to Howland Island, a flat piece of land only around two kilometres long. A ship of the US Coast Guard, the Itasca, was waiting near the island to help guide them by radio.

They took off on 2 July 1937. Early the next morning, local time, the crew of the Itasca heard Earhart's voice, which sounded increasingly worried. In one message she said that they must be on top of the ship but could not see it, and that their fuel was running low. Unfortunately, the radio equipment on the plane and on the ship did not work well together, and neither side could find the direction of the other. Her last confirmed message gave a line of position and said that they were flying north and south along it. Then there was silence. The largest sea search in American history up to that time found nothing, and in 1939 Earhart was officially declared dead.

The most widely accepted explanation, supported by many aviation experts, is known as the “crash and sink” theory. According to this view, the plane ran out of fuel somewhere close to Howland Island and went down in very deep water, where it still lies. Supporters point out that the strength of Earhart's last radio signals suggested she was near the island, and that a small navigation error, combined with cloud and the glare of the morning sun, could easily have caused them to miss such a tiny target. Several expensive deep-sea searches have tried to find the wreck, so far without success.

A second theory, promoted especially by a research group called TIGHAR, argues that Earhart and Noonan followed their line of position towards the south-east and landed on the reef of Gardner Island, now called Nikumaroro, roughly 650 kilometres away. Supporters point to more than a hundred radio messages that were reported in the days after the disappearance, some of which seemed to come from a plane on land. They also mention a set of human bones found on the island in 1940. The doctor who examined them at the time decided that they belonged to a man, but the bones were later lost, and in 2018 a researcher re-examined the old measurements and concluded that they matched Earhart's height and build more closely than those of most people.

Both theories have weaknesses. The deep-sea theory explains the evidence in a simple way, but without the wreck it cannot be proved. The island theory explains the later radio messages, but the bones no longer exist, and many of the objects found on Nikumaroro could have belonged to other people. On balance, the “crash and sink” explanation still seems more likely to most experts. Yet as long as the plane remains undiscovered, Earhart's last flight will continue to attract searchers, and her courage will continue to inspire people who have never seen her fly.

questions.q: What problem made it hard for the Itasca to guide Earhart to Howland Island?
options: The ship had already left the island.
Earhart refused to answer the ship’s messages.
The radio equipment on the plane and the ship did not work well together.
Noonan had forgotten to bring a map of the Pacific.
questions.explain: Uçaktaki ve gemideki telsiz donanımı birbiriyle iyi çalışmadı; iki taraf da diğerinin yönünü bulamadı. Doğru cevap “The radio equipment on the plane and the ship did not work well together.”

questions.q: Which statement best describes the writer’s view of the two theories?
options: The island theory has been proved by the bones found in 1940.
Both theories are equally impossible.
The plane was found near Howland Island in 2018.
The crash and sink theory seems more likely, but neither has been proved.
